Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \cos t\;e^{-x t^{2}}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x(t^{2} - 4t + 4)}\,dt \) by completing the square.
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-1}^{1} e^{x(1 - t^{2})}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{1 + t^{2}}\,e^{-x t^{2}}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{x(2t - t^{2})}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{0}^{\pi} (1 + \cos t)\,e^{x\sin t}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x\cosh t}\,dt \). Note that the dominant contribution comes from the minimum of \( \cosh t \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{x(t^{2} - \frac{1}{4}t^{4})}\,dt \). (Hint: there are two symmetric maxima.)
Find the two-term asymptotic expansion as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (1 + t^{2})\,e^{-x t^{2}}\,dt \), and verify it against the exact value.
Find the two-term asymptotic expansion as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{x\cos t}\,dt = 2\pi I_{0}(x) \), and identify the source of the correction term.
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} t^{2}\,e^{-x t^{2}}\,dt \), and explain why the decay is faster than \( x^{-1/2} \).
Find the two-term asymptotic expansion as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{t}\,e^{-x t^{2}/2}\,dt \), and verify it against the exact closed form.

By writing \( n! = \Gamma(n+1) = \int_{0}^{\infty} t^{n} e^{-t}\,dt \) and substituting \( t = n s \), use Laplace's method to derive Stirling's formula \( n! \sim \sqrt{2\pi n}\,\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^{n} \) as \( n \to \infty \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x(t - \ln t)}}{\sqrt{t}}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x(t + \frac{1}{t})}\,dt \), an integral related to the modified Bessel function \( K_{1} \).

The integral \( I(x) = \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin t\;e^{x\sin t}\,dt \) has an interior maximum of its phase. Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \), and comment on the role of the amplitude.

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{x(\cos t - 1)}\,dt \) (taking the integral over one full period to be representative of the local Gaussian).

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of the ratio \( R(x) = \dfrac{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} t^{2} e^{x\cos t - x}\,dt}{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{x\cos t - x}\,dt} \) over a single period centred at \( t = 0 \). (This is the variance of the von Mises distribution at large concentration.)
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x t^{2}}\cosh(\alpha t)\,dt \) for a fixed constant \( \alpha \), and compare with the exact value.
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( I(x) = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} e^{-x\sin^{2} t}\,dt \), where the phase \( \phi(t) = -\sin^{2} t \) has an interior maximum.

am4b.questionText: Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-x t^2}\,\mathrm{d}t \), and state explicitly the factor of \( \tfrac{1}{2} \) relative to the full Gaussian integral over \( (-\infty, \infty) \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of the linear-endpoint integral \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{1} e^{-x t}\,\mathrm{d}t \).

Using the substitution \( u = \sqrt{x}\,t \), or otherwise, evaluate \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} e^{-x t^2}\,\mathrm{d}t \) exactly in terms of \( \Gamma\!\left(\tfrac12\right) \), and hence in terms of \( \pi \).
The exponent of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{1} e^{x t}\,\mathrm{d}t \) is maximised at the upper endpoint \( t=1 \). Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \).

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\infty} t\, e^{-x t^2}\,\mathrm{d}t \). Comment on why the power of \( x \) differs from the half-Gaussian \( x^{-1/2} \).

An endpoint maximum at \( t=a \) with \( \phi'(a)=0 \) and \( \phi''(a)<0 \) gives the half-Gaussian coefficient. Write down the leading-order Laplace estimate of \( \displaystyle \int_a^{b} e^{x \phi(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t \) for such a case, and apply it to \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-x \sin^2 t}\,\mathrm{d}t \).
Find the leading-order asymptotic behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{x \cos t}\,\mathrm{d}t \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-x \sin t}\,\mathrm{d}t \).
Find the first two terms in the asymptotic expansion as \( x \to \infty \) of the linear-endpoint integral \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{1} e^{-x (t + t^2)}\,\mathrm{d}t \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{1} e^{-x t^2}(1 + t)\,\mathrm{d}t \), and identify which part of the prefactor survives at leading order.

Use Laplace's method to find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{2} e^{x(2t - t^2)}\,\mathrm{d}t \). State carefully whether the maximum is interior or at an endpoint.
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{1} e^{-x t}\,(1+t)\,\mathrm{d}t \).

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{1} \frac{e^{x t}}{\sqrt{1 - t}}\,\mathrm{d}t \), where the exponent is maximised at the upper endpoint \( t=1 \) at which the prefactor has an integrable singularity.

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-x t}\,\sqrt{t}\,\mathrm{d}t \), and state the general rule for a prefactor \( t^{\mu} \) at a linear endpoint.
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{1} e^{-x t^2}\,\cos t\,\mathrm{d}t \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_1^{\infty} e^{-x t}\,\mathrm{d}t \), an endpoint maximum at the finite lower limit \( t=1 \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{1} e^{x(t^2 - 1)}\,\mathrm{d}t \), identifying the dominant endpoint.

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{1} e^{-x t^2}\,\mathrm{d}t \), and explain why the finite upper limit does not change the answer at any algebraic order.
Find the first two terms in the asymptotic expansion as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{x \cos t}\,\mathrm{d}t \).

Find the first two terms (in powers of \( x^{-1/2} \) where appropriate) in the asymptotic expansion as \( x \to \infty \) of the half-Gaussian endpoint integral \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-x (t^2 + t^3)}\,\mathrm{d}t \).

By substituting \( u = \sqrt{t} \), find the first two terms in the asymptotic expansion as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\pi^2/4} e^{x \cos \sqrt{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t \). (Cf. Example Sheet Q13.)

Consider \( \displaystyle I_1(x) = \int_0^{1} e^{-x t (1-t)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t \) as \( x \to \infty \) (cf. Example Sheet Q11). Show the exponent is minimised at the endpoint \( t=0 \) and at the interior point \( t=1 \), determine which dominates, and find the leading-order behaviour.

Derive the general half-Gaussian endpoint formula: if \( \phi \) has its maximum on \( [a,b] \) at the lower endpoint \( t=a \) with \( \phi'(a)=0 \) and \( \phi''(a)<0 \), show that \( \displaystyle \int_a^{b} e^{x \phi(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t \sim e^{x \phi(a)}\,\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{x\,|\phi''(a)|}} \), making the origin of the factor \( \tfrac12 \) explicit.

Derive the general linear (sub-Gaussian) endpoint formula: if \( \phi \) is maximised on \( [a,b] \) at the lower endpoint \( t=a \) with \( \phi'(a) < 0 \), show that \( \displaystyle \int_a^{b} e^{x \phi(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t \sim \frac{e^{x \phi(a)}}{x\,|\phi'(a)|} \), and explain why no factor of \( \tfrac12 \) appears.

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-x t^3 \cos t}\,\mathrm{d}t \), expressing your answer in terms of a Gamma function. (Cf. Example Sheet Q12.)

Find the first two terms in the asymptotic expansion as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x t}}{1 + t}\,\mathrm{d}t \), and relate the result to the exponential integral.

A maximum sits at an endpoint with a vanishing prefactor and zero slope. Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\infty} t^2\, e^{-x t^2}\,\mathrm{d}t \), and state the general scaling for a prefactor \( t^{\mu} \) at a half-Gaussian endpoint.

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_{-1}^{1} e^{-x t^2}\,\mathrm{d}t \), and contrast it with the half-Gaussian endpoint integral \( \int_0^{1} e^{-x t^2}\,\mathrm{d}t \). Explain the factor of \( 2 \).

The Gamma function for large argument can be probed at an endpoint. Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{1} t^{x}\,\mathrm{d}t \) by writing \( t^{x} = e^{x \ln t} \), and confirm against the exact value.

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{1} e^{x\,t(1-t)}\,\mathrm{d}t \). Identify whether the maximum is interior or at an endpoint, and state explicitly whether a \( \tfrac12 \) factor is present.

am4c.questionText: Write the Gamma function as the Laplace-type integral that underlies Stirling's formula: express \( \Gamma(x+1) \) as an integral over \( [0,\infty) \), and rescale \( t = x s \) to display the large parameter \( x \) in the exponent.
The phase in the Stirling integral is \( \phi(s)=\ln s - s \). Find the location of its maximum on \( (0,\infty) \) and the value of \( \phi''(s) \) there.
State the leading-order Stirling formula for \( \Gamma(x+1) \) as \( x\to\infty \), and use it to write down the corresponding leading-order estimate of \( n! \) for large integer \( n \).
Using the half-integer values \( \Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt{\pi} \) and the recurrence \( \Gamma(z+1)=z\,\Gamma(z) \), evaluate \( \Gamma(5/2) \) in closed form.
Use the reflection formula \( \Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\dfrac{\pi}{\sin\pi z} \) to evaluate \( \Gamma(1/4)\,\Gamma(3/4) \) in closed form.
State the Stirling series for \( \ln\Gamma(z) \) as \( z\to\infty \), keeping terms up to and including the \( 1/z \) correction.

Starting from \( \Gamma(x+1)=x^{x+1}\int_0^\infty e^{x(\ln s - s)}\,ds \), apply Laplace's method about the maximum to derive the leading-order Stirling formula \( \Gamma(x+1)\sim\sqrt{2\pi x}\,(x/e)^x \) as \( x\to\infty \).

The Stirling expansion is \( \Gamma(x+1)\sim\sqrt{2\pi x}\,(x/e)^x\left(1+\dfrac{c_1}{x}+\dfrac{c_2}{x^2}+\cdots\right) \). Given the \( \ln\Gamma \) series \( \ln\Gamma(x+1)=(x+\tfrac12)\ln x - x + \tfrac12\ln(2\pi)+\dfrac{1}{12x}+O(x^{-3}) \), determine \( c_1 \) and \( c_2 \).
Use Stirling's formula to find the leading-order asymptotics of the central binomial coefficient \( \dbinom{2n}{n} \) as \( n\to\infty \).
Find the leading-order behaviour of the ratio \( \dfrac{\Gamma(x+a)}{\Gamma(x+b)} \) as \( x\to\infty \), with \( a,b \) fixed.
The Beta function is \( B(x,b)=\dfrac{\Gamma(x)\,\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(x+b)} \). Using the Gamma-ratio asymptotic, find the leading behaviour of \( B(x,b) \) as \( x\to\infty \) with \( b \) fixed.
By recognising it as a Beta integral, find the leading-order asymptotics of \( I(x)=\int_0^1 t^{x-1}(1-t)^2\,dt \) as \( x\to\infty \).
Following Example Sheet 2, derive the leading-order behaviour of \( J(x)=\int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-x\sin^2 t}\,dt \) as \( x\to\infty \) by Laplace's method about the endpoint maximum at \( t=0 \).
The modified Bessel function is \( I_0(x)=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \). Use Laplace's method to find its leading-order asymptotics as \( x\to\infty \).
Use Stirling's formula to estimate \( \ln(100!) \) to the leading two terms, and state the relative error you would expect from omitting the \( 1/(12n) \) correction.
Express the double factorial \( (2n)!! = 2\cdot4\cdots(2n) \) in closed form and hence find its leading-order asymptotics as \( n\to\infty \) via Stirling's formula.
Show that \( \Gamma\!\left(n+\tfrac12\right) = \dfrac{(2n)!}{4^{n}\,n!}\sqrt{\pi} \) for a non-negative integer \( n \), and evaluate it at \( n=3 \).

By substituting \( t=x s \) in \( \Gamma(x+1)=\int_0^\infty t^x e^{-t}\,dt \) and treating the result by Laplace's method, find the leading-order asymptotics of \( \Gamma(x+1) \), and state how the answer changes if instead you analyse \( \Gamma(2x+1) \) the same way.

Obtain the first correction to Stirling's formula, i.e. show that \( \Gamma(x+1)\sim\sqrt{2\pi x}\,(x/e)^x\left(1+\dfrac{1}{12x}+\cdots\right) \) as \( x\to\infty \), by expanding the phase to fourth order in the rescaled Laplace integral.
Derive the next correction in the ratio \( \dfrac{\Gamma(x+a)}{\Gamma(x+b)} \), showing that as \( x\to\infty \) it equals \( x^{a-b}\left(1+\dfrac{(a-b)(a+b-1)}{2x}+\cdots\right) \).

Following Example Sheet 2 Q2, the change of variable \( t\mapsto\pi/2-t \) turns \( \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{x\sin^2 t}\,dt \) into \( \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{x\cos^2 t}\,dt \). Use Laplace's method to obtain the leading-order asymptotics of \( K(x)=\int_0^{\pi/2} e^{x\cos^2 t}\,dt \) as \( x\to+\infty \).

Following Example Sheet 2 Q2, find the first correction to the Bessel asymptotic, i.e. show that \( I_0(x)\sim\dfrac{e^{x}}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{8x}+\cdots\right) \) as \( x\to\infty \), by expanding \( \cos\theta \) to fourth order near \( \theta=0 \).

Following Example Sheet 2 Q2, use the reflection formula \( \Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\pi/\sin\pi z \) to show that the \( n \)-th coefficient in the expansion \( \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-x\sin^2 t}\,dt \sim \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4x}\right)^{1/2}\sum_{n\ge0} d_n (4x)^{-n} \) is \( d_n=\dfrac{1}{n!}\big[1^2\,3^2\cdots(2n-1)^2\big] \). Verify \( d_0,d_1,d_2 \).

A partition-counting argument needs the asymptotics of \( \dfrac{\Gamma(x+\tfrac12)}{\Gamma(x+1)} \) to two terms as \( x\to\infty \). Obtain them, and hence give the leading behaviour of \( \dfrac{(2n)!}{4^n (n!)^2} \).

Find the leading-order asymptotics, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( P(x)=\int_0^{\infty} t^{x}\,e^{-t^2/2}\,dt \), expressing the answer in terms of the Gamma function and then in elementary Stirling form.

By writing the integrand as a single exponential and applying Laplace's method, find the leading-order asymptotics of \( Q(x)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-x(t-\ln t)}\,dt \) as \( x\to\infty \). Comment on its relation to Stirling's formula.

Use Stirling's formula to determine the large-\( n \) behaviour of the ratio of consecutive central binomial coefficients \( r_n=\dfrac{1}{4^{n}}\dbinom{2n}{n} \), showing \( r_{n}/r_{n-1}\to 1 \) and finding the next term in \( n^{-1} \).

Find the leading-order asymptotics of \( R(x)=\int_0^{1} t^{x}(1-t)^{x}\,dt \) as \( x\to\infty \) by Laplace's method, and confirm it against the Beta-function value \( R(x)=B(x+1,x+1) \) using Stirling's formula.
Use Stirling's formula to determine the large-\( n \) growth rate of \( a_n = \dfrac{(3n)!}{(n!)^3} \), giving both the exponential rate and the algebraic prefactor.

Use the saddle-point (Laplace-on-the-real-axis) treatment of \( n!=\int_0^\infty t^{n}e^{-t}\,dt \) to estimate the width of the dominant region around the maximum \( t=n \), and hence explain why the relative error of leading-order Stirling is \( O(1/n) \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 01
am4d.questionText: Locate the point where the exponent is largest in the Laplace-type integral \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \) for large \( x>0 \), and state the value of \( \cos\theta \) there.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 02
am4d.questionText: Near \( \theta=0 \) write \( \cos\theta = 1 - g(\theta) \). Find the leading quadratic behaviour of \( g(\theta) \) as \( \theta\to 0 \), which controls the width of the Laplace peak.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 03
am4d.questionText: Evaluate the Gaussian half-line integral \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} e^{-x\theta^2/2}\,d\theta \) for \( x>0 \), the building block of the Bessel \( I_0 \) Laplace estimate.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 04
am4d.questionText: Using the leading Laplace estimate \( \int_0^{\pi} e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \sim e^{x}\sqrt{2\pi/x}\,\cdot\tfrac12 \cdot 2 \) only through the peak, derive the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( I_0(x)=\tfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 05
am4d.questionText: Show that the substitution \( \cos\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2 u \) (with \( u=\theta/2 \)) turns \( I_0(x)=\tfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \) into a multiple of \( \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-2x\sin^2 u}\,du \), and state that multiple.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 06
am4d.questionText: State the first subleading coefficient \( a_1 \) in the asymptotic series \( I_0(x)\sim \dfrac{e^x}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}\Big(1+\dfrac{a_1}{x}+\cdots\Big) \), and hence write the two-term approximation.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 07
am4d.questionText: By applying Laplace's method to the endpoint maximum, derive the leading large-\( x \) asymptotic of \( I_0(x)=\tfrac1\pi\int_0^\pi e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \), justifying carefully why the upper limit may be sent to infinity.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 08
am4d.questionText: Starting from \( I_0(x)=\dfrac{2e^x}{\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-2x\sin^2 u}\,du \), substitute \( s=\sin u \) and use Watson's lemma to obtain the leading term of \( I_0(x) \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 09
am4d.questionText: Continue the Watson's-lemma expansion of \( I_0(x)=\dfrac{e^x}{\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{1}\dfrac{w^{-1/2}e^{-2xw}}{\sqrt{1-w}}\,dw \) to find the first two terms of the asymptotic series.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 10
am4d.questionText: Compute the next coefficient \( a_2 \) in \( I_0(x)\sim \dfrac{e^x}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}\Big(1+\dfrac{1}{8x}+\dfrac{a_2}{x^2}+\cdots\Big) \) directly from the closed-form coefficient rule, and state it as an exact fraction.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 11
am4d.questionText: Write down the three-term asymptotic expansion of \( I_0(x) \) for large \( x \), and use it to estimate \( I_0(20) \) to leading-order accuracy, commenting on the closeness to the exact value \( I_0(20)\approx 4.3558\times10^{7} \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 12
am4d.questionText: Using \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-X\sin^2 t}\,dt \sim \Big(\frac{\pi}{4X}\Big)^{1/2}\Big(1+\frac{1}{4X}+\cdots\Big) \) from the example sheet, set \( X=2x \) and the prefactor \( 2e^x/\pi \) to recover the first two terms of \( I_0(x) \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 13
am4d.questionText: Find the leading large-\( x \) asymptotic of the related Laplace integral \( \displaystyle J(x)=\int_0^{\pi} \cos\theta\,e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \), and identify it as \( \pi\,I_1(x) \) at leading order.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 14
am4d.questionText: Determine the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle K(x)=\int_0^{\pi} e^{x\cos\theta}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta \), noting that the amplitude vanishes quadratically at the peak.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 15
am4d.questionText: Show that the ratio \( \dfrac{I_0(x)}{I_0(2x)} \) behaves like \( \sqrt{2}\,e^{-x} \) at leading order as \( x\to\infty \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 16
am4d.questionText: Using the integral representation \( I_0(x)=\tfrac1\pi\int_0^\pi e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \), verify by differentiating under the integral sign that \( I_0'(x)=I_1(x) \), and state the leading asymptotic of \( I_0'(x) \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 17
am4d.questionText: Find the leading large-\( x \) asymptotic of the integral \( \displaystyle M(x)=\int_0^{\pi/2} e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \), where the upper limit stops short of \( \pi \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 18
am4d.questionText: By substituting \( v=2x\sin^2 u \) in the leading neighbourhood of \( u=0 \) in \( I_0(x)=\tfrac{2e^x}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}e^{-2x\sin^2u}\,du \), confirm the leading term and identify the small parameter governing the corrections.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 19
am4d.questionText: Following the example sheet, derive the full asymptotic series \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-X\sin^2 t}\,dt \sim \Big(\frac{\pi}{4X}\Big)^{1/2}\sum_{n\ge0} \frac{[1\cdot3\cdots(2n-1)]^2}{n!\,(4X)^n} \) as \( X\to\infty \), then set \( X=2x \) to obtain the corresponding series for \( I_0(x) \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 20
am4d.questionText: Compute the third subleading coefficient \( a_3 \) of the \( I_0 \) series \( I_0(x)\sim\dfrac{e^x}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}\sum_n a_n x^{-n} \), giving it as a fully reduced fraction, and verify the recurrence \( a_{n+1}=\dfrac{(2n+1)^2}{8(n+1)}a_n \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 21
am4d.questionText: Use the example-sheet reflection identity \( \Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\dfrac{\pi}{\sin\pi z} \) to express the coefficient \( \dfrac{\Gamma(1/2)}{\Gamma(1/2-m)\,m!}\,\Gamma(1/2+m) \) appearing in the \( \int_0^{\pi/2}e^{x\sin^2 t}dt \) expansion as \( \dfrac{(-1)^m[1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)]^2}{m!\,4^m} \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 22
am4d.questionText: Derive the subleading asymptotic of \( I_0(x) \) directly by expanding \( e^{x\cos\theta}=e^x e^{-x(\theta^2/2-\theta^4/24+\cdots)} \) about \( \theta=0 \), keeping the \( \theta^4 \) term, and confirm the \( 1/(8x) \) correction.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 23
am4d.questionText: Show that for large \( x \) the modified Bessel functions satisfy \( I_0(x)+I_1(x)\sim \dfrac{e^x}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}\Big(2-\dfrac{1}{4x}+\cdots\Big) \), using \( I_0\sim\frac{e^x}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}(1+\frac{1}{8x}) \) and \( I_1\sim\frac{e^x}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}(1-\frac{3}{8x}) \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 24
am4d.questionText: By writing the integrand as \( e^{x\cos\theta}=e^{x}e^{-x(1-\cos\theta)} \) and substituting \( \tau = 1-\cos\theta \), show \( I_0(x)=\dfrac{e^x}{\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{2}\dfrac{e^{-x\tau}}{\sqrt{\tau(2-\tau)}}\,d\tau \) and obtain its leading large-\( x \) form via Watson's lemma.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 25
am4d.questionText: From the representation \( I_0(x)=\dfrac{e^x}{\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^2 \dfrac{e^{-x\tau}}{\sqrt{2}\,\sqrt\tau}\big(1+\tfrac{\tau}{4}+\tfrac{3\tau^2}{32}+\cdots\big)\,d\tau \), extract the first two terms of the asymptotic series for \( I_0(x) \) by term-by-term Watson's lemma.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 26
am4d.questionText: Verify the recurrence \( a_{n+1}=\dfrac{(2n+1)^2}{8(n+1)}a_n \) implies the \( I_0 \) asymptotic series is divergent for every fixed \( x \), and estimate the optimal truncation index \( N_\star(x) \) (where the terms are smallest).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 27
am4d.questionText: A drum-like average gives \( P(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi} e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \). Show \( P(x)=I_0(x) \) and hence find the two-term large-\( x \) expansion of \( \ln P(x) \).

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 28
am4d.questionText: Find the leading large-\( x \) asymptotic of the generalised integral \( \displaystyle G(x)=\int_0^{\pi} e^{x\cos\theta}\,\theta^{2}\,d\theta \), where the algebraic factor \( \theta^2 \) vanishes at the peak.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 29
am4d.questionText: By relating \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-x\sin^2 t}\,dt \) (the decaying sheet integral) to the growing one via \( t\mapsto \pi/2-t \), and then to \( I_0 \), show the leading behaviour of \( H(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}e^{-x\sin^2 t}\,dt \) is \( \sqrt{\pi/(4x)} \) and explain why it is algebraically small, not exponentially small.

am4d.topicTitle: Laplace integrals for special functions (Bessel I₀) 30
am4d.questionText: For the Bessel asymptotic \( I_0(x)\sim\dfrac{e^x}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}\big(1+\frac{1}{8x}+\frac{9}{128x^2}\big) \), estimate the relative error of the leading-only term at \( x=4 \) and at \( x=10 \), and discuss the regime in which including the \( 1/(8x) \) term is worthwhile.

am5a.questionText: By integrating by parts once, write \( \displaystyle \int_a^b f(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \) as a boundary term plus a remainder integral.

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 03
am5a.questionText: Find the leading term, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle \int_0^1 t\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 04
am5a.questionText: Find the leading term, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle \int_1^2 \frac{e^{i\omega t}}{t}\, dt \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 05
am5a.questionText: Find the leading term, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle \int_0^\infty e^{-t}\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \), and confirm it against the exact value.

am5a.questionText: State the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma for \( \displaystyle \int_a^b f(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \) with \( f \) integrable, and explain in one line why integration by parts gives the rate of decay when \( f \) is also \( C^1 \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 07
am5a.questionText: Obtain the first two terms in the asymptotic expansion, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^1 (2 + t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 08

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 09
am5a.questionText: Find the leading term, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^2 \cos t\; e^{i\omega t}\, dt \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 10
am5a.questionText: Find the leading term, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_1^3 \ln t\; e^{i\omega t}\, dt \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 11
am5a.questionText: Taking \( \omega \to \infty \), find the leading term in the asymptotic approximation of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^1 \cos(\omega t)\, dt \) and of \( \displaystyle J(\omega) = \int_0^1 t\,\cos(\omega t)\, dt \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 12
am5a.questionText: Let \( f \) be smooth on \( [a,b] \). Show by repeated integration by parts that, as \( \omega \to \infty \), \( \displaystyle \int_a^b f(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \sim \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{(i\omega)^{n+1}}\Big[ f^{(n)}(b)e^{i\omega b} - f^{(n)}(a)e^{i\omega a} \Big] \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 13
am5a.questionText: Find the leading behaviour, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^\pi \sin t\; e^{i\omega t}\, dt \). Comment on the order of decay.

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 14
am5a.questionText: Find the leading term, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^1 e^{t}\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \), and verify it against the exact value.

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 15
am5a.questionText: A function \( f \) is smooth on \( [a,c)\cup(c,b) \) but has a jump discontinuity at the interior point \( t=c \). By splitting the range, show that the leading large-\( \omega \) contribution of the jump to \( \displaystyle \int_a^b f(t)e^{i\omega t}\, dt \) is \( \displaystyle -\frac{\big[f(c^+) - f(c^-)\big]\, e^{i\omega c}}{i\omega} \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 16
am5a.questionText: The amplitude \( f(t) = t \) for \( 0\le t<1 \) and \( f(t) = t+1 \) for \( 1\le t\le 2 \). Find the leading large-\( \omega \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^2 f(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 17
am5a.questionText: Find the leading term, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^{1} e^{-2t}\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \), and compare with the exact value.

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 18
am5a.questionText: Explain why \( \displaystyle \int_0^{2\pi} f(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \) decays faster than any power of \( 1/\omega \) when \( f \) is smooth and \( 2\pi \)-periodic with all derivatives matching at the endpoints, taking \( \omega \) integer.

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 19
am5a.questionText: Define \( f(t) = -e^{t} \) for \( t<0 \) and \( f(t) = e^{-t} \) for \( t\ge 0 \). Find the leading large-\( \omega \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \), and check it against the exact value.

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 20
am5a.questionText: Find the first two non-zero terms, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^1 \frac{e^{i\omega t}}{2+t}\, dt \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 21
am5a.questionText: By writing \( g(t)\,e^{i\omega\phi(t)} \) with \( \phi(t) = t^2 \) and observing that \( \phi'(t)\neq 0 \) on \( [1,2] \), find the leading term, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_1^2 e^{i\omega t^2}\, dt \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 22
am5a.questionText: Find the leading term, as \( \omega \to +\infty \), of the real integral \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_1^2 \cos\!\big(\omega\, t^{3}\big)\, dt \). Begin by checking that the phase has no stationary point on \( [1,2] \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 23
am5a.questionText: Find the leading two terms, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t}\cos t\; e^{i\omega t}\, dt \), and verify against the exact transform.

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 24
am5a.questionText: Let \( f \) be smooth on \( [0,1] \) with \( f^{(n)}(0) = f^{(n)}(1) = 0 \) for all \( n \ge 0 \) (a smooth bump compactly supported inside \( (0,1) \)). Prove that \( \displaystyle \int_0^1 f(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \) decays faster than any power of \( 1/\omega \) as \( \omega \to \infty \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 25
am5a.questionText: Find the leading large-\( \omega \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^1 t^{1/2}\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \). Treat the endpoint \( t=1 \) by integration by parts, and explain why the contribution from \( t=0 \) is of order \( \omega^{-3/2} \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 26
am5a.questionText: By using \( \displaystyle \int_0^\infty e^{i x(\frac{1}{3}t^3 + t)}\, dt \sim i\!\left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{2}{x^3} + \cdots\right) \) as \( x\to+\infty \) (a known result), reproduce the leading term by an integration-by-parts argument and identify \( a_1 \) in \( \sim i\sum a_n x^{-n} \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 27
am5a.questionText: Find the first two terms, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^1 e^{t}\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \) by integration by parts, and confirm them by expanding the exact value \( \dfrac{e^{1+i\omega} - 1}{1+i\omega} \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 28
am5a.questionText: Find the leading behaviour, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_{-1}^{1} |t|\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \), and comment on the order of decay relative to a smooth amplitude.

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 29
am5a.questionText: Find the leading large-\( \omega \) behaviour of the real integral \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^1 \frac{\sin(\omega t)}{1 + t^2}\, dt \).

am5a.topicTitle: Integration by parts & the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma 30
am5a.questionText: Find the leading large-\( \omega \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^2 H(t-1)\, e^{t}\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \), where \( H \) is the Heaviside step. Identify both the genuine endpoint and the discontinuity contributions.

am5b.questionText: Evaluate \( I(\omega) = \int_0^1 e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) exactly, then write down its leading behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) and identify which endpoint each term comes from.

For smooth \( f \) with no stationary phase, the leading endpoint contribution to \( \int_a^b f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) comes from one integration by parts. Carry out that single integration by parts and write down the leading term.
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^2 e^{-t}\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).

A function \( f \) is smooth on \( (a,c) \) and on \( (c,b) \) but jumps at \( t = c \), with one-sided limits \( f(c^-) \) and \( f(c^+) \). Write down the extra term this jump adds to the leading asymptotics of \( \int_a^b f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), and explain its sign.

Let \( f(t) = 0 \) for \( t < 0 \) and \( f(t) = 1 \) for \( t \ge 0 \) (a unit step). Find the leading behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1} f(t)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).
Find, to leading order as \( \omega \to +\infty \), the real integral \( \displaystyle J(\omega) = \int_0^1 \cos(\omega t)\,dt \), and state the order of its decay.

A function \( f \) is smooth on \( (a,c) \cup (c,b) \) with one-sided limits of \( f \) and all its derivatives existing at \( a^+,\,c^-,\,c^+,\,b^- \). Show that, as \( |\omega| \to \infty \), \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_a^b f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) has leading behaviour given by the two endpoints plus the jump at \( c \).

Let \( f(t) = -e^{t} \) for \( t < 0 \) and \( f(t) = e^{-t} \) for \( t \ge 0 \). Find the leading behaviour of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to +\infty \), and compare with the exact value.
Find the leading-order asymptotics as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^{\pi} t\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), and give the next-order \( O(\omega^{-2}) \) correction.

Let \( f(t) = 1 \) for \( 0 \le t < 1 \) and \( f(t) = 2 \) for \( 1 \le t \le 3 \). Find the leading behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^3 f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_{-1}^{1} |t|\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \). (Note \( |t| \) is continuous but its derivative jumps at \( t = 0 \).)
Compute the leading two terms (orders \( \omega^{-1} \) and \( \omega^{-2} \)) as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^1 e^{t}\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).

A signal is \( f(t) = \cos t \) for \( 0 \le t < \tfrac{\pi}{2} \) and \( f(t) = 0 \) for \( \tfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \pi \). Find the leading behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^{\pi} f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).
Find the leading two terms as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of the real integral \( \displaystyle J(\omega) = \int_0^1 t\,\cos(\omega t)\,dt \).

Let \( f(t) = t \) for \( 0 \le t < 1 \) and \( f(t) = t - 1 \) for \( 1 \le t \le 2 \) (a sawtooth with a unit drop at \( t = 1 \)). Find the leading behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^2 f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_1^{2} \frac{1}{t}\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).
Find the leading two terms as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^{1} (1 + t^2)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).

Let \( f(t) = e^{-t} \) for \( t \ge 0 \) and \( f(t) = 0 \) for \( t < 0 \). Find the leading behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_{-1}^{1} f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), distinguishing the jump term from the endpoint term.

Let \( f \) be smooth on \( (a,c) \cup (c,b) \) with one-sided derivatives of all orders at the four relevant points. By repeated integration by parts, derive the full asymptotic series for \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_a^b f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( |\omega| \to \infty \), giving the general \( n \)-th term.

Let \( f(t) = t^2 \) for \( 0 \le t < 1 \) and \( f(t) = 1 + 5(t-1) \) for \( 1 \le t \le 2 \) (so \( f \) is continuous at \( t = 1 \) but \( f' \) jumps there). Find the asymptotic expansion of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^2 f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) up to and including \( O(\omega^{-2}) \).

Using part (a)-style reasoning, find the asymptotic expansion of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to +\infty \) for \( f(t) = -e^{t}\ (t<0),\ e^{-t}\ (t \ge 0) \), to two non-zero terms, and confirm against the exact transform.

An oscillatory integral has both an interior stationary point and live endpoints. For \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^1 e^{i\omega t^2}\,dt \), find the leading contribution of the stationary point at \( t = 0 \) and the leading endpoint contribution at \( t = 1 \), and state which dominates as \( \omega \to +\infty \).

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^1 \sqrt{t}\;e^{i\omega t}\,dt \). (Note \( f(t)=\sqrt t \) has an integrable singularity in its derivative at the lower endpoint.)

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^1 \cos\!\big(x\,t^{p}\big)\,dt \) for fixed real \( p > 1 \). Identify the contribution of the stationary point at \( t = 0 \) and that of the endpoint at \( t = 1 \).

A pulse is \( f(t) = \sin(\pi t) \) for \( 0 \le t < 1 \) and \( f(t) = 0 \) for \( 1 \le t \le 2 \). Find the leading behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^2 f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), being careful about continuity of \( f \) and \( f' \) at \( t = 1 \).
Find the asymptotic expansion to two non-zero terms as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^{\pi} \cos t\;e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).

Stokes-style problem. Find the leading behaviour as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_a^{\infty} e^{ix(t^3 - t)}\,dt \) in the case \( a = 1 \), where the phase has stationary points at \( t = \pm 1/\sqrt{3} \) (both lying below the lower limit).

Find the leading two terms as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_0^{1} t\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) by repeated integration by parts, and verify your result by evaluating the integral exactly.

A boxcar window is \( f(t) = 1 \) for \( |t| \le 1 \) and \( 0 \) otherwise. Find the leading behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_{-2}^{2} f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), and express the result as a real function of \( \omega \).

A triangular window is \( f(t) = 1 - |t| \) for \( |t| \le 1 \) and \( 0 \) otherwise. Find the leading behaviour as \( \omega \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega) = \int_{-1}^{1} (1 - |t|)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), and explain why it decays faster than the boxcar window.

am5c.questionText: Consider the Fourier integral \( I(\omega) = \int_a^b f(t)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) with \( f \) smooth on \( [a,b] \). Perform one integration by parts and hence state the leading-order behaviour as \( \omega \to \infty \).
Find the leading-order asymptotic behaviour, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( I(\omega) = \int_0^1 e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), and confirm it against the exact value.
Use the endpoint formula to write down the leading-order behaviour of \( I(\omega) = \int_0^1 (t^2 + 1)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \).
Find the leading-order behaviour of the oscillatory integral \( I(\omega) = \int_0^{\pi} t\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \).

Given the asymptotic series \( I(\omega) \sim -\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(-i\omega)^{n+1}}\big[f^{(n)}(b)e^{i\omega b} - f^{(n)}(a)e^{i\omega a}\big] \) for \( \int_a^b f e^{i\omega t}dt \), write down the first two terms for \( f(t)=e^{t} \) on \( [0,1] \).

A function \( f \) is smooth on \( (a,c) \cup (c,b) \) but has a finite jump at the interior point \( c \). State the leading-order contribution this jump makes to \( I(\omega) = \int_a^b f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \).
By integrating by parts twice, find the two-term asymptotic expansion, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( I(\omega) = \int_0^1 (t^2+1)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).

Find the two-term asymptotic expansion, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( I(\omega) = \int_0^2 e^{-t}\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), and identify the exact closed form of \( I(\omega) \) to confirm the leading term.

Taking the real part of \( \int_0^1 t\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), find the leading-order behaviour of \( J(\omega) = \int_0^1 t\cos(\omega t)\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \), and verify it against the exact value.
Find the leading-order asymptotic behaviour, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( I(\omega) = \int_0^2 \frac{1}{1+t}\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).
Let \( f(t) = 1 \) for \( 0 \le t < 1 \) and \( f(t) = 3 \) for \( 1 \le t \le 2 \). Find the leading-order behaviour of \( I(\omega) = \int_0^2 f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \).
Consider \( f(t) = -e^{t} \) for \( t<0 \) and \( f(t)=e^{-t} \) for \( t\ge 0 \). Compute the exact value of \( I(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) in closed form.
For the piecewise-exponential function with exact transform \( I(\omega) = \dfrac{2i\omega}{1+\omega^2} \), find the asymptotic expansion of \( I(\omega) \) to two terms as \( \omega \to \infty \).
Find the leading-order behaviour of \( I(\omega) = \int_{1}^{3} \ln t\, e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \).

Taking the imaginary part of \( \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), deduce the leading behaviour of \( S(\omega) = \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin(\omega t)\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \), and check against the exact value.
Find the two-term asymptotic expansion, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( I(\omega) = \int_0^1 \cos(\pi t)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \).

A signal has amplitude \( f(t)=2 \) for \( -1 \le t < 0 \) and \( f(t) = 2-t \) for \( 0 \le t \le 1 \), and is zero outside \( [-1,1] \). Find the leading-order behaviour of \( I(\omega) = \int_{-1}^{1} f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \).

Find the leading-order behaviour of \( I(\omega) = \int_a^b f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) when \( f \) is smooth and periodic with \( f(a)=f(b) \) and \( e^{i\omega a}=e^{i\omega b} \). Explain why the decay is faster than \( 1/\omega \).

By repeated integration by parts, show that for \( f \) smooth on \( [a,b] \), \( \int_a^b f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \sim -\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(-i\omega)^{n+1}}\big[f^{(n)}(b)e^{i\omega b} - f^{(n)}(a)e^{i\omega a}\big] \) as \( \omega \to \infty \).

For the piecewise-exponential amplitude \( f(t)=-e^{t} \) (\(t<0\)), \( e^{-t} \) (\(t\ge 0\)), use the interior-jump formula to obtain the leading asymptotics of \( I(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), and reconcile it with the exact result \( 2i\omega/(1+\omega^2) \).

A pulse has amplitude \( f(t)=e^{t} \) for \( -1 \le t < 0 \) and \( f(t)=e^{-2t} \) for \( 0 \le t \le 1 \), and is zero outside \( [-1,1] \). Find the leading-order behaviour of \( I(\omega) = \int_{-1}^{1} f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \).

Compare the smooth and discontinuous cases: find the leading behaviour of (i) \( \int_0^1 t\, e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), and (ii) \( \int_0^2 g(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) where \( g(t)=t \) on \( [0,1) \) and \( g(t)=t-1 \) on \( [1,2] \). Explain the difference in their decay.

Find the leading-order behaviour of \( I(\omega) = \int_0^1 (1-t)^2\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \), being careful about which endpoint dominates. Determine the leading power of \( 1/\omega \) and its coefficient.
For \( \omega \neq 1 \), evaluate \( I(\omega) = \int_0^{\pi} \sin t\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) in closed form, then deduce its leading-order behaviour as \( \omega \to \infty \).

Find the asymptotic expansion to two terms, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( I(\omega) = \int_0^1 e^{t}\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), and confirm both terms by expanding the exact closed form \( (e^{1+i\omega}-1)/(1+i\omega) \).

A signal is \( f(t)=\cos t \) on \( [0,\pi/2) \) and \( f(t)=0 \) on \( [\pi/2,\pi] \). Find the leading-order behaviour of \( I(\omega) = \int_0^{\pi} f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) as \( \omega \to \infty \), accounting for every contributing feature.

Show that for \( f \) smooth on \( [a,b] \) with \( f(a)=f(b)=0 \) and \( f'(a)=f'(b)=0 \), the Fourier integral \( \int_a^b f e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) decays faster than any inverse power if \( f \) is in fact \( C^\infty \) with all derivatives vanishing at both ends. State the decay when only the first two derivatives vanish.

Find the leading large-\(\omega\) behaviour of \( I(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{1+t^2}\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) and contrast it with the algebraic decay seen for amplitudes with jumps or endpoints.

A waveform is \( f(t)=t \) on \( [0,1) \), with a jump to \( f(t)=t-2 \) on \( [1,2] \). Find the asymptotic expansion to two terms, as \( \omega \to \infty \), of \( I(\omega)=\int_0^2 f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), including both endpoint and jump contributions at each order.

Generalise the piecewise-exponential example: for \( f(t)=-e^{\alpha t} \) (\(t<0\)) and \( f(t)=e^{-\beta t} \) (\(t\ge 0\)) with \( \alpha,\beta>0 \), compute the exact transform \( I(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) and find its leading asymptotics, checking consistency with the jump rule.

am5d.questionText: Evaluate the Fresnel-type integral \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} u^{-1/2}\cos u \, du \) using the standard cosine Mellin transform \( \int_0^{\infty} u^{s-1}\cos u \, du = \Gamma(s)\cos\!\big(\tfrac{\pi s}{2}\big) \).

By the substitution \( u = x t^{p} \), reduce \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty}\cos(x t^{p})\,dt \) (with \( p>1 \), \( x>0 \)) to a multiple of \( x^{-1/p} \) times a \( u \)-integral. State the resulting power of \( x \) and the prefactor.
Find the exact value of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty}\cos(t^{2})\,dt \) (the Fresnel cosine integral) using \( \int_0^{\infty} u^{s-1}\cos u\,du = \Gamma(s)\cos(\pi s/2) \).

State the decay rate (the power of \( x \)) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(x t^{p})\,dt \) as \( x\to+\infty \), for \( p>1 \), and explain in one line why the endpoint \( t=0 \) dominates the endpoint \( t=1 \).
Find the exact value of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} u^{-1/2}\sin u \, du \) using \( \int_0^{\infty} u^{s-1}\sin u\,du = \Gamma(s)\sin(\pi s/2) \).

Using one integration by parts, find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of the upper-endpoint contribution \( \displaystyle\int_{1/2}^{1}\cos(x t)\,dt \) (a linear, non-stationary phase). Give the leading term.
Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(x t^{p})\,dt \) for real \( p>1 \).
Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(x t^{3})\,dt \), giving the constant in terms of \( \Gamma(1/3) \).
Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\sin(x t^{2})\,dt \), and hence give its decay rate.
Show that, as \( x\to+\infty \), \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} e^{\,i x t^{p}}\,dt \sim \frac{1}{p}\,\Gamma\!\Big(\frac1p\Big)\,e^{\,i\pi/(2p)}\,x^{-1/p} \) for \( p>1 \).
Find the leading large-\( x \) term of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{2}\cos(x t^{2})\,dt \). Show explicitly that the upper limit does not affect the leading coefficient.
Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(x t^{4})\,dt \), giving the constant in terms of \( \Gamma(1/4) \).
Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos\!\big(x t^{3/2}\big)\,dt \).
Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(a\, x\, t^{2})\,dt \), where \( a>0 \) is a fixed constant, and state how the coefficient scales with \( a \).
Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\sin(x t^{3})\,dt \), giving the constant in terms of \( \Gamma(4/3) \).

Include the next correction: show that, as \( x\to+\infty \), \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(x t^{2})\,dt \sim \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{8}}\,x^{-1/2} + \frac{\sin x}{2x} \), and identify the origin of each term.

For \( p>1 \), find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of the upper-endpoint correction \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(x t^{p})\,dt - \frac1p\Gamma\!\Big(\frac1p\Big)\cos\!\Big(\frac{\pi}{2p}\Big)x^{-1/p} \), i.e. the next term after the fractional power.

Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} e^{-x t^{4}}\,dt \) (a real, decaying algebraic phase), and contrast its rate with that of \( \int_0^\infty \cos(x t^4)\,dt \).
Find the first two terms in the large-\( x \) expansion of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(x t^{3})\,dt \), as \( x\to+\infty \).
Find the first two terms in the large-\( x \) expansion of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(x t^{2})\,dt \), including the second endpoint correction at \( t=1 \) beyond \( \sin x/(2x) \).

The phase \( \phi(t)=t-\sin t \) behaves like \( \tfrac{1}{6}t^{3} \) near \( t=0 \). Using this, show that \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} e^{\,i x (t-\sin t)}\,dt \sim e^{\,i\pi/6}\Big(\frac{6}{x}\Big)^{1/3}\Gamma\!\Big(\frac43\Big) \) as \( x\to+\infty \).

An interior stationary point: find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\cos\!\big(x\,t^{2}\big)\,dt \) by exploiting symmetry, and confirm it is twice the half-range result.

Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\cos\!\big(x\,t^{4}\big)\,dt \), where the phase \( t^4 \) has a quartic (degenerate) stationary point at the interior \( t=0 \).
Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{\,q}\cos(x t^{p})\,dt \), where \( p>1 \) and \( q>-1 \), giving the constant in terms of the Gamma function.
Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} \sqrt{t}\,\cos(x t^{2})\,dt \).
An integrable amplitude singularity at the stationary endpoint: find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{-1/2}\cos(x t^{2})\,dt \).
Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} e^{-t}\cos(x t^{2})\,dt \), where the smooth amplitude \( e^{-t} \) is non-zero at the stationary endpoint.
Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos\!\big(x\,(t^{2}+t^{3})\big)\,dt \), where the phase is \( t^2+t^3 \) (so \( t^2 \) dominates near \( t=0 \)).

Two competing endpoints: find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos\!\big(x\,t^{2}(1-t)^{2}\big)\,dt \), where the phase \( t^2(1-t)^2 \) is flat at both \( t=0 \) and \( t=1 \).

Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos\!\big(x\,(t^{2}-\tfrac12)\big)\,dt \), where the constant phase shift must be handled before extracting the fractional power.

am6a.questionText: State the leading-order stationary-phase approximation, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( I(x) = \int_a^b g(t)\,e^{ix\phi(t)}\,dt \), where \( \phi \) has a single simple stationary point \( t_0 \in (a,b) \) with \( \phi'(t_0)=0 \) and \( \phi''(t_0)>0 \), and \( g(t_0)\neq 0 \).
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-1}^{2} e^{ix t^2}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-2}^{3} e^{-ix t^2}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-1}^{1} e^{ix\,(3t^2)}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{2}^{5} e^{ix\,[\,1+(t-3)^2\,]}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-1}^{1} (2+t)\,e^{ix t^2}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{\pi} e^{ix\sin t}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{\pi} (2+\cos t)\,e^{ix\sin t}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-1}^{1} e^{ix\cos t}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{2} e^{ix\,(t^2-2t)}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-2}^{2} \frac{e^{ix t^2}}{1+t^2}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{\pi} \cos t\,\;e^{ix\,(t-\frac{1}{2}\sin 2t)}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} e^{-ix\cos t}\,dt \).
By taking the real part of a suitable oscillatory integral, find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle J(x)=\int_{0}^{\pi} \cos\!\big(x\sin t\big)\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{3} t\,e^{ix\,(t-2)^2}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-1}^{4} e^{ix\,(t^2-4t+1)}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (1+t^2)\,e^{ix\sin t}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x \to +\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-3}^{3} e^{\,\frac{i}{2}x t^2}\,dt \).

By taking the real part of a suitable oscillatory integral, show that the modified Bessel-type integral \( \displaystyle J(x)=\int_{0}^{\pi}\cos\!\big(x\sin t-t\big)\,dt \) satisfies \( J(x)\sim\sqrt{2\pi/x}\,\cos\!\big(x-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\big) \) as \( x\to+\infty \). (This is \( \pi J_1(x) \).)
Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{\pi} e^{ix\,(2\sin t-\sin 2t)/2}\,dt \), taking care to identify the simple interior stationary point.

A function \( g \) is smooth with \( g(t)\to 0 \) as \( t\to\pm\infty \). Show that, as \( x\to+\infty \), \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(t)\,e^{ix\,(t^2-t)}\,dt \sim g\!\big(\tfrac12\big)\sqrt{\tfrac{2\pi}{x}}\;e^{i(\pi/4 - x/4)} \).
Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{2\pi} e^{ix\cos(t-\frac{\pi}{3})}\,dt \). (Both interior stationary points contribute.)
The integral \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{ix\,(t^2-t)}\,\frac{dt}{1+t^2} \) is to be approximated for large \( x \). Find its leading term and the order of the first correction.
Using the substitution \( u=\sin\theta \) (or otherwise), find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{\pi/2} e^{ix\sin^2\theta}\,d\theta \).

Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-t^2}\,e^{ix\,(t-t^3/3)}\,dt \), and explain why the cubic term in the phase does not affect the leading order.
Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin t\;e^{ix\,(t+\cos t)}\,dt \).

Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\!\!\int \!\!\;e^{ix\cos\theta}\,d\theta \) over \( \theta\in(0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}) \), where the only stationary point is at the endpoint \( \theta=0 \). Hence comment on how the answer differs from the interior-point case.
Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-2}^{2} e^{ix\,(t^3-3t)}\,dt \), summing the contributions of all simple interior stationary points.

Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{0}^{1} t\,e^{ix\,(t^2-t)}\,dt \), and explain carefully why the endpoint contributions are subdominant to the interior stationary point.

Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\cos\big(x\,(t^2+t)\big)}{1+t^4}\,dt \), by relating it to the real part of a stationary-phase integral.

am6b.questionText: Evaluate the regularised oscillatory integral \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} e^{i t^3}\,dt \) by rotating the contour onto the steepest-descent ray.
Show that \( \displaystyle\frac{1}{3}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) = \Gamma\!\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \), the identity that lets the cubic-phase constant be written either way.
For large \( x \), find the leading behaviour of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{i x t^3}\,dt \) by scaling out \( x \).
Use the rescaling \( s = x^{1/p}t \) to find the leading term of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} e^{i x t^{p}}\,dt \) for a fixed real \( p>1 \) and \( x\to\infty \).
A phase \( \phi(t) \) satisfies \( \phi'(t_0)=\phi''(t_0)=0 \) with \( \phi'''(t_0)>0 \). Write the local cubic model of \( \phi \) about the interior point \( t_0 \).
Find the leading behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} e^{i a x t^3}\,dt \) for a real constant \( a>0 \) and \( x\to\infty \).
Show that, as \( x\to+\infty \), \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} e^{\,i x(t-\sin t)}\,dt \sim e^{i\pi/6}\left(\frac{6}{x}\right)^{1/3}\Gamma\!\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \).

How does the leading asymptotics of \( \displaystyle\int_{a}^{\pi} e^{\,i x(t-\sin t)}\,dt \) differ when the lower limit is changed from \( a=0 \) to \( a=-\pi \)? Give the leading term for \( a=-\pi \) as \( x\to+\infty \).
Find the leading term, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} \cos\!\left(x t^{3}\right)\,dt \).
Taking \( x\to\infty \), find the leading term of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos\!\left(x t^{p}\right)\,dt \) for a fixed real \( p>1 \).

A smooth phase has an interior order-2 stationary point at \( t_0 \) with \( \phi'''(t_0)=c>0 \). Find the leading contribution to \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(t)\,e^{\,i x\phi(t)}\,dt \) for \( x\to\infty \), where \( g \) is smooth with \( g(t_0)\neq 0 \).
Find the leading behaviour, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} e^{\,i x(\sin t - t)}\,dt \), i.e. the conjugate phase to the canonical model.

The phase \( \phi(t)=t^3-t \) has stationary points where \( \phi'(t)=0 \). Consider \( \displaystyle\int_{a}^{\infty} f(t)\,e^{\,i x(t^3-t)}\,dt \) with \( f \) smooth, \( f\to 0 \) at infinity. For the choice \( a=-1/\sqrt{3} \), explain why the stationary point coincides with the endpoint and give the resulting leading power of \( x \).

For the same phase \( \phi(t)=t^3-t \), now take the lower limit \( a=1 \) in \( \displaystyle\int_{1}^{\infty} f(t)\,e^{\,i x(t^3-t)}\,dt \), with \( f \) smooth and \( f\to 0 \) at infinity. Determine the leading behaviour as \( x\to\infty \).
Find the leading behaviour, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} t^{\,\sigma-1}\, e^{\,i x t^{3}}\,dt \) for a constant \( \sigma>0 \) (an algebraically weighted cubic phase).
Find the leading term, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\!\left(x\cos\theta\right)\,d\theta \) (the \( \gamma=0 \) case of the sheet's weighted family).

Find the leading behaviour, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} e^{\,i x(t^{3}/3 + t)}\,dt \) (a cubic-plus-linear phase with no real stationary point), and identify the leading power.
Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,i t^{3}/3}\,dt \) by relating it to the Airy function value \( \mathrm{Ai}(0)=\dfrac{1}{3^{2/3}\Gamma(2/3)} \).
Obtain the first TWO terms (leading plus first correction) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} e^{\,i x(t-\sin t)}\,dt \) as \( x\to+\infty \), keeping the next term in the local expansion of the phase.

A wave-packet integral has the form \( \displaystyle u(x)=\int_0^{\infty} A(k)\,e^{\,i x\,\omega(k)}\,dk \), where the group velocity is stationary: \( \omega'(k_0)=\omega''(k_0)=0 \), \( \omega'''(k_0)=\beta\neq 0 \), and \( k_0>0 \) is interior. Derive the leading behaviour of \( u(x) \) as \( x\to\infty \) (a caustic / Airy-type focusing).

Find the leading behaviour, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}\right)^{\!-3/4}\cos\!\left(x\cos\theta\right)\,d\theta \) (the \( \gamma=-3/4 \) case of the sheet's weighted family). Identify which endpoint dominates and the resulting power of \( x \).

For the \( \gamma=-1/2 \) case, find the leading behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}\right)^{\!-1/2}\cos\!\left(x\cos\theta\right)\,d\theta \) as \( x\to\infty \), and state whether the two endpoints contribute at the same order.
Show that, for \( x\to\infty \), \( \displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi} e^{\,i x(t-\sin t)}\,dt \) has TWO degenerate stationary points and find the leading behaviour, combining their contributions.

Find the leading behaviour, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\frac{\cos(x t^{3})}{\sqrt{t}}\,dt \) (a cubic phase with an integrable inverse-square-root weight at the stationary point).

A phase has an interior stationary point of order 3 at \( t_0 \): \( \phi'=\phi''=\phi'''=0 \), \( \phi^{(4)}(t_0)=d>0 \). Derive the leading contribution of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(t)e^{\,i x\phi(t)}\,dt \) and contrast its decay rate with the cubic (order-2) case.

By writing \( \mathrm{Ai}(-\xi) \) as an oscillatory integral and applying stationary phase, derive its large-\( \xi \) asymptotics for \( \xi\to+\infty \), and explain why a degenerate (cubic) phase appears precisely at \( \xi=0 \).

Find the leading behaviour, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} (\pi - |t|)\,e^{\,i x(t-\sin t)}\,dt \), where the smooth-looking weight vanishes linearly at the endpoints but is finite (and even) at the stationary point.
Find the leading behaviour, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} e^{\,i x(t^{3}-3t^{2}+3t)}\,dt \) by recognising a perfect-cube phase and reducing to the canonical cubic integral.

Find the leading behaviour, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} \sin t\; e^{\,i x(t-\sin t)}\,dt \), where the smooth weight \( \sin t \) VANISHES at the stationary point \( t=0 \), so the leading cubic term is suppressed.

Two simple stationary points of a phase \( \phi \) are about to coalesce: \( \phi'(t)= (t^2 - \epsilon) \,h(t) \) with \( h(0)>0 \) and a small \( \epsilon\to 0^{+} \). Explain, using the uniform Airy description, what happens to \( \displaystyle\int g\,e^{\,i x\phi}\,dt \) as \( \epsilon\to 0 \) at fixed large \( x \), and give the decay rate exactly at coalescence \( \epsilon=0 \).

am6c.questionText: State the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of the algebraic-endpoint integral \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{\gamma} e^{i x t}\,dt \), for fixed \( \gamma > -1 \). (You may quote the standard result obtained by extending the upper limit to \( \infty \).)
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{-1/2}\cos(x t)\,dt \).

For the weight \( w(\theta) = \big(1 - \tfrac{2\theta}{\pi}\big)^{\gamma} \) on \( [0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}] \), determine where \( w \) is singular when \( \gamma < 0 \), and write the local behaviour of \( w \) near that point in terms of \( s = \tfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta \).
By extending the upper limit to infinity, find the leading behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} \cos(x t^2)\,dt \).

Two contributions to an oscillatory integral scale as \( A\,x^{-1/2} \) (a stationary point) and \( B\,x^{-(\gamma+1)} \) (a singular endpoint of strength \( \gamma \)). State, in terms of \( \gamma \), which contribution dominates as \( x\to\infty \), and find the value of \( \gamma \) at which the two are of equal order.
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( \omega \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), where the amplitude is smooth (\( g\equiv 1 \)), and state the decay rate.
Find the leading-order asymptotic behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x)=\int_0^{\pi/2} \Big(1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}\Big)^{-3/4}\cos(x\cos\theta)\,d\theta. \)

Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle J(x)=\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos(x\cos\theta)\,d\theta \) (the case \( \gamma=0 \)), and state why the weight singularity plays no role here.

Consider \( \displaystyle K(x)=\int_0^{\pi/2} \Big(1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}\Big)^{-1/2}\cos(x\cos\theta)\,d\theta. \) Show that the stationary point and the singular endpoint contribute at the *same* order, and write down both leading terms.
Find the leading behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(x t^3)\,dt \), giving the constant in terms of a Gamma function.

Using the result \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\cos(x t^p)\,dt \sim \tfrac1p\Gamma\!\big(\tfrac1p\big)\cos\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2p}\big)x^{-1/p} \) for \( p>1 \), find the leading behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}\sin(x t^4)\,dt \) as \( x\to\infty \).

Find the leading behaviour as \( \omega \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}(1+t)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), a smooth-amplitude oscillatory integral with no stationary point, and identify the endpoint contributions.
Find the leading-order behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\Big(1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}\Big)^{-1/4}\cos(x\cos\theta)\,d\theta. \)
Find the leading behaviour as \( x \to \infty \) of the weighted endpoint integral \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{-2/3}\,e^{i x t}\,dt \), and give its modulus and argument.

An oscillatory integral over \( [a,b] \) has a smooth amplitude \( f \) with a jump discontinuity at an interior point \( c\in(a,b) \). Write down the leading-order asymptotic form as \( \omega \to \infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega)=\int_a^b f(t)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \), explaining the role of the jump.

Find the leading behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{1/2}\cos(x t)\,dt \). Identify which endpoint dominates, given that the amplitude *vanishes* at the lower endpoint (\( \gamma=+\tfrac12 \)) but is smooth and non-zero at the upper endpoint.
Find the leading behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\Big(1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}\Big)^{-3/4}\sin(x\cos\theta)\,d\theta. \)

The integral \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{\gamma}\cos(x t)\,dt \) has a singular weight at \( t=0 \). For what range of \( \gamma \) does this endpoint produce a contribution that decays *more slowly* than the \( x^{-1/2} \) of a quadratic stationary point? Justify your answer.

For \( \displaystyle I_\gamma(x)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\Big(1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}\Big)^{\gamma}\cos(x\cos\theta)\,d\theta \), derive the leading-order behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) for each of \( \gamma=0 \), \( \gamma=-\tfrac12 \) and \( \gamma=-\tfrac34 \), exhibiting in each case which critical point dominates.

Show that as \( x\to+\infty \), \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} e^{i x(t-\sin t)}\,dt \sim e^{i\pi/6}\Big(\frac{6}{x}\Big)^{1/3}\Gamma\!\Big(\frac{4}{3}\Big), \) treating \( t=0 \) as a degenerate stationary point lying at the endpoint.

An oscillatory integral has both a weight singularity \( t^{\gamma} \) at the lower endpoint *and* the phase \( e^{ixt} \). For the two-term expansion, evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{\gamma}(1 + b t)\,e^{i x t}\,dt \) to two orders as \( x\to\infty \), with \( \gamma>-1 \) and \( b \) constant.

Find the leading behaviour as \( \omega\to\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) for the function \( f(t)=-e^{t} \) for \( t<0 \) and \( f(t)=e^{-t} \) for \( t\ge 0 \), and compare with the exact value of \( I(\omega) \).

Find the leading behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{-1/2}\,e^{i\lambda(t+t^2)}\,dt \) (take \( \lambda=x\to\infty \)), where the weight is singular at the lower endpoint and the phase has no interior stationary point on \( (0,1) \).

Consider the weighted integral \( \displaystyle I_\gamma(x)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\Big(1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}\Big)^{\gamma}\cos(x\cos\theta)\,d\theta. \) Determine the critical exponent \( \gamma^\star \) at which the *next-order* correction to the dominant endpoint term first competes with the stationary contribution, for \( \gamma<-\tfrac12 \).
Find the leading behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1}(1-t)^{-1/2}\,e^{i x t}\,dt \), where the weight is singular at the *upper* endpoint \( t=1 \).
An integral has a stationary point *and* a singular weight at the **same** endpoint: find the leading behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{-1/2}\cos(x t^2)\,dt \).

Generalise: for the coincident case \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{\gamma}\cos(x t^p)\,dt \) with \( \gamma>-1 \) and \( p>0 \), derive the leading behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) and state the decay exponent.

Find the leading behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\Big(1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}\Big)^{-2/3}\cos(x\cos\theta)\,d\theta, \) and state both the dominant term and the order of the first subdominant correction.

For \( \displaystyle\int_0^{1} t^{-1/2}\,e^{i\lambda(t+t^2)}\,dt \sim \frac{c_1}{\lambda^{1/2}} + c_2\frac{e^{2i\lambda}}{\lambda} + \cdots \) as \( \lambda\to\infty \), determine \( c_1 \) from the singular lower endpoint and explain the origin and \( \lambda \)-order of the \( c_2 \) term.

A weighted amplitude has an *interior* algebraic singularity: find the leading behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{2} |t-1|^{-1/2}\,e^{i x t}\,dt \), where the integrand is singular at the interior point \( t=1 \) and there is no stationary point.

am7a.topicTitle: Saddle points & paths of steepest descent 18

For \( I(k) = \displaystyle\int_{\gamma-i\infty}^{\gamma+i\infty}\frac{e^{k(z-2z^{1/2})}}{z - c}\,dz \) with \( c \) real and \( c<1 \), use the parametrisation to obtain the leading behaviour.
