am7b.questionText: Evaluate the Gaussian integral \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-a t^2}\,dt \) for \( a>0 \). This is the local integral that appears once a steepest-descent contour has been straightened at a saddle.
By rotating the contour onto the steepest-descent ray, evaluate the Fresnel-type integral \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,i x t^2}\,dt \) for \( x>0 \).
Find the value of the half-line stationary-phase integral \( \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty} \cos\!\big(x t^2\big)\,dt \) for \( x>0 \), the building block for an endpoint at a stationary point.
Locate the saddle point of the phase \( \phi(t) = t - \tfrac13 t^3 \) on the real axis and state the local quadratic approximation of \( \phi \) there.

Given a single non-degenerate saddle at \( t_0 \) with \( \phi''(t_0) < 0 \), state the leading-order steepest-descent estimate of \( \displaystyle\int_C g(t)\,e^{\lambda\phi(t)}\,dt \) as \( \lambda\to\infty \), assuming \( g(t_0)\neq 0 \).
Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x(t^2 - 2 t)}\,dt \) for \( x>0 \) by completing the square, the move that recentres a contour on its saddle.
Use the method of steepest descent to find the leading-order behaviour, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x(t^2-1)^2/2}\,dt \).
Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of the oscillatory integral \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,i x (t^2 + 2 t)}\,dt \).
Determine the leading-order asymptotics, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \cos\!\big(x(t^2+2t)\big)\,dt \).
Apply the method of steepest descent to obtain the leading term, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x(t^2-2t)}}{1+t^2}\,dt \).
Find the leading-order steepest-descent estimate, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,x(2t - t^2)}\,t^2\,dt \).
The phase \( \phi(t) = i\big(t + \tfrac13 t^3\big) \) has saddles where \( \phi'=0 \). Find the saddle points, the value of \( \phi \) at each, and the curvature \( \phi'' \) there.

Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( \lambda\to\infty \), of the endpoint-dominated integral \( \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty} t^{-1/2}\,e^{\,i\lambda t}\,dt \). (This is the algebraic-endpoint contribution that appears in steepest-descent problems with a branch point at an endpoint.)

Use steepest descent to find the leading term, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,i x t^2}\,e^{-t^2}\,dt \). Treat \( x\to\infty \) and keep the genuine large-parameter contribution.

Find the leading-order asymptotics, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x\,t^2}\cos t\,dt \) and comment on why the \( \cos t \) factor only contributes its value at the endpoint.
For \( x\to+\infty \), find the leading term of \( \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty} \cos\!\big(x\,t^3\big)\,dt \). (A cubic endpoint stationary point.)
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x\cosh t}\,dt \) using steepest descent about the saddle on the real axis.

Find the leading-order asymptotics, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,i x t^2}\,e^{-t^4}\,dt \). The smooth weight \( e^{-t^4} \) is non-singular at the stationary point \( t=0 \).

For \( \theta>0 \) define \( \displaystyle f(\theta) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{C} \exp\!\Big(\theta\big(t + \tfrac13 t^3\big)\Big)\,dt \), where \( C \) runs from \( \infty \) in \( -\tfrac{\pi}{2}<\arg t<-\tfrac{\pi}{6} \) to \( \infty \) in \( \tfrac{\pi}{6}<\arg t<\tfrac{\pi}{2} \). Show that, as \( \theta\to\infty \), \( f(\theta) \sim (\pi\theta)^{-1/2}\cos\!\big(\tfrac{2}{3}\theta - \tfrac{\pi}{4}\big) \).

Show that, as \( x\to+\infty \), \( \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} \exp\!\big[i x(t-\sin t)\big]\,dt \sim e^{i\pi/6}\Big(\frac{6}{x}\Big)^{1/3}\Gamma\!\Big(\frac{4}{3}\Big) \), and identify why the decay is \( x^{-1/3} \) rather than \( x^{-1/2} \).

Use the method of steepest descent to obtain the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty} \exp\!\Big[i x\big(\tfrac13 t^3 + t\big)\Big]\,dt \). Confirm the leading coefficient by an integration-by-parts argument.

Let \( h(t)=i(t+t^2) \). By integrating along the constant-imaginary-phase (steepest) path through the endpoint \( t=0 \), find the leading-order term, as \( \lambda\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} t^{-1/2}\exp\!\big[i\lambda(t+t^2)\big]\,dt \), i.e. the constant \( c_1 \) in \( \sim c_1\lambda^{-1/2} \).
Using steepest descent, find the leading-order behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) of the modified Bessel function \( \displaystyle I_0(x)=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} e^{\,x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \).

By the method of steepest descent applied to \( \displaystyle\Gamma(x+1)=\int_{0}^{\infty} t^{x}e^{-t}\,dt \), derive the leading-order Stirling formula \( \Gamma(x+1)\sim \sqrt{2\pi x}\,\big(x/e\big)^{x} \) as \( x\to\infty \).

The phase \( h(z)=k\big(z-2z^{1/2}\big) \) has a saddle where \( h'=0 \). Find the saddle point, verify that the steepest-descent paths leaving it are \( z_{\pm}(\tau)=1-\tau^2\pm 2 i\tau \) (\( \tau\ge 0 \)), and give the parabola they trace in real form \( x=x(y) \) with \( z=x+iy \).

Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{\,i x(t^3/3 - t)}}{1 + t^2}\,dt \), keeping only the contribution of the dominant real stationary point and explaining which one it is.
Find the leading-order asymptotics, as \( x\to\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x(t-\ln t)}\,dt \) by steepest descent about its interior saddle.
Find the leading term, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\exp\!\big[i x(t-\sin t)\big]\,dt \), and contrast it with the result for the integral over \( [0,\pi] \).

Using steepest descent on \( \displaystyle J(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp\!\big[\,x(i t - \tfrac12 t^2)\big]\,dt \), find its exact leading behaviour as \( x\to\infty \) and identify the (complex) saddle.

Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( x\to+\infty \), of \( \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{\cos(x t^2)}{1+t}\,dt \), arising from a stationary point at the endpoint with a slowly-varying algebraic prefactor.

am7c.questionText: By integrating by parts once, find the leading two terms of the asymptotic expansion as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_x^{\infty} \frac{e^{-t}}{t}\,dt \).
Using Watson's lemma, write down the first two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x t}}{1+t}\,dt \).
Find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x t}}{\sqrt{1+t}}\,dt \) by Watson's lemma.
Evaluate exactly the Watson-lemma building block \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} t^{1/2}\, e^{-x t}\,dt \) for \( x > 0 \), giving the answer as a power of \( x \) times a Gamma value.

By integrating by parts twice, find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} e^{-x t}\cos t \,dt \), and confirm them against the exact value \( \dfrac{x}{x^{2}+1} \).
State the first correction term in Stirling's formula: write the next term in \( \Gamma(x+1) \sim \sqrt{2\pi x}\,(x/e)^{x}\,(1 + \cdots) \) as \( x \to \infty \), and identify its order in \( 1/x \).
Find the first three terms of the asymptotic expansion as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x t}}{1+t^{2}}\,dt \), and state the order of the first omitted term.

Derive, via Laplace's method including the first correction, the expansion as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x\left(\frac{1}{2}t^{2} + \frac{1}{4}t^{4}\right)}\,dt \).
Find the first three terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_x^{\infty} \frac{e^{-t}}{t}\,dt \) by repeated integration by parts, and explain why the resulting series does not converge.

By Laplace's method, find the leading term and first correction as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} t^{x} e^{-x t}\,dt \), and verify it equals \( \Gamma(x+1)/x^{x+1} \) expanded by Stirling.

Find the leading two non-zero terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of the endpoint expansion of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{\,i x\left(\frac{1}{3}t^{3} + t\right)}\,dt \), by repeated integration by parts.
Using Watson's lemma, find the first two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} t^{1/2}\, e^{-x t}\,(1 + t)^{-1}\,dt \).
Find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{1} \frac{e^{-x t}}{1+t}\,dt \) and explain why the upper limit \( t = 1 \) does not contribute to the asymptotic series.
Find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} e^{-x t}\ln(1+t)\,dt \), and check the leading term by integration by parts.

Given the expansion \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-x\sin^{2}t}\,dt \sim \left(\frac{\pi}{4x}\right)^{1/2}\!\left(1 + \frac{1}{4x} + \cdots\right) \) as \( x \to +\infty \), use it to find the leading two terms of the asymptotic expansion of the same integral, showing how the first correction arises.
Find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} e^{-x t}\,(1 + t)^{2}\,e^{-t}\,dt \), and cross-check the leading term against the exact value.
Find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x t}}{(1+t)^{2}}\,dt \) by Watson's lemma, and confirm the leading term by one integration by parts.

Given the Bessel-function representation \( \displaystyle I_0(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} e^{x\cos\theta}\,d\theta \), use Laplace's method with its first correction to obtain the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \).

Find the leading three non-zero terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle I(x) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{\,i x\left(\frac{1}{3}t^{3} + t\right)}\,dt \) and give a general expression for the coefficient \( a_n \) in \( I(x) \sim i\sum_{n} a_n x^{-(2n+1)} \).

Show by repeated integration by parts that \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x t}}{1+t^{2}}\,dt \) has the asymptotic expansion \( \sum_{k\ge0} (-1)^{k}(2k)!\,x^{-(2k+1)} \), reproducing the Watson result.

Obtain the first two terms of Stirling's series, i.e. show \( \Gamma(x+1) \sim \sqrt{2\pi x}\,(x/e)^{x}\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{12x} + \cdots\right) \) as \( x \to \infty \), by applying Laplace's method to \( \Gamma(x+1) = \int_0^{\infty} t^{x} e^{-t}\,dt \) including the cubic and quartic curvature terms.

For the incomplete Gamma function \( \displaystyle \Gamma(a, x) = \int_x^{\infty} t^{a-1} e^{-t}\,dt \), find the first three terms of its asymptotic expansion as \( x \to +\infty \) (with \( a \) fixed) by repeated integration by parts, and give the general term.

Find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x\left(\frac{1}{2}t^{2} + \frac{1}{6}t^{3} + \frac{1}{4}t^{4}\right)}\,dt \), explaining carefully why the cubic term contributes at the same order as the quartic.

Find the first two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} e^{-x t}\,e^{-t^{2}}\,dt \) by Watson's lemma, and independently by completing the square; confirm the two leading-order results agree.

Find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \frac{\cos t}{x^{2} + t^{2}}\,dt \) by integration by parts, and explain the structure of the resulting expansion.

Find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} e^{-x\left(t + \frac{1}{t}\right)} t^{-1/2}\,dt \) by Laplace's method at the interior saddle, and identify the leading behaviour with a modified Bessel function.

Find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x t}}{\sqrt{t}\,(1+t)}\,dt \) by Watson's lemma, and explain why the expansion proceeds in half-integer powers of \( 1/x \).

Find the first two non-zero terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} e^{\,i x\left(\frac{1}{3}t^{3} + t\right)}\,\frac{dt}{1+t} \) by integration by parts, treating the amplitude carefully at the endpoint.

The complementary error function satisfies \( \operatorname{erfc}(z) = \frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_z^{\infty} e^{-s^{2}}\,ds \). By integration by parts, show that as \( z \to +\infty \), \( \operatorname{erfc}(z) \sim \dfrac{e^{-z^{2}}}{z\sqrt\pi}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2z^{2}} + \cdots\right) \), and give the general coefficient.

Find the leading two terms as \( x \to +\infty \) of \( \displaystyle \int_0^{1} (1-t)^{x}\,(1+t)\,dt \), first exactly and then by recognising it as a Laplace-type endpoint integral; confirm the two agree.

am7d.questionText: For the phase \( h(t) = i t^2 \), find the saddle point and determine the directions \( \arg t \) of the constant-phase line \( \operatorname{Im} h = 0 \) through it. State which of these directions is the path of steepest descent for \( e^{\lambda h} \) as \( \lambda \to +\infty \).

Evaluate the Gaussian contribution \( \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{i\lambda t^2}\,dt \) for \( \lambda > 0 \) by integrating along the constant-phase (steepest-descent) line \( t = r e^{i\pi/4} \).
The phase is \( h(t) = t + \tfrac{1}{3}t^3 \). Find both saddle points and evaluate \( h \) at each. Comment on the relationship between the two values of \( h \).
For \( h(t) = i(t + t^2) \), show that the line \( \operatorname{Im} h = 0 \) through the point \( t = 0 \) leaves the origin tangent to the real axis, and find the second derivative \( h''(0) \).
Given two saddle contributions \( A e^{i\phi} \) and \( A e^{-i\phi} \) (with \( A \) real and positive), write their sum as a single real expression.

For the steepest-descent integral through a single saddle \( t_s \), the standard formula is \( g(t_s)\sqrt{\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda\,|h''(t_s)|}}\,e^{\lambda h(t_s)+i\theta} \), where \( \theta \) sets the descent direction. For \( h(t)=t+\tfrac13 t^3 \) at the saddle \( t=i \), compute \( h''(i) \) and \( |h''(i)| \).

Two saddles \( t = \pm i \) of \( h(t)=t+\tfrac13 t^3 \) each contribute \( \tfrac12(\pi\theta)^{-1/2} e^{\pm i(2\theta/3 - \pi/4)} \) to \( f(\theta)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_C e^{\theta h(t)}\,dt \). Combine the two contributions to obtain the leading asymptotics of \( f(\theta) \) as \( \theta\to\infty \).

The integral \( J(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,i x (t^3/3 - t)}\,dt \) has two real stationary points. By scaling \( s = x^{1/3} t \), express \( J(x) \) in terms of the Airy function \( \operatorname{Ai}(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,i(s^3/3 + z s)}\,ds \).

Using \( \operatorname{Ai}(-X)\sim \pi^{-1/2}X^{-1/4}\sin\!\big(\tfrac23 X^{3/2}+\tfrac{\pi}{4}\big) \) for \( X\to+\infty \), deduce the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( J(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,i x(t^3/3 - t)}\,dt = 2\pi x^{-1/3}\operatorname{Ai}(-x^{2/3}) \).

Consider \( I(\lambda)=\int_0^1 t^{-1/2}\,e^{\,i\lambda(t+t^2)}\,dt \) with \( h(t)=i(t+t^2) \). The constant-phase path through the endpoint \( t=0 \) gives the dominant contribution. Find its leading term, of the form \( c_1\lambda^{-1/2} \), as \( \lambda\to\infty \).

Continuing \( I(\lambda)=\int_0^1 t^{-1/2}e^{\,i\lambda(t+t^2)}\,dt \), find the contribution of the upper endpoint \( t=1 \) (the second constant-phase path), giving the term \( c_2\,e^{2i\lambda}\lambda^{-1} \).

For \( h(z)=z - 2\sqrt{z} \) (principal branch, cut along the negative real axis), find the saddle point in \( z \) and verify that the curves \( z_{\pm}(\tau)=1-\tau^2\pm 2i\tau \), \( \tau\ge 0 \), are constant-phase paths through it by checking \( \operatorname{Im} h \) along them.
Show that the two parametrised curves \( z_{\pm}(\tau)=1-\tau^2\pm 2i\tau \) form the two halves of a single parabola, and find its equation in the real variables \( z=x+iy \).

A contour passes through two saddles \( t_1 \) and \( t_2 \) with \( h(t_1)=h(t_2)=h_0 \) real (equal heights), prefactors \( g(t_1)=g(t_2)=g_0 \), and curvatures \( h''(t_1)=\rho e^{i\beta} \), \( h''(t_2)=\rho e^{-i\beta} \). Write the combined leading steepest-descent estimate of \( \int g\,e^{\lambda h}\,dt \).

For \( h(t)=i(t+t^2) \), find the saddle point \( t_s \), the saddle value \( h(t_s) \), and the equation of the constant-phase line \( \operatorname{Im} h = \operatorname{Im} h(t_s) \) through it in terms of \( t=x+iy \).

An integral \( \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,i x \phi(t)}\,dt \) has two real stationary points \( t_1, t_2 \) with \( \phi''(t_1)>0 \) and \( \phi''(t_2)<0 \). Write the leading stationary-phase sum, and simplify the case \( \phi(t_1)=-\phi(t_2)=A \), \( |\phi''(t_1)|=|\phi''(t_2)|=B \).

Combine the two endpoint contributions of am7d Q10/Q11 to state the full leading asymptotic expansion of \( I(\lambda)=\int_0^1 t^{-1/2}e^{\,i\lambda(t+t^2)}\,dt \) to two terms as \( \lambda\to\infty \).

For \( h(z)=z-2\sqrt z \) with saddle \( z=1 \), the steepest-descent integral \( \int_C \frac{e^{k h(z)}}{z-c}\,dz \) is dominated by the saddle when no pole is crossed. Using the parametrisation \( z=1-\tau^2+2i\tau \) (upper half), find \( dz \) and \( h \) as functions of \( \tau \), and write the saddle contribution as a \( \tau \)-integral over \( (-\infty,\infty) \).

For \( h(t)=t+\tfrac13 t^3 \) with \( t=x+iy \), show that the constant-phase paths \( \operatorname{Im} h = \operatorname{Im} h(\pm i) \) through the saddles \( t=\pm i \) are \( x = +\big(\tfrac{2+y}{3y}\big)^{1/2}(y-1) \) for \( y>0 \) and \( x = -\big(\tfrac{y-2}{3y}\big)^{1/2}(y+1) \) for \( y<0 \). Derive the level-set equation and indicate how the sign of each square root is fixed.

For \( f(\theta)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_C e^{\theta(t+t^3/3)}\,dt \), with \( C \) running from \( \infty \) in \( -\tfrac{\pi}{2}<\arg t<-\tfrac{\pi}{6} \) to \( \infty \) in \( \tfrac{\pi}{6}<\arg t<\tfrac{\pi}{2} \), apply the method of steepest descent through both saddles \( t=\pm i \) and show \( f(\theta)\sim(\pi\theta)^{-1/2}\cos\!\big(\tfrac23\theta-\tfrac{\pi}{4}\big) \).

Apply the method of steepest descent to the two-saddle integral and obtain the first two non-zero terms of \( \int_0^{\infty} e^{\,ix(t^3/3 + t)}\,dt \sim i\big(\tfrac1x + \tfrac{2}{x^3} + \cdots\big) \) as \( x\to+\infty \), and confirm the \( 1/x \) term by integration by parts.

Determine the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \int_{a}^{\infty} f(t)\,e^{\,ix(t^3 - t)}\,dt \) (with \( f \) smooth, \( f\to 0 \) at \( \pm\infty \)) in the two cases \( a=-1/\sqrt3 \) and \( a=1 \), where \( t=\pm 1/\sqrt3 \) are the stationary points.

Show that \( \int_0^{\pi} e^{\,ix(t-\sin t)}\,dt \sim e^{\,i\pi/6}\big(\tfrac{6}{x}\big)^{1/3}\Gamma\!\big(\tfrac43\big) \) as \( x\to+\infty \), and explain how the answer changes if the lower limit becomes \( -\pi \).

For \( I(k)=\int_{\gamma-i\infty}^{\gamma+i\infty}\frac{e^{k(z-2\sqrt z)}}{z-c}\,dz \) (\( \gamma>1 \), cut on the negative real axis), with steepest-descent parabola \( z=1-\tau^2+2i\tau \) through the saddle \( z=1 \), find the leading asymptotics as \( k\to+\infty \) when \( c \) is real with \( c<1 \) (no pole crossed).

For the same \( I(k)=\int_{\gamma-i\infty}^{\gamma+i\infty}\frac{e^{k(z-2\sqrt z)}}{z-c}\,dz \) with \( 1<c<\gamma \), the leftward deformation onto the steepest-descent parabola now sweeps across the simple pole at \( z=c \). Write \( I(k) \) as the sum of the residue term and the saddle term as \( k\to+\infty \).

Two saddles of \( h(t)=-\tfrac12 t^2 + i\beta t \) (with \( \beta \) real) — actually one saddle — illustrate the conjugate principle differently: consider instead \( \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,\lambda(i t - t^4/4)}\,dt \), whose two relevant saddles are complex. Find the saddles, their \( h \)-values, and the leading combined behaviour as \( \lambda\to\infty \).

Derive the full two-term asymptotics \( \int_0^1 t^{-1/2}e^{\,i\lambda(t+t^2)}\,dt \sim \dfrac{c_1}{\lambda^{1/2}} + c_2\dfrac{e^{2i\lambda}}{\lambda} \) by integrating along the constant-phase paths through \( t=0 \) and \( t=1 \), determining both \( c_1 \) and \( c_2 \).

The Bessel function \( J_0(x)=\tfrac{1}{\pi}\operatorname{Re}\!\int_0^{\pi} e^{\,ix\cos\theta}\,d\theta \) has stationary points where \( \sin\theta=0 \). Identify the two stationary points in \( [0,\pi] \), combine their (half- and half-) contributions, and derive \( J_0(x)\sim\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{\pi x}}\cos\!\big(x-\tfrac{\pi}{4}\big) \).

For \( I(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{\,ix(t^3/3 - t)}}{t^2+1}\,dt \), the deformation onto the steepest-descent paths of the two real saddles \( t=\pm1 \) also encounters poles at \( t=\pm i \). Discuss whether the poles are crossed, and give the leading large-\( x \) behaviour from the two saddles, evaluating the smooth factor \( 1/(t^2+1) \) at each.

For \( I(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\,ix(t^3/3 - a^2 t)}\,dt \) with real \( a>0 \), find the two real saddles, evaluate \( \phi \) and \( \phi'' \) at each, and combine the contributions to obtain the leading asymptotics. Check it reduces to the \( a=1 \) Airy result.

am8a.questionText: To evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ixt}}{t^2+1}\,dt \) with \( x>0 \) by closing the contour, decide which half-plane the closing arc must lie in and name the single pole it then encloses.
Compute the residue of \( \dfrac{e^{ixt}}{t^2+1} \) at the simple pole \( t=i \), where \( x>0 \).

While deforming a contour, a simple pole of residue \( R \) is swept across so that it ends up encircled once anticlockwise. State the extra contribution this adds to the integral, and what changes if the encirclement is clockwise.
For the steepest-descent phase \( \varphi(z)=z-2z^{1/2} \) (principal branch, cut along \( (-\infty,0] \)), locate the saddle point and evaluate \( \varphi \) there.

The steepest-descent paths through the saddle \( z=1 \) of \( \varphi(z)=z-2z^{1/2} \) are \( z_\pm(\tau)=1-\tau^2\pm 2i\tau \) for \( \tau\ge 0 \). Writing \( z=x+iy \), eliminate \( \tau \) to find the parabola they trace.
The contribution from wrapping a contour around a branch point has the local form \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} t^{s-1}e^{-xt}\,dt \) with \( s>0 \) and \( x>0 \). Evaluate it in closed form.
Evaluate \( I(x)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ixt}}{t^2+1}\,dt \) for \( x>0 \) by closing the contour and picking up the enclosed residue.
Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ixt}}{t^2+a^2}\,dt \) for \( x>0,\ a>0 \) by deforming onto the enclosed pole.
Using even symmetry and a contour deformation, evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\cos xt}{t^2+1}\,dt \) for \( x>0 \).

For \( I(k)=\dfrac{1}{2\pi i}\displaystyle\int_{\gamma-i\infty}^{\gamma+i\infty}\frac{e^{k(z-2z^{1/2})}}{z-c}\,dz \) with \( \gamma>1 \), the Bromwich line is moved leftward onto the steepest-descent parabola through \( z=1 \). For a real pole with \( 1<c<\gamma \), find the residue contribution and its exponential rate.

For the integral of am8a-010 with a real pole at \( c<1 \), state whether deforming \( \operatorname{Re}z=\gamma \) onto the steepest-descent parabola crosses the pole, and identify the dominant contribution as \( k\to+\infty \).

Find the leading large-\( x \) behaviour of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty}\frac{t^{a-1}e^{-xt}}{1+t}\,dt \) with \( 0<a<1 \), where \( t^{a-1} \) carries a branch point at \( t=0 \), and give the next correction.
Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ixt}}{(t^2+1)(t^2+4)}\,dt \) for \( x>0 \) by deforming onto the two enclosed poles.
Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ixt}}{(t^2+1)^2}\,dt \) for \( x>0 \), noting the contour is deformed onto a double pole.

When the simple pole \( z=c \) for \( I(k) \) of am8a-010 lies on the deformed contour itself, the integral is taken as a principal value with a small semicircular indentation. State the contribution the indentation arc makes.

Across the branch cut of \( z^{1/2} \) (principal branch, cut on \( (-\infty,0] \)), evaluate the discontinuity \( z^{1/2}\big|_{\text{above}}-z^{1/2}\big|_{\text{below}} \) at \( z=-r \) with \( r>0 \).

A Hankel-type loop is wrapped tightly around the branch cut of \( t^{1/2} \) on \( (-\infty,0] \) for \( \displaystyle\oint t^{1/2}e^{-x|t|}\,dt \). Using the discontinuity, reduce the loop to a single integral over \( r=|t|\in(0,\infty) \) and evaluate it for \( x>0 \).

For the oscillatory phase \( h(t)=i(t+t^2) \), find the saddle point and the local steepest-descent direction, as needed to deform a contour onto the constant-\( \operatorname{Im}h \) path through it.

For \( \varphi(z)=z-2z^{1/2} \) (principal branch), show that the curves \( z_\pm(\tau)=1-\tau^2\pm 2i\tau \) are the steepest-descent paths through the saddle \( z=1 \) by proving \( \operatorname{Im}\varphi\equiv 0 \) and \( \operatorname{Re}\varphi \) strictly decreasing along them.

Using \( \varphi(z_\pm(\tau))=-(1+\tau^2) \), evaluate the leading saddle-point contribution to \( I(k)=\dfrac{1}{2\pi i}\displaystyle\int_{\gamma-i\infty}^{\gamma+i\infty}\frac{e^{k\varphi(z)}}{z-c}\,dz \) as \( k\to+\infty \) when no pole is crossed (\( c>\gamma \)).

For \( I(k) \) of am8a-020 with a real pole at \( 1<c<\gamma \), combine the residue picked up on deformation with the saddle term to write the full two-term asymptotics as \( k\to+\infty \), and identify the dominant term.

For \( I(k) \) of am8a-020 with a complex pole \( c=ib \), \( b \) real and \( b>2 \), determine whether deforming onto the steepest-descent parabola crosses the pole, and hence give the leading asymptotics as \( k\to+\infty \).
For \( I(k) \) of am8a-020 with real \( c \), explain how the leading asymptotics changes discontinuously as \( c \) passes through \( c=1 \), and relate this to the Stokes phenomenon.
By deforming onto the branch cut, find the full asymptotic series as \( x\to+\infty \) of \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty}\frac{t^{a-1}e^{-xt}}{1+t}\,dt \) with \( 0<a<1 \), giving the general term.

Compare two singularities at the same height. Evaluate the pole case \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ixt}}{t^2+1}\,dt \) for \( x>0 \), and give the leading large-\( x \) form that a square-root branch point at \( t=i \) (i.e. \( (t^2+1)^{-1/2} \)) would instead produce; compare the decay rates.

Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ixt}}{(t^2+1)(t^2+4)}\,dt \) for \( x>0 \), and from the result identify which pole sets the leading large-\( x \) decay after the deformation.

Deform onto the branch cut of \( t^{1/2} \) along \( (-\infty,0] \) to evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty}t^{1/2}e^{-xt}\,dt \) for \( x>0 \), and state the algebraic decay order of this branch-point contribution.

Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ixt}}{t-i\alpha}\,dt \) with \( \alpha>0,\ x>0 \) by deformation, then describe what happens as \( \alpha\to 0^+ \) (the pole approaching the real contour).

For \( \displaystyle\int_0^1 t^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda(t+t^2)}\,dt \) with \( h(t)=i(t+t^2) \), describe the constant-\( \operatorname{Im}h \) paths through the endpoints \( t=0 \) and \( t=1 \), and explain how deforming onto them yields a branch-point contribution at \( t=0 \) together with an ordinary endpoint term at \( t=1 \) as \( \lambda\to\infty \).

A Fourier integral \( I(\omega)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt \) has \( f \) with a simple pole at \( t_0=\sigma+i\beta \) (\( \beta>0 \)) and residue \( R \). For \( \omega\to+\infty \), give the leading contribution from deforming into the upper half-plane, and describe how it changes as the pole crosses the real axis (\( \beta \) passing through \( 0 \)).

The equation \( \cot x = x \) has large positive roots near \( x = n\pi \). Writing \( x_n = n\pi + \delta \) with small \( \delta \), set up a fixed-point iteration and find the first two terms of \( x_n \) for large \( n \).

Find the first three terms of the large root of \( \tan x = x \) near \( (n+\tfrac{1}{2})\pi \), continuing the iteration \( x = (n+\tfrac{1}{2})\pi - \arctan(1/x) \) past the leading correction. Let \( c = (n+\tfrac{1}{2})\pi \).

Find the first three terms in the small-\( \varepsilon \) expansion of the positive root of \( x^2 + \varepsilon x - 1 = 0 \), and verify the constant term by comparison with the exact quadratic formula.

The equation \( x = t - e^{-x} \) has a root that grows with \( t \) as \( t \to +\infty \). Find the first three terms of the asymptotic expansion of the root, where the correction is exponentially small.

Find the first three terms in the expansion of the root of \( \tan x = \dfrac{1}{x} \) near \( x = n\pi \) for large \( n \). Write \( x_n = n\pi + \delta \) with small \( \delta \), and let \( c = n\pi \).
Find the first four terms in the small-\( \varepsilon \) expansion of the regular root of \( \varepsilon x^2 + x - 1 = 0 \) near \( x = 1 \), using \( x = 1 - \varepsilon x^2 \).

The equation \( x = N + \ln x \) has a large root as \( N \to +\infty \). Find the first four terms of its expansion, keeping all contributions through order \( (\ln N)/N \) and \( (\ln N)^2 / N^2 \).

am9b.questionText: Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + \ln x = t \).
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + x^{1/2} = t \).
The solution of \( x + \ln x = t \) satisfies \( x \sim t \) as \( t \to \infty \). Find the next term in the expansion of \( x(t) \).
The solution of \( x + x^{1/2} = t \) satisfies \( x \sim t \). Find the next term in the expansion of \( x(t) \) as \( t \to \infty \).
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x^2 + \ln x = t \).
The equation \( x + x^{1/2} + 2\ln x = t + \ln t \) has a solution with \( x \to \infty \) as \( t \to \infty \). State its leading-order behaviour.
Find the first three terms in the asymptotic expansion, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + \ln x = t \).
Find the first three terms in the asymptotic expansion, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x - \ln x = t \).
Find the first three terms in the asymptotic expansion, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + 2\ln x = t \).

The equation \( x + x^{1/2} = t \) can be solved exactly. By treating it as a quadratic in \( u = x^{1/2} \), find \( x(t) \) in closed form, and hence give its three-term expansion as \( t \to \infty \).
Find the first three terms in the asymptotic expansion, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x^2 + \ln x = t \).
Find the first three terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + x^{1/2} + \ln x = t \).
Find the first three terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + 3x^{1/2} = t \), by iteration (do not use the exact quadratic solution).
Find the first three terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + x^{1/2} + 2\ln x = t + \ln t \).

Find the first two terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of the transcendental equation \( x\,e^{x} = t \). (You may quote the relation \( x = W(t) \) but should derive the asymptotics directly.)
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x\,\ln x = t \), and state the form of the first correction.
Find the first three terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + x^{1/3} + \ln x = t \).
Find the first three terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + (\ln x)^2 = t \).
Consider \( x + x^{1/2} + 2\ln x = t + \ln t \). Find the first four terms in the asymptotic expansion of \( x(t) \) as \( t \to \infty \).
For the equation \( x + x^{1/2} + 2\ln x = t + \ln t \), show that for all \( t \ge 10 \) there is a unique solution \( x(t) \), and that \( x(t) \to \infty \) as \( t \to \infty \).
Find the first four terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + 3x^{1/2} + \ln x = t + 2\ln t \).

Show that the solution of \( x + c\,x^{1/2} + b\ln x = t + a\ln t \) has the four-term expansion \( x \sim t + (a-b)\ln t - c\,t^{1/2} + \tfrac12 c^{2} \) as \( t \to \infty \), for constants \( a,b,c \).
Find the first three terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x\,e^{x} = t \) (the Lambert \( W \) function \( x = W(t) \)).
Find the first four terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + x^{1/2} + \ln x = t \).
Find the first four terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + x^{1/3} + \ln x = t \), including the term beyond \( -\ln t \).
Find the first four terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + \ln x = t \), beyond the term \( +\dfrac{\ln t}{t} \).
Find the first three terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x^{2} + x + \ln x = t \).
The equation \( x + x^{1/2} + 2\ln x = t + \ln t \) has solution \( x \sim t - t^{1/2} - \ln t + \tfrac12 \). Find the next (fifth) term in the expansion.
Find the first three terms, as \( t \to \infty \), of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x\,\ln x = t \). Express the answer using \( L = \ln t \) and \( \ell = \ln\ln t \).

The seed balance \( x + x^{1/2} + 2\ln x = t + \ln t \) gives a large root \( x_{+}(t)\sim t \). Consider instead the companion equation \( x + x^{1/2} + 2\ln x = -(t + \ln t) \). Show that for each large \( t \) it has a small root \( x_{-}(t) \to 0^{+} \), and find the leading behaviour of \( x_{-}(t) \) as \( t \to \infty \).

am9c.questionText: Consider \( \varepsilon x^{2} + x - 1 = 0 \) with \( 0 < \varepsilon \ll 1 \). By identifying the dominant balance, find the leading-order approximation to the root that remains \( O(1) \) as \( \varepsilon \to 0 \).

For \( \varepsilon x^{2} + x - 1 = 0 \) with \( 0 < \varepsilon \ll 1 \), the equation has two roots but the reduced equation has only one. Use the rescaling \( x = X/\varepsilon \) to locate the leading-order behaviour of the lost (large) root.
Find the leading-order approximation, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), to the root of \( x = 2 + \varepsilon x^{3} \) that is \( O(1) \).
As \( t \to \infty \), determine the leading-order behaviour of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + \ln x = t \).
Find the leading-order approximation, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), to the small root of \( x^{3} - x + \varepsilon = 0 \) (the root near \( x = 0 \)).

The equation \( \varepsilon x^{2} - x + 1 = 0 \) has a regular root near \( x = 1 \) and a singular root. Using the rescaling \( x = X/\varepsilon \), find the leading-order behaviour of the singular root as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \).
Find the first two terms in the asymptotic expansion, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), of the regular root of \( \varepsilon x^{2} + x - 1 = 0 \).
Find the first two terms, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), of the singular root of \( \varepsilon x^{2} + x - 1 = 0 \).
Find the first two terms, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), in the expansion of the root of \( x = 2 + \varepsilon x^{3} \) near \( x = 2 \).
Find the first two terms, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), in the expansion of the root of \( x = 1 + \varepsilon \sin x \) near \( x = 1 \).
As \( t \to \infty \), find the first two terms in the asymptotic expansion of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + \ln x = t \).
Find the first two terms, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), in the expansion of the root of \( \varepsilon x^{2} + 2x - 1 = 0 \) that stays bounded.
The cubic \( x^{3} - x + \varepsilon = 0 \) has three real roots for small \( \varepsilon > 0 \). Find the first two terms of each of the three roots as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \).
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), of the two large roots of \( \varepsilon x^{3} + x - 1 = 0 \).
As \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), find the leading-order behaviour of the (large, positive) solution of the transcendental equation \( x\, e^{x} = \dfrac{1}{\varepsilon} \).
Find the leading-order location of the large positive roots of \( \tan x = \dfrac{1}{x} \), and the first correction, as the root index \( n \to \infty \).
Find the first two terms, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), of the small positive root of \( x = \varepsilon\, e^{x} \).
Find the leading-order location of the large positive roots of \( \cos x = \varepsilon x \) (with \( 0 < \varepsilon \ll 1 \)) near \( x = (n + \tfrac12)\pi \), and the first correction.
Consider \( x + x^{1/2} + 2\ln x = t + \ln t \). Find the first four terms in the asymptotic expansion of \( x(t) \) as \( t \to \infty \).
Find the first three terms, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), of the regular root of \( \varepsilon x^{2} + x - 1 = 0 \), and verify the third term against the exact quadratic formula.
The quartic \( \varepsilon x^{4} + x^{3} - 1 = 0 \) has three \( O(1) \) roots and one large root as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \). Find the first two terms of the large root.
As \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), find the first three terms in the asymptotic expansion of the large positive root of \( x^{2} e^{-x} = \varepsilon \).

Find the first two terms, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), of the two roots of \( \varepsilon x^{2} + x - 1 = 0 \) that arise from the singular balance, using the rescaling \( x = X/\varepsilon \) and continuing one order beyond leading order. Hence state both the regular and singular roots to two terms.
As \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), find the first two terms of the large positive root of \( e^{-x} = \varepsilon x \).
The equation \( \varepsilon x^{3} - x^{2} + 1 = 0 \) has two \( O(1) \) roots and one large root as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \). Find the first two terms of the large root.
Find the first three terms, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), in the expansion of the root near \( x = 1 \) of the transcendental equation \( x\, e^{-\varepsilon x} = 1 \).
Find the first two terms, as \( n \to \infty \), of the large positive roots of \( x \tan x = 1 \).

The quadratic \( x^{2} - 2x + (1 - \varepsilon) = 0 \) has a double root at \( \varepsilon = 0 \). Find the leading-order behaviour of the splitting of the two roots for small \( \varepsilon > 0 \), and identify the appropriate local scaling.
As \( t \to \infty \), find the first three terms in the asymptotic expansion of the solution \( x(t) \) of \( x + \sqrt{x} = t \).
Find the leading-order behaviour, as \( \varepsilon \to 0^{+} \), of all three roots of \( \varepsilon^{2} x^{3} + \varepsilon x^{2} - x + 1 = 0 \), identifying every distinguished scaling.

am10a.questionText: For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = q(x)\, y \) substitute the Liouville–Green ansatz \( y = \exp\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon} S(x)\right) \) and show that the equation becomes \( (S')^{2} + \varepsilon S'' = q \).
From \( (S')^{2} + \varepsilon S'' = q \), with \( S = S_{0} + \varepsilon S_{1} + \cdots \), write down the leading-order equation and hence give \( S_{0} \) as an integral.
For the equation \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = (1 + x^{2})\, y \), compute \( S_{0} = \displaystyle\int \sqrt{q}\; dx \) (take the \( + \) sign, constant of integration omitted).
Solve the order-\( \varepsilon \) equation \( 2 S_{0}' S_{1}' + S_{0}'' = 0 \) for \( S_{1}' \) in terms of \( q \), and hence write \( S_{1} \).
Using \( S_{0} = \pm\displaystyle\int\sqrt{q}\,dx \) and \( S_{1} = -\tfrac14 \ln q \), write down the leading Liouville–Green approximation to \( y \) for \( q(x) > 0 \).
The Liouville–Green prefactor is \( q^{-1/4} \). At what points of the \( x \)-axis does this break down, and what is such a point called?

Substitute \( y = \exp\!\big(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}(S_{0} + \varepsilon S_{1} + \varepsilon^{2} S_{2} + \cdots)\big) \) into \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = q\, y \) and derive the first three equations of the Liouville–Green hierarchy.
For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = (1 + x)\, y \), find the two-term Liouville–Green approximation \( y \sim q^{-1/4}\exp\!\big(\pm\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\int\sqrt{q}\,dx\big) \).
For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = e^{x}\, y \), find the two-term Liouville–Green approximation to \( y \).
For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = -(1 + x^{2})\, y \) (so \( q < 0 \)), write the leading oscillatory Liouville–Green solution. Put \( q = -p \) with \( p = 1 + x^{2} > 0 \).
Derive the general formula \( S_{2}' = -\dfrac{(S_{1}')^{2} + S_{1}''}{2 S_{0}'} \), and hence show \( S_{2}' = \dfrac{4 q q'' - 5(q')^{2}}{32\, q^{5/2}} \) for the \( + \) branch.
For \( q(x) = e^{x} \), use \( S_{2}' = \dfrac{4qq''-5(q')^{2}}{32 q^{5/2}} \) to find \( S_{2}' \) and \( S_{2} \) (constant omitted).
For \( q(x) = x^{2} \) on \( x > 0 \) (so \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = x^{2} y \)), find \( S_{0} \), \( S_{1} \) and the leading LG approximation to \( y \).

The Liouville–Green expansion orders as \( S_{0} \gg \varepsilon S_{1} \gg \varepsilon^{2} S_{2} \). Show that the validity of the leading term requires \( \varepsilon \left| \dfrac{q'}{q^{3/2}} \right| \ll 1 \).

For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = x\, y \) (\( x > 0 \)), compute the validity quantity \( \varepsilon\left|q'/q^{3/2}\right| \) and deduce how close to the turning point \( x=0 \) the LG approximation remains valid.
For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = (1+x)\, y \), use \( S_{2}' = \dfrac{4qq''-5(q')^{2}}{32 q^{5/2}} \) to find \( S_{2} \) (constant omitted).
Show that for constant \( q = k > 0 \) the Liouville–Green series terminates: find \( S_{0}, S_{1}, S_{2} \) and confirm the LG form is exact.
Explain why \( S_{1} = -\tfrac14 \ln q \) is the same for both choices of sign in \( S_{0}' = \pm\sqrt{q} \), and state the consequence for the prefactor of the two LG solutions.

For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = (1 + x^{2})\, y \), compute the three-term Liouville–Green exponent \( \tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}S_{0} + S_{1} + \varepsilon S_{2} \), giving \( S_{0} \), \( S_{1} \) and \( S_{2} \) explicitly (take the \( + \) branch, constants omitted).

For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = x\, y \) on \( x>0 \), find the three-term LG approximation \( y \sim q^{-1/4}\exp\!\big(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}S_{0} + \varepsilon S_{2}\big) \), i.e. compute \( S_{0} \) and \( S_{2} \) for \( q=x \).

Show that \( S_{2}' = \dfrac{4qq''-5(q')^{2}}{32 q^{5/2}} \) can be written as \( S_{2}' = \dfrac{1}{8}\dfrac{q''}{q^{3/2}} - \dfrac{5}{32}\dfrac{(q')^{2}}{q^{5/2}} \), and confirm it gives \( S_{2}'\equiv0 \) when \( q \) is constant.
For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = (1+x)\,y \), write the full three-term LG solution \( y \sim q^{-1/4}\exp\!\big(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}S_{0}+\varepsilon S_{2}\big) \) on the decaying branch.
For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = e^{x}\, y \), assemble the full three-term LG approximation \( y \sim q^{-1/4}\exp\!\big(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}S_{0} + \varepsilon S_{2}\big) \) on the growing branch.

Substitute the LG amplitude form \( y = q^{-1/4} u \) into \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = q y \) to obtain \( \varepsilon^{2}\big(u'' - \tfrac{q'}{2q}u'\big) = \big(q + \varepsilon^{2} R\big) u \), and find the remainder \( R \) in terms of \( q \). Hence relate \( R \) to the next LG correction \( S_{2} \).
For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = (1 - x^{2})\, y \) on \( -1 < x < 1 \) (where \( q>0 \)), find the leading LG solution and state where the approximation fails.

For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = x^{2}\, y \) on \( x>0 \), compute \( S_{2} \) and write the three-term LG approximation \( y \sim q^{-1/4}\exp\!\big(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}S_{0}+\varepsilon S_{2}\big) \) on the growing branch.

For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = -\omega^{2}(x)\, y \) with \( \omega^{2}>0 \), derive the oscillatory LG solution and show the \( O(\varepsilon) \) phase correction comes from \( S_{2} \), giving the leading frequency and amplitude.

The general LG solution is \( y = q^{-1/4}\big(c_{+}e^{S_{0}/\varepsilon} + c_{-}e^{-S_{0}/\varepsilon}\big)(1 + O(\varepsilon)) \). For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = (1+x)\,y \), find the constants in the relative correction so that the bracket reads \( 1 + \varepsilon S_{2} + \cdots \) on each branch, giving the two values of \( S_{2} \).
For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = e^{2x}\, y \), compute \( S_{0}, S_{1}, S_{2} \) and assemble the three-term LG approximation on the decaying branch.

For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = x\, y \) near the turning point \( x=0 \), introduce the inner variable \( X = x/\varepsilon^{2/3} \), show the equation becomes \( \dfrac{d^{2}Y}{dX^{2}} = X\,Y \) (Airy's equation), and confirm \( \varepsilon^{2/3} \) is the breakdown scale predicted by LG.

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 01
am10b.questionText: Write down the leading-order asymptotic form of \( \mathrm{Ai}(x) \) as \( x \to +\infty \), stating the prefactor and the exponential decay rate.

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 02
am10b.questionText: Write down the leading-order oscillatory asymptotic form of \( \mathrm{Ai}(-x) \) as \( x \to +\infty \), including the \( \tfrac{\pi}{4} \) phase.

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 03

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 04

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 05

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 06

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 07
am10b.questionText: Write down the two-term large-\( x \) asymptotic expansion of \( \mathrm{Ai}(x) \), including the first algebraic correction inside the bracket.

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 08
am10b.questionText: By substituting \( \xi = (q'(a)/\varepsilon^{2})^{1/3}(x - a) \) into \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = q'(a)(x - a)\,y \), show that the local equation reduces to the Airy equation \( W'' = \xi\,W \).

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 09
am10b.questionText: For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = q(x)\,y \) with a simple turning point at \( x = a \), state the connection formula linking the Liouville–Green solution that decays as \( x \to +\infty \) on the forbidden side \( (x > a) \) to the oscillatory solution on the allowed side \( (x < a) \).

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 10

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 11

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 13

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 19

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 21

For \( y'' + \lambda(1 - x)\,y = 0 \) on \( x < 1 \) with \( y \to 0 \) as \( x \to +\infty \) (past the turning point \( x = 1 \)) and \( y(0) = 0 \), use the connection formula to derive the large-\( \lambda \) quantisation condition for the allowed-region phase.

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 22

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 25
am10b.questionText: For \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = (x^{2} - 1)\,y \) there are turning points at \( x = \pm 1 \). Near the simple turning point \( x = 1 \), find the appropriate local Airy variable \( \xi \) (note \( q'(1) = 2 \)).

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 26
am10b.questionText: Compare the two-term Airy asymptotic with the leading term at \( x = 2 \): compute \( \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}} x^{-1/4} e^{-\frac{2}{3} x^{3/2}} \) and its correction factor \( (1 - \tfrac{5}{48} x^{-3/2}) \) at \( x = 2 \), and state which is closer to the true \( \mathrm{Ai}(2) = 0.0349241 \). Give the corrected estimate to 4 decimal places (\( \times 10^{-2} \)).

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 27
am10b.questionText: A particle in a linear potential is governed by \( -\psi'' + x\,\psi = E\,\psi \) on \( x \ge 0 \) with \( \psi(0) = 0 \) and \( \psi \to 0 \) as \( x \to +\infty \). Express the exact eigenfunctions in terms of \( \mathrm{Ai} \), and give the quantisation condition for \( E \).

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 28
am10b.questionText: From the relation \( \mathrm{Ai}(-x) \sim \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} x^{-1/4} \sin(\tfrac{2}{3} x^{3/2} + \tfrac{\pi}{4}) \), find the leading-order spacing \( a_{s+1} - a_{s} \) between consecutive large zeros of \( \mathrm{Ai}(-x) \) as \( s \to \infty \).

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 29
am10b.questionText: Two simple turning points bound a classically allowed well in \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = q(x)\,y \) (with \( q < 0 \) between \( x = a \) and \( x = b \), \( q > 0 \) outside). Applying the \( -\tfrac{\pi}{4} \) connection at each end, derive the Bohr–Sommerfeld quantisation condition.

am10b.topicTitle: Airy asymptotics, turning points & connection formulae 30
am10b.questionText: Apply the Bohr–Sommerfeld condition \( \tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{-q}\,dt = (n + \tfrac12)\pi \) to the harmonic-oscillator-type problem \( \varepsilon^{2} y'' = (x^{2} - E)\,y \) (turning points \( x = \pm\sqrt{E} \)), and find the quantised energies \( E_{n} \).

am10c.questionText: For \( y'' + p\,y' + r\,y = 0 \) the substitution \( y = w\,\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12\int p\,dx\right) \) removes the first-derivative term. State the resulting equation for \( w \) and the invariant \( I \).
Compute the invariant \( I \) of \( y'' + 2x\,y' + x^{2}\,y = 0 \).
Reduce the spherical-Bessel equation \( y'' + \dfrac{2}{x}y' + \left(1 - \dfrac{\ell(\ell+1)}{x^{2}}\right)y = 0 \) to normal form, giving the substitution and the resulting equation for \( w \).

An ODE \( y'' + P(t)\,y_{t} + R(t)\,y = 0 \) has a point \( t = 0 \). State the pole-order test that decides whether \( t = 0 \) is an ordinary point, a regular singular point, or an irregular singular point.
Compute the invariant \( I \) of the Bessel equation \( y'' + \dfrac{1}{x}y' + \left(1 - \dfrac{\nu^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)y = 0 \).
Write the normal form \( w'' + I\,w = 0 \) in the equivalent shape \( W'' = Q(z)W \), and express \( Q \) in terms of \( p \) and \( r \).
Reduce the Bessel equation \( y'' + \dfrac{1}{x}y' + \left(1 - \dfrac{\nu^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)y = 0 \) to normal form and hence find the leading LG (large-\( x \)) form of \( y \).
Classify the point \( z = \infty \) for the oscillator \( y'' + y = 0 \) by substituting \( z = 1/t \) and inspecting the transformed coefficients at \( t = 0 \).
Classify \( z = \infty \) for the Bessel equation \( y'' + \dfrac{1}{z}y' + \left(1 - \dfrac{\nu^{2}}{z^{2}}\right)y = 0 \) using \( z = 1/t \).

For the constant-coefficient damped equation \( y'' + 2b\,y' + (b^{2} + \omega_{0}^{2})\,y = 0 \) (\( b,\omega_{0} \) constants), find the invariant and verify that the normal form recovers the exact solution.

Reduce the spherical-Bessel equation \( y'' + \dfrac{2}{x}y' + \left(1 - \dfrac{\ell(\ell+1)}{x^{2}}\right)y = 0 \) to normal form, and for \( \ell = 1 \) compare the LG leading form with the exact solution \( j_{1}(x) = \dfrac{\sin x}{x^{2}} - \dfrac{\cos x}{x} \).
Find the invariant of the modified Bessel equation \( y'' + \dfrac{1}{x}y' - \left(1 + \dfrac{\nu^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)y = 0 \), and hence give the two LG leading forms as \( x \to \infty \).
Reduce \( y'' + \dfrac{2}{x}y' + y = 0 \) to normal form, solve it exactly, and confirm that \( y = \dfrac{\cos x}{x} \) and \( y = \dfrac{\sin x}{x} \) are solutions.
Classify \( z = \infty \) for the Airy equation \( y'' - z\,y = 0 \) using \( z = 1/t \).
Distinguish a regular from an irregular singular point at \( x = 0 \) for the pair (a) \( y'' + \dfrac{1}{x}y' + \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}y = 0 \); (b) \( y'' + \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}y' + \dfrac{1}{x}y = 0 \).
Reduce the Cauchy–Euler equation \( y'' + \dfrac{a}{x}y' + \dfrac{b}{x^{2}}y = 0 \) (\( a,b \) constants) to normal form and show the invariant has the form \( I = c/x^{2} \). Find \( c \).

The Weber (parabolic-cylinder) equation is \( y'' + \left(\nu + \tfrac12 - \tfrac14 x^{2}\right)y = 0 \). It is already in normal form. Use LG/WKB to give the leading large-\( x \) exponential factor.
Reduce the Coulomb-wave equation \( y'' + \left(1 - \dfrac{2\eta}{x} - \dfrac{\ell(\ell+1)}{x^{2}}\right)y = 0 \) and state the leading LG form as \( x \to \infty \).
Reduce the Hermite equation \( y'' - 2x\,y' + 2n\,y = 0 \) to normal form, identify the resulting equation, and state the exponential factor governing the large-\( x \) behaviour.

For the normal form \( W'' = Q(z)W \) with \( Q \sim z^{m} \) as \( z \to \infty \), find the leading exponential factor of the solutions and hence the growth exponent ("rank") of the irregular singular point at \( \infty \).
Classify \( z = \infty \) for the Hermite equation \( y'' - 2z\,y' + 2n\,y = 0 \) via \( z = 1/t \), giving the pole orders of the transformed coefficients.
Reduce \( y'' + 2\,y' + \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)y = 0 \) to normal form, solve the normal form exactly (Cauchy–Euler), and write the general solution \( y(x) \).

For the Airy equation \( y'' = z\,y \) (already in normal form), use LG to obtain the leading recessive form as \( z \to +\infty \) and compare numerically with \( \mathrm{Ai}(z) \sim \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}z^{-1/4}e^{-\frac23 z^{3/2}} \).
Reduce the Legendre equation in the angular variable \( y'' + \cot\theta\,y' + \lambda\,y = 0 \) to normal form, and state the invariant.
Classify \( z = \infty \) for \( y'' + \dfrac{4}{z}y' + \left(1 - \dfrac{m^{2}}{z^{2}}\right)y = 0 \), then reduce to normal form and give the leading LG amplitude exponent.
Reduce \( y'' + \dfrac{1}{x}y' - \left(k^{2} + \dfrac{\nu^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)y = 0 \) (with \( k > 0 \) constant) to normal form, and give the two leading LG forms as \( x \to \infty \).
Show that the invariant \( I \) is unchanged under the gauge transformation \( y \mapsto \tilde{y} = f(x)\,y \), explaining why \( I \) (not \( p \) or \( r \)) characterises the equation.
Determine the number of formal exponential solutions and their leading factors at \( z = \infty \) for \( W'' = (z^{4} + z)\,W \), and state the rank of the irregular point.
Reduce \( y'' + (\tan x)\,y' + y = 0 \) to normal form, giving the substitution and the invariant \( I \). Hence write the normal-form equation.

am10d.questionText: State the Bohr–Sommerfeld quantisation condition for a particle of mass \( m \) and energy \( E \) trapped between two soft (linear) turning points \( x_{1} < x_{2} \) of a potential \( V(x) \), and identify the turning points.
For the harmonic oscillator \( V = \tfrac12 m\omega^{2}x^{2} \) and energy \( E \), find the two classical turning points.

A particle of mass \( m \) and energy \( E \) meets a rectangular barrier of height \( V_{0} > E \) and width \( L \). Write down the WKB tunnelling exponent \( \gamma \) defined by \( T \approx e^{-2\gamma} \), where \( \gamma = \tfrac1\hbar\int \sqrt{2m(V-E)}\,dx \) over the forbidden region.

For the harmonic oscillator the action integral evaluates to \( \displaystyle\int_{x_{1}}^{x_{2}} \sqrt{2m\left(E-\tfrac12 m\omega^{2}x^{2}\right)}\,dx = \dfrac{\pi E}{\omega} \). Apply Bohr–Sommerfeld to find the energy levels \( E_{n} \).

A particle of mass \( m \) and energy \( E \) tunnels through a rectangular barrier of height \( V_{0} = 4\,\text{(units)} \), with \( E = 1 \), width \( L = 0.8 \), taking \( m = \hbar = 1 \). Compute the tunnelling exponent \( \gamma \) and hence \( 2\gamma \).

Explain why the WKB quantisation of an infinite square well of width \( L \) (hard walls at both ends) uses the phase index that gives \( N = 1,2,3,\dots \) rather than \( (n+\tfrac12) \). State the resulting condition on \( \sqrt{2mE}\,L \).

Evaluate the harmonic-oscillator action \( \displaystyle\int_{-x_{t}}^{x_{t}} \sqrt{2m\left(E-\tfrac12 m\omega^{2}x^{2}\right)}\,dx \) from scratch (with \( x_{t}=\sqrt{2E/(m\omega^{2})} \)) and hence derive \( E_{n} \).

A ball of mass \( m \) bounces under gravity above a hard floor: \( V = Fx \) for \( x>0 \) and \( V=\infty \) for \( x<0 \). Using one soft turning point and one hard wall, find the quantised energies \( E_{n} \).
Find the WKB energy levels of the symmetric linear well \( V = F|x| \) (two soft turning points at \( x=\pm E/F \)).
Derive the WKB spectrum of the infinite square well \( V=0 \) for \( 0<x<L \), \( V=\infty \) otherwise, and confirm it is exact.
A half-harmonic oscillator has \( V=\tfrac12 m\omega^{2}x^{2} \) for \( x>0 \) and a hard wall \( V=\infty \) at \( x=0 \). Find its WKB energy levels.

Show, by reducing the action integral to a standard form, that the quartic well \( V=\alpha x^{4} \) has \( \displaystyle\int_{-x_{t}}^{x_{t}}\sqrt{2m(E-\alpha x^{4})}\,dx = 2\sqrt{2mE}\,(E/\alpha)^{1/4}\,C \) with \( C=\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-u^{4}}\,du \). Evaluate \( C \) in terms of \( \Gamma \)-functions.

Using the result \( \displaystyle\int_{-x_{t}}^{x_{t}}\sqrt{2m(E-\alpha x^{4})}\,dx = 2C\sqrt{2m}\,\alpha^{-1/4}E^{3/4} \) with \( C\approx 0.8740 \), apply Bohr–Sommerfeld to show \( E_{n}\propto (n+\tfrac12)^{4/3} \) and give the constant.

Evaluate the tunnelling exponent \( \gamma = \tfrac1\hbar\int_{-x_{*}}^{x_{*}}\sqrt{2m(V-E)}\,dx \) for the parabolic barrier \( V=V_{0}(1-x^{2}/a^{2}) \), where \( \pm x_{*} \) are the points with \( V=E \).
For field emission the barrier is triangular: \( V(x)=V_{0}-Fx \) for \( x>0 \), with electron energy \( E<V_{0} \). Find the Fowler–Nordheim tunnelling exponent \( \gamma \).

Explain, from the turning-point connection formula, why each soft turning point contributes \( -\tfrac{\pi}{4} \) to the phase, and hence why a well with two soft turning points obeys \( \oint p\,dx = (n+\tfrac12)\,2\pi\hbar \).
A metastable state of frequency \( \omega \) sits behind a barrier with WKB exponent \( \gamma \). Estimate its decay rate \( \Gamma \) and lifetime \( \tau \) using the attempt-frequency picture.
Compute the quartic-well WKB ground-state energy for \( V=x^{4} \) (taking \( m=\hbar=1 \), \( \alpha=1 \)) and compare with the accurate value \( E_{0}^{\text{exact}}\approx 0.6680 \).

For the quartic well \( V=\alpha x^{4} \), derive the complete WKB spectrum \( E_{n} \) in closed form including the \( \Gamma \)-function constant, and verify the \( (n+\tfrac12)^{4/3} \) law numerically.

For the Pöschl–Teller well \( V=-\dfrac{\hbar^{2}\alpha^{2}\lambda(\lambda-1)}{2m}\,\operatorname{sech}^{2}(\alpha x) \) it is known that \( \dfrac1\hbar\int\sqrt{2m(E-V)}\,dx = \pi\!\left[\sqrt{\lambda(\lambda-1)}-\dfrac{\sqrt{2m|E|}}{\hbar\alpha}\right] \) for a bound state \( E=-|E| \). Derive the WKB bound-state energies.

The exact Pöschl–Teller spectrum is \( E_{n}^{\text{exact}}=-\dfrac{\hbar^{2}\alpha^{2}}{2m}(\lambda-1-n)^{2} \). Compare it with the WKB result of the previous question and identify the source of the discrepancy.

For the double-power well \( V=\tfrac12 m\omega^{2}x^{2}+\lambda x^{4} \) with small \( \lambda \), find the leading WKB energy and the first-order shift in \( \lambda \), using the action \( S(E)=\int\sqrt{2m(E-V)}\,dx \).

Derive the Gamow factor for alpha decay: a particle of energy \( E>0 \) escaping a Coulomb tail \( V(r)=B/r \) (for \( r>R \)), with outer turning point \( r_{b}=B/E \). Find \( \gamma = \tfrac1\hbar\int_{R}^{r_{b}}\sqrt{2m(B/r-E)}\,dr \) in closed form.

A symmetric double well has barrier exponent \( \gamma \) between the two minima, each of frequency \( \omega \). Estimate the tunnel splitting \( \Delta E \) between the symmetric and antisymmetric ground states.
Derive the energy levels of the power-law well \( V=\beta|x|^{s} \) (with \( s>0 \)) and show \( E_{n}\propto (n+\tfrac12)^{2s/(s+2)} \). Check the cases \( s=2 \) and \( s=4 \).
A particle tunnels through the smooth barrier \( V(x)=V_{0}\,\operatorname{sech}^{2}(x/a) \) at energy \( E<V_{0} \). Find the tunnelling exponent \( \gamma \) in closed form.

For the relativistic-like dispersion mock potential, consider the well \( V=\tfrac12 m\omega^{2}x^{2} \) but now find the number of bound states \( N \) below a cut-off energy \( E_{\max} \) using the WKB density-of-states formula \( N\approx \tfrac{1}{\pi\hbar}\int_{x_{1}}^{x_{2}}\sqrt{2m(E_{\max}-V)}\,dx \).

Estimate the tunnelling rate out of the cubic metastable well \( V=\tfrac12 m\omega^{2}x^{2}-bx^{3} \) (\( b>0 \)) for a particle near the bottom (\( E\approx \tfrac12\hbar\omega \)), expressing the answer through the barrier exponent \( \gamma \) and attempt frequency.

Compute the WKB ground-state energy of the linear well \( V=F|x| \) (with \( m=F=\hbar=1 \)) and compare with the exact value, which is set by the first zero of the derivative of the Airy function, \( E_{0}^{\text{exact}}\approx 0.8086 \).

A parabolic barrier near its top, \( V(x)=V_{0}-\tfrac12 m\Omega^{2}x^{2} \), gives the near-exact transmission \( T=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{2\gamma}} \) with \( \gamma=\dfrac{\pi(V_{0}-E)}{\hbar\Omega} \). Verify the WKB exponent \( 2\gamma \) reproduces the leading \( e^{-2\gamma} \) and discuss \( E=V_{0} \).

(b) Find the cost of a 12 km journey.

(c) A journey costs £14. How far did the taxi travel?

(a) Write an equation for the height \( h \) (in cm) after \( t \) hours.

(b) How tall is the candle after 6 hours?

(c) After how many hours does the candle burn out (reach height 0)?

Two phone contracts are available:

- Contract A: £10 per month plus 5p per minute of calls.
- Contract B: £25 per month with unlimited calls.

(a) Write equations for the monthly cost \( C_A \) and \( C_B \) in terms of minutes used \( m \).

(b) Find the number of minutes at which both contracts cost the same.

(c) Which contract is cheaper if you use 400 minutes per month?

Find the equation of the line passing through \( (2, 7) \) and \( (6, 3) \).
Find the gradient of the line \( 5x + 2y - 8 = 0 \).
A line has gradient \( \frac{2}{3} \) and passes through \( (-3, 1) \). Find where it crosses the y-axis.
Find the equation of the line through \( (0, -2) \) and \( (4, 6) \). Give your answer in the form \( ax + by + c = 0 \).
Find the midpoint of \( A(3, -1) \) and \( B(7, 5) \).
Find the distance between \( P(1, 3) \) and \( Q(4, 7) \).
The line \( L \) passes through \( (1, 4) \) and is parallel to \( y = 2x - 3 \). Find the equation of \( L \).
The line \( L \) passes through \( (3, 1) \) and is perpendicular to \( y = \frac{1}{2}x + 5 \). Find the equation of \( L \).
Find where the lines \( y = 3x - 1 \) and \( y = -x + 7 \) intersect.

Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining \( A(2, 4) \) and \( B(6, 0) \).

Find the value of \( k \) if the line through \( (2, 3) \) and \( (k, 7) \) has gradient \( \frac{4}{3} \).

Find the equation of the line through \( (-2, 5) \) and \( (4, -1) \) in the form \( ax + by + c = 0 \).
Find the gradient of a line perpendicular to \( 4x - 3y + 12 = 0 \).

A triangle has vertices \( A(0, 0) \), \( B(6, 0) \) and \( C(3, 4) \). Find the equation of the median from \( C \).

Find the distance from the origin to the line \( 3x + 4y - 10 = 0 \).
Find the equation of the line with x-intercept 4 and y-intercept -3.
Determine whether the lines \( 2x + 3y = 6 \) and \( 4x + 6y = 5 \) are parallel, perpendicular, or neither.

A line passes through \( (a, 2a) \) and \( (3a, 5a) \). Find the equation of the line.
Find the equation of the line through \( (5, -2) \) that makes an angle of \( 45° \) with the positive x-axis.

Find the shortest distance from \( P(4, 1) \) to the line \( y = 2x + 3 \).

\( AB \) has \( A = (1, 4) \) and \( B = (7, -2) \). The point \( P \) lies on \( AB \) such that \( AP = 2 \). Find \( P \).

CG3.questionText:
State which of the following lines are parallel to \( y = 4x - 3 \).

a) \( 2y = 8x + 5 \)
b) \( y - 4x + 1 = 0 \)
c) \( 8y + 32x = 1 \)
d) \( \frac{1}{2}(y + 2) = 2x \)
e) \( -12y - 3 = -48x \)
f) \( 4y = x \)

a) \( y = 3x + 1 \) and \( y = 3x - 5 \)
b) \( y = 2x + 4 \) and \( y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x + 1 \)
c) \( y = 5x - 2 \) and \( y = -5x + 2 \)
d) \( 2x - 4y + 3 = 0 \) and \( x - 2y - 1 = 0 \)

a) \( 3x + y - 4 = 0 \) and \( 6x + 2y + 1 = 0 \)
b) \( 4x - y + 2 = 0 \) and \( x + 4y - 8 = 0 \)
c) \( 2x + 5y - 10 = 0 \) and \( 5x - 2y + 3 = 0 \)

Find the equation of the line parallel to \( y = -2x + 5 \) passing through \( (3, 1) \). Give your answer in the form \( ax + by + c = 0 \).
Line \( L \) passes through \( (0, 5) \) and is parallel to \( 3x - 6y + 4 = 0 \). Find the equation of \( L \) in the form \( y = mx + c \).
Find the equation of the line parallel to \( 5x + 2y - 6 = 0 \) that passes through \( (4, -3) \). Give your answer in the form \( ax + by + c = 0 \), where \( a \), \( b \) and \( c \) are integers.
Find the equation of the line parallel to \( 4x - 3y + 9 = 0 \) passing through \( (-3, 2) \). Give your answer in the form \( ax + by + c = 0 \).

Find the equation of the line parallel to \( \dfrac{x}{3} + \dfrac{y}{2} = 1 \) that passes through \( (6, 5) \). Give your answer in the form \( ax + by + c = 0 \).
Two parallel lines each have gradient \( \frac{3}{2} \). One passes through \( (2, 4) \) and the other through \( (6, 3) \). Find the equations of both lines in the form \( ax + by + c = 0 \).
Find the equation of the line perpendicular to \( y = 2x - 1 \) that passes through \( (4, 3) \). Give your answer in the form \( y = mx + c \).

Find the equation of the line perpendicular to \( 3x + 5y - 2 = 0 \) that passes through \( (-5, 4) \). Give your answer in the form \( ax + by + c = 0 \).
Find the equation of the line perpendicular to \( 2x + 6y - 3 = 0 \) passing through \( (3, -4) \). Give your answer in the form \( y = mx + c \).
Line \( M \) is perpendicular to the line joining \( A(1, 5) \) and \( B(4, 11) \), and passes through the midpoint of \( AB \). Find the equation of \( M \) in the form \( y = mx + c \).
Find the value of \( k \) such that the line \( kx - 2y + 5 = 0 \) is perpendicular to \( y = 4x - 1 \).
Find the equation of the line that is perpendicular to \( 6x - 4y + 1 = 0 \) and passes through the point \( (3, 7) \). Give your answer in the form \( ax + by + c = 0 \).
Line \( Q \) passes through \( (a, b) \) and is perpendicular to \( 5x - 2y = 10 \). Find an equation for \( Q \) in terms of \( a \) and \( b \).

(a) Find the gradients of all four sides.

(b) Show that \( ABCD \) is a rectangle.

(b) Find the coordinates of the point where \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) intersect.

(c) Find the exact distance between the point \( (4, 1) \) and the intersection point.
