Test at the 5% significance level whether the proportion of premium items differs from 30%. You are given \(P(X \ge 10) = 0.0480\) where \(X \sim B(20, 0.3)\).

A school claims that 15% of its students achieve an A* grade. This year, 7 out of 20 students achieve an A*. Test at the 5% significance level whether the proportion achieving A* has increased. You are given \(P(X \ge 7) = 0.0219\) where \(X \sim B(20, 0.15)\).

A bakery believes that 20% of loaves are undercooked. After adjusting the oven, 8 out of 15 loaves are undercooked. Test at the 1% significance level whether the proportion of undercooked loaves has increased. You are given \(P(X \ge 8) = 0.0042\) where \(X \sim B(15, 0.2)\).

A survey suggests that 45% of adults exercise regularly. A health authority surveys 20 adults in a particular town and finds that 5 exercise regularly. Test at the 5% significance level whether the proportion who exercise regularly in this town is lower than the national figure. You are given \(P(X \le 5) = 0.0553\) where \(X \sim B(20, 0.45)\). State the p-value of the test.

A website claims that 25% of visitors make a purchase. After a redesign, 9 out of 20 visitors make a purchase. Test at the 5% significance level whether the redesign has increased the purchase rate. You are given \(P(X \ge 9) = 0.0409\) where \(X \sim B(20, 0.25)\).

A supermarket claims that 40% of customers use self-checkout. In a random sample of 15 customers, 2 use self-checkout. Test at the 5% significance level whether the proportion using self-checkout differs from 40%. You are given \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0271\) where \(X \sim B(15, 0.4)\).

A charity claims that 35% of people donate when asked. A fundraiser approaches 18 people and 3 donate. Test at the 5% significance level whether the donation rate is lower than claimed. You are given \(P(X \le 3) = 0.0783\) where \(X \sim B(18, 0.35)\).

An insurance company states that 10% of claims are fraudulent. An investigator examines 20 claims and finds that 5 are fraudulent. Test at the 5% significance level whether the fraud rate has increased. You are given \(P(X \ge 5) = 0.0432\) where \(X \sim B(20, 0.1)\).

A dice manufacturer claims their dice are fair, with \(P(6) = \frac{1}{6}\). A die is rolled 18 times and a 6 appears 7 times. Test at the 5% significance level whether the die is biased with respect to the probability of rolling a 6. You are given \(P(X \ge 7) = 0.0206\) where \(X \sim B(18, \frac{1}{6})\).

A phone company claims that 90% of calls are connected on the first attempt. A customer makes 15 calls and only 11 connect on the first attempt. Test at the 5% significance level whether the connection rate is lower than claimed. You are given \(P(X \le 11) = 0.0556\) where \(X \sim B(15, 0.9)\).

A restaurant claims that 20% of meals are returned by customers. After changing supplier, 8 out of 18 meals are returned. Test at the 5% significance level whether the return rate has increased. You are given \(P(X \ge 8) = 0.0163\) where \(X \sim B(18, 0.2)\). Would the conclusion change at the 1% significance level?

A manufacturer claims that 75% of its products pass quality control. In a sample of 12 products, 7 pass. Test at the 5% significance level whether the pass rate is lower than claimed. You are given \(P(X \le 7) = 0.1576\) where \(X \sim B(12, 0.75)\).

A company claims that 50% of job applicants are shortlisted. In a sample of 16 applicants, 12 are shortlisted. Test at the 5% significance level whether the shortlisting rate differs from 50%. You are given \(P(X \ge 12) = 0.0384\) where \(X \sim B(16, 0.5)\). State the p-value of the test.

A politician claims that 60% of voters support a policy. A journalist surveys 20 voters and finds that 8 support the policy. (a) State suitable hypotheses to test whether the level of support is lower than claimed. (b) You are given \(P(X \le 8) = 0.0565\) where \(X \sim B(20, 0.6)\). Carry out the test at the 5% significance level. (c) State the conclusion at the 10% significance level. (d) Explain why the conclusions differ.

A machine is set to produce 35% of items in colour A and 65% in colour B. After maintenance, a sample of 20 items contains 12 in colour A. Test at the 5% significance level whether the proportion of colour A items has changed. You are given \(P(X \ge 12) = 0.0196\) and \(P(X \le 3) = 0.0444\) where \(X \sim B(20, 0.35)\).

A researcher conducts a one-tailed hypothesis test for a binomial parameter. The probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the observed value is 0.038. (a) State the conclusion at the 5% significance level. (b) State the conclusion at the 1% significance level. (c) Explain the meaning of 'the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the observed value'.

A doctor claims that a treatment is effective for 55% of patients. After modifying the dosage, a trial of 18 patients is conducted and 14 respond positively. (a) Explain whether a one-tailed or two-tailed test is appropriate if the doctor wants to know whether the effectiveness has changed. (b) Carry out the appropriate test at the 5% significance level. You are given \(P(X \ge 14) = 0.0338\) where \(X \sim B(18, 0.55)\).

A factory produces bolts where historically 15% are oversized. A new machine is installed and a sample of 20 bolts is tested. (a) State hypotheses to test whether the proportion of oversized bolts has changed. (b) If 0 bolts are oversized, carry out the test at the 5% level. You are given \(P(X = 0) = 0.0388\) where \(X \sim B(20, 0.15)\). (c) Would the conclusion change at the 10% level?

Let \(X \sim B(8, 0.5)\). (a) Show that \(P(X \ge 7) = 0.03516\) (to 5 significant figures). (b) A coin is tossed 8 times and 7 heads are obtained. Using part (a), test at the 5% significance level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

A health authority claims that 30% of adults in a region are overweight. A researcher surveys 20 adults and finds 10 are overweight. (a) Test at the 5% significance level whether the proportion of overweight adults has increased. You are given \(P(X \ge 10) = 0.0480\) where \(X \sim B(20, 0.3)\). (b) State the conclusion at the 1% level.

A company claims that 20% of emails it sends are opened by recipients. In a sample of 15 emails, 7 are opened. (a) Show that \(P(X \ge 7) = 0.0181\) (to 3 significant figures) where \(X \sim B(15, 0.2)\). You may use: \(P(X \le 6) = 0.9819\). (b) Test at the 5% significance level whether the open rate has increased.

A seed packet states that 85% of seeds germinate. A gardener plants 16 seeds and only 10 germinate. (a) State suitable hypotheses to test whether the germination rate is lower than stated. (b) Calculate \(P(X \le 10)\) where \(X \sim B(16, 0.85)\). You are given \(P(X \le 10) = 0.0235\). (c) Carry out the test at the 5% level. (d) Carry out the test at the 1% level. (e) Comment on the difference.

A bus company claims that 40% of buses arrive on time. A commuter records 20 bus arrivals and finds that 3 arrive on time. (a) Test at the 5% significance level whether the proportion of on-time buses differs from 40%. You are given \(P(X \le 3) = 0.0160\) where \(X \sim B(20, 0.4)\). (b) State the p-value of this two-tailed test.

Let \(X \sim B(10, 0.3)\). (a) Show that \(P(X = 0) = 0.0282\) to 3 significant figures. (b) Show that \(P(X \le 0) = 0.0282\) and hence determine whether observing \(X = 0\) would lead to rejection of \(H_0: p = 0.3\) in favour of \(H_1: p < 0.3\) at the 5% significance level. (c) Find \(P(X \le 1)\), given \(P(X = 1) = 0.1211\), and determine whether observing \(X = 1\) would lead to rejection of \(H_0\) at the 5% level.

A manufacturer claims that 50% of customers prefer product A over product B. A market researcher surveys 18 customers and finds that 13 prefer product A. (a) State hypotheses to test whether the preference differs from 50%. (b) You are given \(P(X \ge 13) = 0.0481\) where \(X \sim B(18, 0.5)\). Carry out the test at the 10% significance level. (c) Carry out the test at the 5% significance level. (d) A colleague argues that a one-tailed test should be used. If \(H_1: p > 0.5\), state the conclusion at the 5% level and explain why it differs from part (c).

y1ht3.questionText: Define what is meant by a critical region in the context of a hypothesis test.
Define what is meant by a critical value in the context of a hypothesis test.

A test uses \(X \sim B(15, p)\) with \(H_0: p = 0.4\) and \(H_1: p < 0.4\) at the 5% significance level. Given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0271\) and \(P(X \le 3) = 0.0905\) under \(H_0\), state the critical region for this test.

A test uses \(X \sim B(20, p)\) with \(H_0: p = 0.5\) and \(H_1: p < 0.5\) at the 5% significance level. Given that \(P(X \le 5) = 0.0207\) and \(P(X \le 6) = 0.0577\) under \(H_0\), state the critical value for this test.
The critical region for a test is \(X \le 3\). The observed value of the test statistic is \(X = 2\). State whether the null hypothesis should be rejected.
The critical region for a test is \(X \ge 14\) where \(X \sim B(20, p)\). The observed value is \(X = 12\). State whether the null hypothesis should be rejected.
Define what is meant by the actual significance level of a hypothesis test.
The critical region for a one-tailed test is \(X \le 2\), where \(X \sim B(15, 0.4)\) under \(H_0\). Given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0271\), state the actual significance level of the test.

The random variable \(X \sim B(10, 0.5)\). Find the critical region for a test of \(H_0: p = 0.5\) against \(H_1: p < 0.5\) at the 5% significance level. You are given that \(P(X \le 0) = 0.0010\), \(P(X \le 1) = 0.0107\) and \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0547\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(10, 0.5)\). Find the critical region for a test of \(H_0: p = 0.5\) against \(H_1: p > 0.5\) at the 5% significance level. You are given that \(P(X \ge 8) = 0.0547\) and \(P(X \ge 9) = 0.0107\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(20, 0.3)\). Find the critical region for a test of \(H_0: p = 0.3\) against \(H_1: p < 0.3\) at the 5% significance level. You are given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0355\) and \(P(X \le 3) = 0.1071\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(20, 0.3)\). Find the critical region for a test of \(H_0: p = 0.3\) against \(H_1: p < 0.3\) at the 1% significance level. You are given that \(P(X \le 0) = 0.0008\), \(P(X \le 1) = 0.0076\) and \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0355\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(20, 0.3)\). Find the critical region for a test of \(H_0: p = 0.3\) against \(H_1: p > 0.3\) at the 5% significance level. You are given that \(P(X \le 9) = 0.9520\) and \(P(X \le 10) = 0.9829\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(20, 0.5)\). Find the critical region for a two-tailed test of \(H_0: p = 0.5\) against \(H_1: p \ne 0.5\) at the 5% significance level. You are given that \(P(X \le 5) = 0.0207\), \(P(X \le 6) = 0.0577\), \(P(X \ge 15) = 0.0207\) and \(P(X \ge 14) = 0.0577\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(20, 0.5)\). The critical region for a two-tailed test is \(X \le 5\) or \(X \ge 15\). Given that \(P(X \le 5) = 0.0207\) and \(P(X \ge 15) = 0.0207\), find the actual significance level of this test.
Explain why the actual significance level of a hypothesis test using a binomial distribution may differ from the stated significance level.

The random variable \(X \sim B(25, 0.2)\). Find the critical region for a test of \(H_0: p = 0.2\) against \(H_1: p < 0.2\) at the 5% significance level and state the actual significance level. You are given that \(P(X \le 1) = 0.0274\), \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0982\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(20, 0.3)\). Find the critical region for a two-tailed test of \(H_0: p = 0.3\) against \(H_1: p \ne 0.3\) at the 10% significance level. You are given: \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0355\), \(P(X \le 3) = 0.1071\), \(P(X \ge 10) = 0.0480\) and \(P(X \ge 9) = 0.1133\).

A factory claims that 30% of its products are defective. A quality control inspector tests 20 items and finds that 2 are defective. The critical region for a one-tailed test at the 5% level, where \(X \sim B(20, 0.3)\) and \(H_1: p < 0.3\), is \(X \le 2\). State whether there is sufficient evidence to reject the factory's claim.

A doctor believes that a new treatment is more effective than the current treatment which has a 40% success rate. She trials the new treatment on 15 patients and 10 are successfully treated. The critical region for a one-tailed test at the 5% level, where \(X \sim B(15, 0.4)\) and \(H_1: p > 0.4\), is \(X \ge 10\). State whether there is sufficient evidence to support the doctor's belief.

The random variable \(X \sim B(20, 0.3)\). The critical region for a two-tailed test is \(X \le 2\) or \(X \ge 10\). Given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0355\) and \(P(X \ge 10) = 0.0480\), find the actual significance level of the test.

The random variable \(X \sim B(30, 0.25)\). Find the critical region for a test of \(H_0: p = 0.25\) against \(H_1: p > 0.25\) at the 1% significance level. You are given: \(P(X \le 13) = 0.9918\) and \(P(X \le 12) = 0.9784\).

An opinion poll suggests that 35% of voters support a particular party. A researcher believes the true proportion has changed. She surveys 25 randomly selected voters and uses a two-tailed test at the 5% significance level with \(X \sim B(25, 0.35)\). Given: \(P(X \le 4) = 0.0239\), \(P(X \le 5) = 0.0636\), \(P(X \ge 13) = 0.0442\) and \(P(X \ge 14) = 0.0195\). Find the critical region for this test.

The random variable \(X \sim B(20, 0.5)\). The critical region for a lower-tailed test at the 5% level is \(X \le 5\) and the critical region at the 1% level is \(X \le 3\). Given that \(P(X \le 5) = 0.0207\) and \(P(X \le 3) = 0.0013\), state the actual significance level at each level and comment on the difference.

A pharmaceutical company claims that a drug cures 60% of patients. A health authority suspects the drug is less effective than claimed and tests it on 18 patients. Using \(X \sim B(18, 0.6)\) with \(H_1: p < 0.6\) at the 5% significance level, find the critical region. You are given: \(P(X \le 6) = 0.0203\) and \(P(X \le 7) = 0.0596\).

A manufacturer claims that 25% of items produced are premium quality. An inspector believes the proportion may have changed and takes a sample of 30 items. Using \(X \sim B(30, 0.25)\) with \(H_1: p \ne 0.25\) at the 5% significance level, find the critical region and the actual significance level. You are given: \(P(X \le 3) = 0.0374\), \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0106\), \(P(X \ge 12) = 0.0507\) and \(P(X \ge 13) = 0.0216\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(25, 0.4)\) under \(H_0\). The critical region for a one-tailed test (\(H_1: p < 0.4\)) at the 5% level is \(X \le 5\). An observed value of \(X = 6\) is obtained. State the conclusion of the test, giving a reason.

A teacher believes that fewer than 50% of students pass a particular exam. She takes a random sample of 12 students. Using \(X \sim B(12, 0.5)\) with \(H_1: p < 0.5\) at the 10% significance level, find the critical region and state the actual significance level. You are given: \(P(X \le 3) = 0.0730\), \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0193\) and \(P(X \le 4) = 0.1938\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(25, 0.3)\). A one-tailed test is conducted with \(H_0: p = 0.3\) and \(H_1: p < 0.3\) at the 5% significance level. You are given: \(P(X \le 3) = 0.0332\) and \(P(X \le 4) = 0.0905\). (a) Find the critical region. (b) State the actual significance level. (c) An observed value of \(X = 3\) is obtained. State the conclusion of the test in context.

A coin is thought to be biased. To test this, the coin is flipped 20 times. Let \(X\) denote the number of heads. The hypotheses are \(H_0: p = 0.5\) and \(H_1: p \ne 0.5\). The test is conducted at the 5% significance level. You are given: \(P(X \le 5) = 0.0207\), \(P(X \le 6) = 0.0577\), \(P(X \ge 15) = 0.0207\), \(P(X \ge 14) = 0.0577\). (a) Find the critical region. (b) Find the actual significance level. (c) The coin is flipped 20 times and 15 heads are observed. State the conclusion in context.

The critical region for a two-tailed test is \(X \le 2\) or \(X \ge 9\) where \(X \sim B(12, 0.5)\) under \(H_0\). Find the actual significance level. You are given: \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0193\) and \(P(X \ge 9) = 0.0730\).
The random variable \(X \sim B(10, 0.3)\). Show that the critical region for a one-tailed test of \(H_0: p = 0.3\) against \(H_1: p < 0.3\) at the 5% significance level is \(X \le 0\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(n, 0.15)\). Find the largest value of \(n\) such that \(X = 0\) does not lie in the critical region for a one-tailed test of \(H_0: p = 0.15\) against \(H_1: p < 0.15\) at the 5% significance level.

A company claims that 20% of its emails are spam. An IT manager suspects the true proportion is higher. He examines a random sample of 30 emails. (a) Write down suitable hypotheses for this test. (b) Using \(X \sim B(30, 0.2)\) with the cumulative probabilities \(P(X \le 9) = 0.9163\) and \(P(X \le 10) = 0.9639\), find the critical region at the 5% significance level. (c) State the actual significance level. (d) In the sample, 11 emails are spam. State the conclusion of the test in context.
The random variable \(X \sim B(8, 0.5)\). Show that the critical region for an upper-tailed test at the 5% significance level is \(X \ge 7\).

A seed company states that 45% of seeds from a particular batch will germinate. A gardener thinks this proportion is wrong and plants 20 seeds. Let \(X\) denote the number that germinate. (a) State suitable hypotheses. (b) Find the critical region at the 10% significance level for a two-tailed test. You are given: \(P(X \le 4) = 0.0189\), \(P(X \le 5) = 0.0553\), \(P(X \ge 13) = 0.0580\), \(P(X \ge 14) = 0.0214\). (c) State the actual significance level. (d) 14 seeds germinate. State the conclusion in context.

The random variable \(X \sim B(n, 0.1)\). For a one-tailed test of \(H_0: p = 0.1\) against \(H_1: p < 0.1\) at the 5% significance level, find the smallest value of \(n\) for which the critical region is non-empty (i.e. the smallest \(n\) such that \(P(X = 0) < 0.05\)).

A political party claims that 40% of residents in a town support their policies. A journalist believes the support is lower and surveys 16 randomly selected residents. (a) Write down suitable hypotheses. (b) Find the critical region at the 5% significance level. You are given: \(P(X \le 3) = 0.0651\) and \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0183\) where \(X \sim B(16, 0.4)\). (c) State the actual significance level. (d) In the survey, 2 residents expressed support. State the conclusion in context.

A machine fills packets of cereal and the probability that a randomly chosen packet is underweight is \(p\). To test whether \(p\) has changed from 0.2, 30 packets are randomly selected. (a) State suitable hypotheses. (b) Find the critical region for a two-tailed test at the 5% significance level. You are given: \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0442\), \(P(X \le 1) = 0.0105\), \(P(X \ge 11) = 0.0256\), \(P(X \ge 12) = 0.0095\), where \(X \sim B(30, 0.2)\). (c) Find the actual significance level. (d) 12 packets are found to be underweight. State the conclusion.

A health authority reports that 15% of adults in a region have a certain condition. A researcher suspects the rate has increased and tests a random sample of 40 adults. Let \(X\) denote the number with the condition, where \(X \sim B(40, 0.15)\) under \(H_0\). (a) State the hypotheses. (b) Given that \(P(X \le 9) = 0.9256\) and \(P(X \le 10) = 0.9671\), find the critical region at the 5% significance level. (c) State the actual significance level. (d) Given instead that the test is at the 1% level and \(P(X \le 11) = 0.9870\), find the critical region at this level. (e) In the sample, 11 adults have the condition. State the conclusion at each significance level.

y1k1.questionText: A runner completes one full lap of a circular track of circumference \(400\) m, returning to the starting point. State the total distance travelled and the total displacement.
A car travels \(120\) m due east in \(8\) s, then \(50\) m due north in \(4\) s. Find (a) the average speed and (b) the magnitude of the average velocity for the whole journey.

A particle moves \(7\) m to the right, then \(3\) m to the left along a straight line. Taking rightward as positive, state (a) the total distance travelled and (b) the displacement from the starting point.

A ball is thrown vertically upward with a speed of \(12\) m/s. Taking upward as positive, write down the initial velocity and the acceleration due to gravity acting on the ball. State the velocity of the ball at its highest point.

A displacement--time graph for a particle shows the following: from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 4\) s the displacement increases uniformly from \(0\) to \(20\) m, and from \(t = 4\) to \(t = 10\) s the displacement remains at \(20\) m. Find the velocity of the particle in each stage.
A velocity--time graph for a car shows a straight line from \((0,\, 0)\) to \((5,\, 15)\). Find (a) the acceleration and (b) the displacement of the car during this \(5\) s interval.
A cyclist accelerates uniformly from rest to \(8\) m/s in \(10\) s, travels at \(8\) m/s for \(20\) s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in \(5\) s. Calculate the total displacement.
A displacement--time graph for a particle is a straight line from \((0,\, 12)\) to \((6,\, 0)\). What is the velocity of the particle? Interpret the sign of your answer.

A particle moves along a straight line. Its velocity--time graph consists of three straight-line segments: the velocity increases uniformly from \(0\) to \(V\) m/s over a time interval of \(T_1\) seconds, remains constant at \(V\) m/s for \(T_2\) seconds, then decreases uniformly from \(V\) to \(0\) over \(T_3\) seconds. (a) Show that the total displacement is \(\dfrac{V(T_1 + 2T_2 + T_3)}{2}\). (b) Given that \(T_1 = T_3\), show that the total displacement simplifies to \(V(T_1 + T_2)\). (c) Explain geometrically why the result in (b) is equivalent to the area of a rectangle of width \((T_1 + T_2)\) and height \(V\).

A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at \(a\) m/s\(^2\) for \(T\) seconds, reaching a final speed of \(V\) m/s. During this time it covers a total distance of \(D\) metres. (a) By forming two equations in \(a\) and \(T\), show that \(T = \dfrac{2D}{V}\) and \(a = \dfrac{V^2}{2D}\). (b) Given that \(V = 30\) and \(D = 225\), find the values of \(a\) and \(T\).
A car accelerates uniformly from \(10\) m/s at \(2\) m/s\(^2\) for \(6\) s. Find the final velocity.
A particle starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at \(3\) m/s\(^2\). Find the displacement after \(4\) s.
A car is travelling at \(20\) m/s when the brakes are applied, producing a deceleration of \(4\) m/s\(^2\). Find the distance the car travels before coming to rest.
A train decelerates uniformly from \(30\) m/s to \(10\) m/s over a distance of \(200\) m. Find the time taken.

A ball is thrown vertically upward from ground level with a speed of \(19.6\) m/s. Taking \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\) and upward as positive, find (a) the time taken to reach the highest point and (b) the maximum height.

A stone is dropped from rest from the top of a cliff \(44.1\) m above the sea. Taking \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\), find (a) the time for the stone to reach the sea and (b) the speed at which it hits the sea.

A particle starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at \(a\) m/s\(^2\) for \(t_1\) seconds, reaching speed \(V\) m/s. It then decelerates uniformly at \(2a\) m/s\(^2\) until it comes to rest. (a) Show that \(t_1 = \dfrac{V}{a}\). (b) Find the time for the deceleration phase in terms of \(V\) and \(a\). (c) Show that the total distance travelled is \(\dfrac{3V^2}{4a}\). (d) Hence find the total distance when \(V = 12\) and \(a = 3\).

Two particles \(P\) and \(Q\) are initially at points \(A\) and \(B\) respectively, where \(AB = d\) metres. At time \(t = 0\), particle \(P\) is projected from \(A\) toward \(B\) with speed \(u_1\) m/s and constant acceleration \(a\) m/s\(^2\) in the direction \(AB\). At the same instant, particle \(Q\) is projected from \(B\) toward \(A\) with speed \(u_2\) m/s and the same constant acceleration \(a\) m/s\(^2\) in the direction \(BA\). (a) Show that the particles meet at time \(t = \dfrac{d}{u_1 + u_2}\). (b) Show that the distance from \(A\) to the meeting point is \(\dfrac{d\,u_1}{u_1 + u_2} + \dfrac{a d^2}{2(u_1 + u_2)^2}\). (c) State the condition on \(u_1\), \(u_2\) and \(a\) for the meeting point to be exactly at the midpoint of \(AB\).

A ball is projected vertically upward with speed \(U\) m/s from a point \(h\) metres above the ground. (a) Show that the speed of the ball when it hits the ground is \(\sqrt{U^2 + 2gh}\), regardless of whether the ball is projected upward or downward. (b) Explain in one sentence why the direction of projection does not affect the final speed. (c) Given \(U = 10\) and \(h = 15\), find the speed at which the ball hits the ground. Take \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\).

A particle \(P\) travels along a straight line with constant acceleration. In the 3rd second of its motion it travels \(5\) m, and in the 7th second it travels \(13\) m. (a) Using the formula for the distance covered in the \(n\)th second, \(s_n = u + \tfrac{1}{2}a(2n - 1)\), form two simultaneous equations. (b) Find the initial speed \(u\) and the acceleration \(a\). (c) Find the total distance travelled in the first \(10\) seconds.

A cyclist accelerates uniformly from rest at \(1.5\) m/s\(^2\) for \(10\) s, then decelerates uniformly at \(0.5\) m/s\(^2\) until coming to rest. Find (a) the maximum speed and (b) the total distance travelled.
A ball is thrown vertically upward from ground level at \(29.4\) m/s. Taking \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\), find (a) the maximum height reached and (b) the total time for the ball to return to ground level.

A car travels at a constant speed of \(25\) m/s for \(12\) s, then brakes with a uniform deceleration of \(5\) m/s\(^2\) until it comes to rest. Find (a) the braking time and (b) the total distance covered.
A stone is thrown vertically upward from ground level at \(14.7\) m/s. Taking \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\), find the speed of the stone when it is \(9.8\) m above the ground.

A particle starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at \(a\) m/s\(^2\) for \(T\) seconds, reaching speed \(V\) m/s. It then decelerates uniformly at \(2a\) m/s\(^2\) until it stops. Show that the total distance travelled is \(\dfrac{3V^2}{4a}\).

Two cars start from the same point on a straight road. Car A starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at \(2\) m/s\(^2\). Three seconds later, car B passes the same point travelling at a constant speed of \(12\) m/s. Find the time after car A starts at which car B overtakes car A.
A ball is projected vertically upward from ground level at \(24.5\) m/s. Taking \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\), find the two times at which the ball is \(19.6\) m above the ground.

A particle moves in a straight line with constant acceleration. It passes point \(A\) with speed \(6\) m/s and point \(B\), which is \(40\) m from \(A\), with speed \(14\) m/s. Find (a) the acceleration and (b) the time to travel from \(A\) to \(B\).
A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly, covering \(20\) m in the first \(4\) s. Show that the car covers \(60\) m in the next \(4\) s.

A car is travelling along a straight road at \(30\) m/s. The driver sees an obstacle and reacts for \(0.8\) s before applying the brakes. Under braking, the car decelerates uniformly at \(6\) m/s\(^2\). Find (a) the thinking distance, (b) the braking distance, (c) the total stopping distance, and (d) the total time from seeing the obstacle to stopping.

A ball is thrown vertically upward from a point \(1.2\) m above the ground with speed \(9.8\) m/s. Taking \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\), find (a) the greatest height above the ground reached by the ball, (b) the time taken from throwing to reaching the greatest height, (c) the speed of the ball when it hits the ground, and (d) the total time of flight.

A velocity--time graph for a particle is described as follows: from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 5\) s, velocity increases uniformly from \(0\) to \(10\) m/s; from \(t = 5\) to \(t = 15\) s, velocity remains at \(10\) m/s; from \(t = 15\) to \(t = 20\) s, velocity decreases uniformly from \(10\) to \(0\) m/s. Find (a) the acceleration in the first stage, (b) the deceleration in the last stage, (c) the total displacement, and (d) the average speed for the entire journey.

Two particles are projected vertically upward from the same point \(O\). Particle \(P\) is projected with speed \(U\) m/s at \(t = 0\). At \(t = T\) seconds, particle \(Q\) is projected from \(O\) with speed \(2U\) m/s. Both move under gravity \(g\). (a) Write expressions for the heights of \(P\) and \(Q\) above \(O\) at time \(t\) seconds after \(P\) is projected, for \(t > T\). (b) Show that the two particles are at the same height when \(t = \dfrac{T(4U + gT)}{2(U + gT)}\). (c) State the condition on \(U\), \(g\) and \(T\) for both particles to still be in flight at this instant.

A particle moves along a straight line with initial speed \(u\) m/s and constant acceleration \(a\) m/s\(^2\). (a) By considering the displacement from \(t = 0\) to \(t = n\) and from \(t = 0\) to \(t = n - 1\), show that the distance covered in the \(n\)th second of motion is \(u + \tfrac{1}{2}a(2n - 1)\). (b) A car has initial speed \(4\) m/s and constant acceleration \(3\) m/s\(^2\). Using the result from (a), find the distance covered in the 5th second. (c) Verify your answer to (b) by computing the total distances in the first 5 and first 4 seconds and subtracting.

A car travels from \(A\) to \(B\), a distance \(d\), at constant speed \(v_1\). It immediately returns from \(B\) to \(A\) at constant speed \(v_2\). (a) Find the total time for the round trip in terms of \(d\), \(v_1\) and \(v_2\). (b) Show that the average speed for the whole journey is \(\dfrac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\). (c) Explain why the average speed is not \(\dfrac{v_1 + v_2}{2}\). (d) Given \(v_1 = 40\) km/h and \(v_2 = 60\) km/h, find the average speed for the round trip.

A ball is dropped from rest from a height \(H\) metres above the ground. Each time it bounces, it rises to a fraction \(e\) of the height from which it fell (where \(0 < e < 1\)). Assume the bounces are instantaneous and take \(g\) as the acceleration due to gravity. (a) Show that the time for the ball to fall from height \(H\) is \(\sqrt{2H/g}\). (b) Show that the time between the first and second bounces is \(2\sqrt{2eH/g}\). (c) Show that the total distance the ball travels before coming to rest is \(H \cdot \dfrac{1 + e}{1 - e}\). (d) Given \(H = 5\) m and \(e = 0.64\), find the total distance.

A particle \(P\) is projected vertically upward from a point \(O\) on the ground with speed \(u\) m/s. At the instant when \(P\) has been moving for \(T\) seconds (where \(T < u/g\)), a second particle \(Q\) is projected vertically upward from \(O\) with speed \(2u\) m/s. (a) Show that, at time \(t\) seconds after \(Q\) is projected, the height of \(P\) above \(O\) is \(u(t + T) - \tfrac{1}{2}g(t + T)^2\). (b) Find the height of \(Q\) above \(O\) at this time. (c) Show that the two particles are at the same height when \(t = \dfrac{uT - \tfrac{1}{2}gT^2}{u + gT}\). (d) Given \(u = 25\), \(g = 10\) and \(T = 1\), find \(t\) and the height at which they meet.

A particle moves along a straight line. At \(t = 0\) it is at the origin \(O\) with velocity \(u\) m/s. It has constant acceleration \(a\) m/s\(^2\), where \(a\) and \(u\) have opposite signs. (a) Explain why the particle will initially move away from \(O\) and then return. (b) Show that the particle returns to \(O\) at time \(t = -\dfrac{2u}{a}\), and verify that this is positive. (c) Find the velocity of the particle when it returns to \(O\), in terms of \(u\). (d) Find the maximum distance from \(O\) reached by the particle, in terms of \(u\) and \(a\).

Particles \(A\) and \(B\) move along a straight road. At \(t = 0\), particle \(A\) passes a point \(O\) travelling in the positive direction with speed \(5\) m/s and constant acceleration \(2\) m/s\(^2\). At the same instant, particle \(B\) is \(50\) m ahead of \(O\) (in the positive direction), travelling toward \(O\) with speed \(10\) m/s and decelerating at \(1\) m/s\(^2\) (so its acceleration is \(+1\) m/s\(^2\) since it opposes the motion toward \(O\)). (a) Write expressions for the positions of \(A\) and \(B\) relative to \(O\) at time \(t\). (b) Find the time(s) at which they meet. (c) Find the position(s) at which they meet. (d) Explain what happens physically at each meeting.

A particle moves along a straight line with constant acceleration \(a\) m/s\(^2\). In two consecutive time intervals, each of length \(T\) seconds, it covers distances \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) respectively. Let \(u\) be the speed at the start of the first interval. (a) Show that \(d_1 = uT + \tfrac{1}{2}aT^2\). (b) By finding the speed at the start of the second interval, show that \(d_2 = uT + \tfrac{3}{2}aT^2\). (c) Hence show that \(a = \dfrac{d_2 - d_1}{T^2}\). (d) Find \(u\) in terms of \(d_1\), \(d_2\) and \(T\). (e) Given \(d_1 = 20\), \(d_2 = 32\), and \(T = 4\), find \(a\) and \(u\).

y1k2.questionText: A particle moves along a straight line such that its displacement at time \(t\) seconds is given by \(s = 4t^2 + 3t\), where \(s\) is measured in metres. Find the velocity of the particle at time \(t\).
A particle has velocity \(v = 3t^2 - 12t + 9\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t\) seconds. Find the acceleration of the particle at time \(t\).
A particle moves along a straight line with displacement \(s = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t + 2\) metres at time \(t\) seconds. Find expressions for the velocity \(v\) and the acceleration \(a\) at time \(t\).
A particle has displacement \(s = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t\) metres at time \(t\) seconds. Find the velocity of the particle when \(t = 2\).
A particle moves along a straight line with displacement \(s = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t\) metres at time \(t \geq 0\) seconds. Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest.
A particle has displacement \(s = t^4 - 4t^3 + 6\) metres at time \(t\) seconds. Find the acceleration of the particle when \(t = 3\).
A particle moves with displacement \(s = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t + 2\) metres at time \(t\) seconds. Find the time at which the acceleration of the particle is zero.

A particle moves along a straight line with displacement \(s = 5t^2 - t^3\) metres at time \(t \geq 0\) seconds. Find the velocity when the acceleration is zero, and determine the displacement of the particle at that instant.

A particle moves along a straight line with acceleration \(a = 6t - 4\) m s\(^{-2}\) at time \(t\) seconds. Given that the initial velocity is \(5\) m s\(^{-1}\), find an expression for the velocity \(v\) at time \(t\).
A particle has velocity \(v = 4t - t^2\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t\) seconds. Given that the particle starts at the origin, find an expression for the displacement \(s\) at time \(t\).
A particle moves with acceleration \(a = 10 - 6t\) m s\(^{-2}\) at time \(t\) seconds. When \(t = 0\) the velocity is \(2\) m s\(^{-1}\). Find the velocity when \(t = 3\).

A particle moves along a straight line with velocity \(v = 3t^2 - 10t + 7\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t\) seconds. When \(t = 0\) the displacement is \(4\) m from the origin. Find the displacement when \(t = 3\).
A particle has velocity \(v = 6t - 2\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t\) seconds. Find the displacement of the particle between \(t = 1\) and \(t = 4\).
A particle starts from rest and moves with acceleration \(a = 12t - 6\) m s\(^{-2}\). Find an expression for the displacement \(s\) at time \(t\), given that \(s = 0\) when \(t = 0\).

At time \(t = 0\), a particle passes through a point \(O\) with velocity \(8\) m s\(^{-1}\). The acceleration of the particle is \(a = 6 - 4t\) m s\(^{-2}\). Find the displacement of the particle from \(O\) when the particle is next instantaneously at rest.
A particle has velocity \(v = t^2 - 6t + 8\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t\) seconds. Find the displacement of the particle between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 5\).

A particle \(P\) moves along a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds (\(t \geq 0\)), the displacement of \(P\) from a fixed point \(O\) on the line is \(s\) metres, where \(s = t^3 - 5t^2 + 3t + 5\). (a) Find an expression for the velocity of \(P\) at time \(t\). (b) Find the times when \(P\) is instantaneously at rest. (c) Find the acceleration of \(P\) at each of these times.

A particle moves along a straight line with displacement \(s = 12t + 3t^2 - 2t^3\) metres at time \(t \geq 0\) seconds. Show that the maximum displacement of the particle from its initial position is \(20\) m, and find the time at which this maximum occurs.
A particle moves along a straight line with velocity \(v = t^2 - 4t + 3\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t \geq 0\) seconds. Find the total distance travelled by the particle between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 4\).

A particle moves along a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds (\(t \geq 0\)), the displacement of the particle from a fixed point \(O\) is given by \(s = pt^3 - 18t^2 + qt\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are positive constants. The particle is instantaneously at rest when \(t = 1\) and when \(t = 3\). (a) Show that \(p = 3\) and find the value of \(q\). (b) Find the acceleration of the particle when \(t = 2\). (c) Find the total distance travelled by the particle between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 4\).

A particle moves along a straight line with acceleration \(a = 4t - 6\) m s\(^{-2}\) at time \(t\) seconds. When \(t = 0\), the velocity is \(3\) m s\(^{-1}\) and the displacement from the origin is \(0\). Find expressions for the velocity and displacement at time \(t\).

A particle has acceleration \(a = 6t\) m s\(^{-2}\) at time \(t\) seconds. When \(t = 0\), the velocity is \(4\) m s\(^{-1}\) and the displacement from a fixed point \(O\) is \(2\) m. Find the displacement when \(t = 3\).
A particle has velocity \(v = 3t^2 - 2t\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t\) seconds. Use a definite integral to find the displacement of the particle between \(t = 1\) and \(t = 3\).
A particle has velocity \(v = 6t - t^2 - 8\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t \geq 0\) seconds. Find the total distance travelled by the particle between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 6\).
A particle has velocity \(v = 4t^{1/2} - 2\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t > 0\) seconds. Given that \(s = 0\) when \(t = 1\), find an expression for the displacement \(s\) at time \(t\).

A particle has acceleration \(a = 3t^{-1/2}\) m s\(^{-2}\) for \(t > 0\). When \(t = 4\), the velocity is \(15\) m s\(^{-1}\) and the displacement from the origin is \(0\). Find the displacement when \(t = 9\).

A particle \(P\) moves along the \(x\)-axis. At time \(t\) seconds, the velocity of \(P\) is \(v\) m s\(^{-1}\) where \(v = kt^2 - 12t + c\). When \(t = 0\), \(v = 5\) and when \(t = 2\), \(v = 1\). (a) Find the values of \(k\) and \(c\). (b) Find the acceleration when \(t = 3\). (c) Find the values of \(t\) for which the particle is at rest.

A particle moves along a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds, the displacement of the particle from a fixed point \(O\) is \(s = at^3 + bt^2 + ct\) metres, where \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are constants. When \(t = 0\) the velocity is \(6\) m s\(^{-1}\). When \(t = 1\) the velocity is \(0\). When \(t = 2\) the acceleration is \(0\). (a) Find the values of \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\). (b) Find the displacement of the particle when \(t = 3\).
A particle moves along a straight line with velocity \(v = 12t - 3t^2 + 1\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t \geq 0\) seconds. Find the maximum velocity of the particle.

A particle starts from rest at the origin and moves along a straight line with acceleration \(a = 2t + 4\) m s\(^{-2}\) for \(t \geq 0\). (a) Find expressions for the velocity and displacement at time \(t\). (b) Show that the particle never returns to its starting point.

A particle \(P\) moves along a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds (\(t \geq 0\)), the acceleration of \(P\) is \(a = (8 - 4t)\) m s\(^{-2}\). When \(t = 0\), \(P\) is at rest at the origin. (a) Find the velocity of \(P\) at time \(t\). (b) Find the maximum velocity of \(P\). (c) Find the displacement of \(P\) from the origin when the velocity is at its maximum.

A particle \(P\) moves along a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds, the velocity of \(P\) is \(v = At^2 + Bt + C\) m s\(^{-1}\), where \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) are constants. When \(t = 0\), \(v = 10\). When \(t = 1\), \(v = 3\). When \(t = 3\), \(v = 1\). (a) Find the values of \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\). (b) Find the times at which the particle is at rest. (c) Find the displacement of the particle from its initial position between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 5\).

A particle moves along a straight line with displacement \(s = 2t^3 - 3t^2 + 6t\) metres from a fixed point \(O\) at time \(t \geq 0\) seconds. (a) Show that the velocity of the particle is always positive. (b) Find the minimum velocity of the particle. (c) Hence explain why the particle never returns to \(O\).

A particle starts from rest at a point \(O\) and moves along a straight line. The acceleration of the particle at time \(t\) seconds is \(a = (6 - 3t)\) m s\(^{-2}\). (a) Find the velocity of the particle at time \(t\). (b) Find the time at which the particle is next at rest. (c) Find the maximum displacement from \(O\). (d) Find the displacement of the particle from \(O\) when \(t = 6\).

A particle has velocity \(v = At^2 + Bt\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t \geq 0\) seconds, where \(A\) and \(B\) are non-zero constants with \(A\) and \(B\) having opposite signs. The particle starts from the origin. (a) Show that the particle returns to the origin at time \(T = -\dfrac{3B}{2A}\). (b) Show that this time \(T\) is positive. (c) Find, in terms of \(A\) and \(B\), the maximum displacement of the particle from the origin.

A particle has acceleration \(a = 6 - 2t\) m s\(^{-2}\) at time \(t\) seconds. The particle starts from rest. (a) Find the velocity at time \(t\). (b) Find the times when the particle is at rest. (c) Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first \(9\) seconds.

Particles \(A\) and \(B\) move along a straight line. At time \(t = 0\), both particles are at the origin. The velocity of \(A\) at time \(t\) seconds is \(v_A = 6t - t^2\) m s\(^{-1}\) and the velocity of \(B\) is \(v_B = 3t\) m s\(^{-1}\). (a) Find the time \(t > 0\) at which \(A\) and \(B\) have the same velocity. (b) Find the time \(t > 0\) at which \(A\) and \(B\) have the same displacement from the origin.

A particle moves along a straight line with velocity \(v = pt^2 - qt\) m s\(^{-1}\) at time \(t \geq 0\) seconds, where \(p\) and \(q\) are positive constants. (a) Find the times at which the speed of the particle is zero. (b) Given that the speed of the particle is the same at times \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) where \(0 < t_1 < t_2\), show that \(t_1 + t_2 = \dfrac{q}{p}\).

Particle \(A\) starts from rest at the origin and moves with constant acceleration \(4\) m s\(^{-2}\). At the same instant, particle \(B\) passes through the origin with velocity \(20\) m s\(^{-1}\) and acceleration \(a_B = -2t\) m s\(^{-2}\). (a) Find expressions for the velocities \(v_A\) and \(v_B\) at time \(t\). (b) Find the time at which the velocities are equal. (c) Find expressions for the displacements \(s_A\) and \(s_B\) from the origin at time \(t\). (d) Find the time \(t > 0\) at which the particles are at the same point.

A particle \(P\) moves along a straight line. At time \(t = 0\), \(P\) is at a point \(O\) with velocity \(12\) m s\(^{-1}\). The acceleration of \(P\) at time \(t\) seconds is \(a = (4 - 2t)\) m s\(^{-2}\). (a) Show that the velocity of \(P\) at time \(t\) is \(v = 12 + 4t - t^2\). (b) Find the maximum velocity of \(P\). (c) Show that \(P\) is at rest when \(t = 6\). (d) Find the total distance travelled by \(P\) between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 8\).

y1pr1.questionText: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. Find the probability that the score is (a) a 4, (b) an even number.
The probability that it rains tomorrow is \(0.42\). Find the probability that it does not rain tomorrow.
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Find the probability that the total is 7.
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled and the scores are added. Find the probability that the total is (a) 11, (b) at least 4.
A card is drawn at random from a standard pack of 52 playing cards. Find the probability that the card is (a) a club, (b) a face card (jack, queen, king), (c) a club or a face card.
In a class of 30 pupils, 18 study French and 14 study German; 6 study both. (a) How many study neither? (b) Find the probability a randomly chosen pupil studies French only.

A survey of 200 commuters records mode of transport (Bus or Train) and gender. \(\;\) Female Bus: 48; Female Train: 52; Male Bus: 36; Male Train: 64. Find the probability that a randomly chosen commuter is (a) male, (b) female and travels by train, (c) travels by bus.

A class of 60 pupils is surveyed: 35 own a bike, 28 own a skateboard, 12 own both. A pupil is chosen at random. Find the probability that the pupil owns (a) a bike or a skateboard (or both), (b) neither.

A garage records 80 cars: 50 are petrol, 30 are diesel; 32 are saloons and 48 are hatchbacks. 18 of the petrol cars are saloons. A car is chosen at random. Find (a) the probability it is a diesel hatchback, (b) the probability it is petrol or a saloon.
A school of 240 pupils is surveyed: \(x\) study Spanish, 90 study Latin, and 28 study both. The number who study neither is twice the number who study only Spanish. Find \(x\).
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.5, \ P(B) = 0.4, \ P(A \cap B) = 0.2\). Find \(P(A \cup B)\).
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.6, \ P(B) = 0.5, \ P(A \cup B) = 0.8\). Find \(P(A \cap B)\) and \(P(A' \cap B')\).

In a survey of 50 students, 28 study Maths (M), 22 study Physics (P), and 10 study both. (a) Draw a Venn diagram (or describe the regions) and state how many study neither. A student is chosen at random; find (b) \(P(M \cap P')\) and (c) \(P(M' \cap P')\).

Of 100 sixth-formers, 60 study Maths (M), 45 study Further Maths (F), 40 study Physics (P). 30 study M and F, 25 study M and P, 20 study F and P, and 15 study all three. Find the number who study at least one of these three subjects.

A class of 40 students is surveyed about whether they like coffee (C) or tea (T). 24 like coffee, 18 like tea, 8 like both. A student is chosen at random. Find (a) \(P(C \cup T)\), (b) \(P(C' \cap T)\), (c) \(P(\text{exactly one of C and T})\).
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.5, \ P(B) = x, \ P(A \cap B) = 0.2, \ P(A' \cap B') = 0.1\). Find \(x\).

A leisure centre offers Swimming (S), Tennis (T), and Yoga (Y). Of 80 members surveyed: 40 do S, 30 do T, 35 do Y; 12 do both S and T, 15 do both S and Y, 10 do both T and Y, and 5 do all three. Find the probability that a randomly chosen member does (a) at least one activity, (b) exactly one activity.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive with \(P(A) = 0.3\) and \(P(B) = 0.45\). Find \(P(A \cup B)\) and \(P(A \cap B)\).
A fair die is rolled. Let \(A\) be the event ‘score is 1 or 2' and \(B\) the event ‘score is 5 or 6'. Find \(P(A \cup B)\) and state whether \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.4, \ P(B) = 0.35, \ P(A \cup B) = 0.65\). Determine whether \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive, justifying your answer.
A bag contains 12 red counters, 8 blue counters and 5 green counters. A counter is drawn at random. Find the probability it is (a) red or blue, (b) not green.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent with \(P(A) = 0.6\) and \(P(B) = 0.4\). Find \(P(A \cap B)\).
A fair coin is tossed twice. Find the probability of obtaining (a) two heads, (b) at least one head.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.5, \ P(B) = 0.4, \ P(A \cap B) = 0.2\). Determine whether \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, justifying your answer.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.6, \ P(B) = 0.3, \ P(A \cup B) = 0.78\). Show whether \(A\) and \(B\) are independent.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent with \(P(A) = 0.4\) and \(P(A \cup B) = 0.7\). Find \(P(B)\).
The probability that a train arrives on time is 0.8. Two trains travel independently. Find the probability that (a) both arrive on time, (b) exactly one arrives on time.
A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue counters. Two counters are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that (a) both are red, (b) one is red and one is blue.

A factory has two machines. Machine A makes 60% of the output and 4% of its items are faulty. Machine B makes the rest, with 6% faulty. An item is chosen at random. Find (a) the probability it is faulty, (b) the probability it was made by Machine A and is not faulty.

Each morning Alice cycles to school with probability 0.7, otherwise she walks. If she cycles, she is late with probability 0.05; if she walks, she is late with probability 0.20. Find (a) the probability that, on a given morning, she is late, (b) the probability that on two independent mornings she is late on at least one of them.
A fair eight-sided spinner has sides labelled 1 to 8. Find the probability of obtaining (a) a multiple of 3, (b) a number greater than 5.
Two fair coins are tossed. Find the probability of obtaining (a) two tails, (b) at least one head.
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Find the probability that the absolute difference between the scores is 2.
A fair coin is tossed and a fair six-sided die is rolled. Find the probability of (a) a head and an even number, (b) a tail and a prime number.
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Find the probability that the product of the scores is greater than 20.

A class of 50 pupils is split by gender (Boy/Girl) and whether they wear glasses. 14 boys wear glasses, 12 girls wear glasses, and there are 28 boys in total. Find the probability that a randomly chosen pupil (a) is a girl who does not wear glasses, (b) does not wear glasses.

75 sixth-formers are studying one of Maths, History or Art. Of the 30 boys, 12 study Maths and 8 study History. Of the 45 girls, 18 study Maths and 15 study Art. A student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student is (a) a boy studying Art, (b) studying History.

A library records borrowers by age (Adult / Child) and by genre most recently borrowed (Fiction / Non-fiction). Of 120 borrowers: 70 are adults, and 80 borrowed Fiction. 50 adults borrowed Fiction. Find the probability that a randomly chosen borrower is (a) a child who borrowed Non-fiction, (b) an adult or borrowed Fiction.

A market researcher classifies 200 shoppers by store (X or Y) and by membership (Member / Non-member). 60% of shoppers were at store X, and a quarter of all shoppers are Members. 32 shoppers are Members at store Y. Find the probability that a randomly chosen shopper is (a) a Member at store X, (b) a Non-member.

A two-way table classifies 150 people by smoker/non-smoker and by exercise (Yes/No). The number of smokers who do not exercise is twice the number of smokers who exercise. The number of non-smokers who exercise is three times the number of smokers who exercise. There are 30 non-smokers who do not exercise. Find the number of smokers in total.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.55, \ P(B) = 0.30, \ P(A \cap B) = 0.18\). Find \(P(A \cup B)\) and \(P(A' \cap B')\).
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.4, \ P(B) = 0.5, \ P(A \cap B) = 0.1\). Find \(P(A \cap B')\) and \(P(A' \cap B)\).

In a survey of 60 commuters: 35 read a newspaper (N), 22 listen to a podcast (P), and 14 do both. Find the probability that a randomly chosen commuter (a) does at least one of these, (b) does neither.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.45, \ P(B) = 0.35, \ P(A \cap B) = 0.12\). Find the probability that exactly one of \(A, B\) occurs.

Of 80 students surveyed about sports clubs: 30 play Football (F), 28 play Hockey (H), 25 play Cricket (C). 12 play F and H, 10 play F and C, 9 play H and C, and 4 play all three. Find the number of students who play at least one of these sports.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 2x, \ P(B) = x, \ P(A \cap B) = 0.05, \ P(A \cup B) = 0.55\). Find \(x\) and hence \(P(A)\).

100 readers were surveyed about three magazines, A, B and C. The numbers reading exactly two of the three magazines were: A and B only, 8; A and C only, 6; B and C only, 5. The number reading all three was 4. Of those reading at least one magazine, 50 read A, 40 read B and 35 read C. Find the number reading none of the magazines.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive with \(P(A) = 0.25\) and \(P(A \cup B) = 0.6\). Find \(P(B)\).

A bag of marbles contains red, blue, green and yellow marbles. The probabilities of drawing red, blue and green are 0.4, 0.25 and 0.15 respectively. Find the probability of drawing (a) red or green, (b) yellow.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.3, \ P(B) = 0.45, \ P(A \cap B) = 0.0\). State whether \(A\) and \(B\) are (i) mutually exclusive, (ii) independent, justifying each answer.

A box contains 50 raffle tickets numbered 1 to 50. One ticket is drawn at random. Find the probability that the number drawn is (a) a multiple of 5 or a multiple of 7, (b) a prime number less than 20.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent with \(P(A) = 0.7\) and \(P(B) = 0.2\). Find \(P(A \cup B)\).
The probability that a particular alarm sounds when triggered is 0.95. Two alarms are triggered independently. Find the probability that at least one alarm sounds.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(P(A) = 0.4, \ P(B) = 0.25, \ P(A \cup B) = 0.55\). Determine whether \(A\) and \(B\) are independent.
The probability that a randomly chosen lightbulb is faulty is 0.04. Five bulbs are tested independently. Find, to 4 d.p., the probability that (a) none are faulty, (b) at least one is faulty.
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent with \(P(A) = 0.3\) and \(P(A \cup B) = 0.58\). Find \(P(B)\).
A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue counters. A counter is drawn, its colour noted, and replaced; then a second counter is drawn. Find the probability that both are red.
A bag contains 6 white and 4 black balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that (a) both are the same colour, (b) the balls are of different colours.

A diagnostic test gives a positive result for 98% of people who have a particular condition, and a positive result for 3% of people who do not have the condition. In a population, 5% of people have the condition. A randomly chosen person is tested. Find (a) the probability the test is positive, (b) the probability the person has the condition and tests negative.

Each day Sam revises with probability 0.8. If he revises, he passes a daily test with probability 0.9; if he does not revise, he passes with probability 0.4. Tests on different days are independent. Find (a) the probability he passes a single day's test, (b) the probability he passes both tests on two consecutive days.

y1sd1.questionText: The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.4 & k \end{array}\]Find the value of \(k\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.05 & 0.2 & a & 0.3 & 0.15 \end{array}\]Find the value of \(a\) and hence find \(P(X \le 2)\).
The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.4 & 0.3 \end{array}\]Find \(E(X)\).
The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.5 & 0.3 & 0.2 \end{array}\]Find \(E(X)\) and \(\text{Var}(X)\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.3 & 0.2 \end{array}\]Find the standard deviation of \(X\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 2k & 3k & 4k & k \end{array}\]Find the value of \(k\) and calculate \(E(X)\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.1 & 2c & c & 2c & 0.1 \end{array}\]Find the value of \(c\), and hence find \(E(X)\) and \(\text{Var}(X)\).

The number of customers, \(X\), arriving at a shop counter in a one-minute interval has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.2 & 0.35 & 0.25 & 0.15 & 0.05 \end{array}\]Find the expected number of customers and the standard deviation.
The discrete random variable \(X\) has \(E(X) = 5\) and \(\text{Var}(X) = 3\). Find:\[(a)\; E(3X + 2) \qquad (b)\; \text{Var}(3X + 2) \qquad (c)\; E(4 - 2X)\]

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 2 & 4 & 6 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.25 & 0.5 & 0.25 \end{array}\]Find \(E(X)\), \(\text{Var}(X)\), and hence find \(E(5X - 3)\) and \(\text{Var}(5X - 3)\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & a & b & 0.3 & 0.1 \end{array}\]Given that \(E(X) = 2.3\), find the values of \(a\) and \(b\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline P(X=x) & p & p & q \end{array}\]Given that \(\text{Var}(X) = 0.5\), find the possible values of \(p\) and \(q\).

A game costs \(\pounds 3\) to play. A fair spinner has outcomes 1, 2, 3, 4 with respective probabilities \(0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1\). The player wins \(\pounds X\) where \(X\) is the score shown. Let \(Y\) be the player's profit. (a) Write \(Y\) in terms of \(X\). (b) Find \(E(Y)\) and interpret your answer. (c) Find the standard deviation of \(Y\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has \(E(X) = 4\) and \(\text{Var}(X) = 6\). The random variable \(Y\) is defined by \(Y = aX + b\) where \(a > 0\). Given that \(E(Y) = 10\) and \(\text{Var}(Y) = 24\), find the values of \(a\) and \(b\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.1 & a & 2a & a & 0.1 \end{array}\](a) Find the value of \(a\). (b) Find \(E(X)\) and \(\text{Var}(X)\). (c) The random variable \(Y = 3X - 1\). Find \(E(Y)\) and the standard deviation of \(Y\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & k & 4k & 9k & 16k \end{array}\]where \(P(X=x) = kx^2\). Find the value of \(k\) and state \(P(X \ge 3)\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2 \end{array}\]Find \(E(X^2)\) and hence calculate \(\text{Var}(X)\) using the formula \(\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.15 & 0.25 & 0.35 & 0.25 \end{array}\]Write down the cumulative distribution function \(F(x)\) and find \(F(3)\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 1 & 2 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.5 & 0.3 & 0.2 \end{array}\]Find \(E\!\left(\dfrac{1}{X}\right)\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline P(X=x) & k^2 & 2k & 3k^2 \end{array}\]where \(k > 0\). Find the value of \(k\) and calculate \(E(X)\).

The cumulative distribution function of the discrete random variable \(X\) is given by:\[\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline F(x) & 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.85 & 1 \end{array}\](a) Find the probability distribution of \(X\). (b) Find \(P(2 < X \le 4)\). (c) Find \(E(X)\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.2 \end{array}\]Find \(E(X^2)\) and \(E(2X^2 - 3X + 1)\).

An insurance company offers a policy that pays out for storm damage. The random variable \(X\) represents the payout (in thousands of pounds) with the following distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 0 & 5 & 20 & 50 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.85 & 0.08 & 0.05 & 0.02 \end{array}\]The annual premium is \(\pounds 2500\). (a) Find the expected payout per policy. (b) Find the expected profit per policy for the insurer. (c) Find the standard deviation of the payout.

A game involves rolling two fair six-sided dice. Let \(X\) be the absolute difference between the two scores. The probability distribution of \(X\) is:\[\begin{array}{c|cccccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline P(X=x) & \frac{6}{36} & \frac{10}{36} & \frac{8}{36} & \frac{6}{36} & \frac{4}{36} & \frac{2}{36} \end{array}\]A player pays \(\pounds 2\) to play and wins \(\pounds X\). Find the expected profit and determine whether the game is fair.

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.4 & 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.1 \end{array}\](a) Find \(E(X)\) and \(E\!\left(\dfrac{1}{X}\right)\). (b) Verify that \(E\!\left(\dfrac{1}{X}\right) \ne \dfrac{1}{E(X)}\).

The cumulative distribution function of the discrete random variable \(X\) is given by:\[F(x) = \frac{x^2}{a}, \quad x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\](a) Find the value of \(a\). (b) Find the probability distribution of \(X\). (c) Find \(E(X)\) and \(\text{Var}(X)\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & a & b & c & 0.1 \end{array}\]Given that \(E(X) = 2.3\) and \(\text{Var}(X) = 0.61\), find the values of \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).

In a fairground game, a player spins a spinner that lands on 1, 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities \(\frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{1}{4}\), \(\frac{1}{8}\) and \(\frac{1}{8}\) respectively. The player wins \(\pounds 2^X\) where \(X\) is the score. The game costs \(\pounds 5\) to play. (a) Find \(E(2^X)\). (b) Find the player's expected profit. (c) Find the entry fee that would make the game fair.

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline P(X=x) & a & b & c \end{array}\]Given that \(E(X) = 0.8\) and \(\text{Var}(X) = 0.56\), find the values of \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).

The discrete random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\[\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & k & 3k & 5k & 3k & k \end{array}\]where \(k\) is a constant. (a) Show that \(k = \dfrac{1}{13}\). (b) Write down the cumulative distribution function \(F(x)\). (c) Find \(E(X)\), \(E(X^2)\) and \(\text{Var}(X)\). (d) Find \(E(3X^2 - 2X + 5)\).

y1sd2.questionText: State the four conditions that must be satisfied for a random variable \(X\) to follow a binomial distribution.
A fair coin is tossed 10 times and \(X\) is the number of heads obtained. Explain why \(X\) can be modelled by a binomial distribution and state the values of \(n\) and \(p\).
A fair coin is tossed 5 times. Find the probability of obtaining exactly 3 heads.
A fair six-sided die is rolled 4 times. Find the probability that exactly 2 of the rolls show a six.
A machine produces items with a defect rate of 10%. A random sample of 6 items is taken. Find the probability that exactly 1 item is defective.

In a multiple-choice test, each question has 4 options, only one of which is correct. A student guesses every answer. Given that the test has 8 questions, find the probability that the student gets exactly 4 correct.
The probability that a seed germinates is 0.8. Five seeds are planted. Find the probability that (a) all five germinate, (b) none of them germinate.
A biased coin has \(P(\text{Head}) = 0.6\). The coin is tossed 7 times. Find the probability that at least one head is obtained.
A factory produces light bulbs and 5% are faulty. A box contains 10 bulbs. Find the probability that at most 1 bulb in the box is faulty.
A spinner has a 0.3 probability of landing on red. The spinner is spun 6 times. Find the probability that it lands on red exactly 2 or exactly 3 times.
An archer hits the target with probability 0.7 on each independent shot. She fires 8 arrows. Find the probability that she hits the target at least 7 times.
A random variable \(X \sim B(5,\, p)\). Given that \(P(X = 0) = 0.16807\), find the value of \(p\).
A random variable \(X \sim B(n,\, 0.1)\). Given that \(P(X = 0) < 0.05\), find the smallest value of \(n\).
A random variable \(X \sim B\!\left(6,\, \dfrac{3}{7}\right)\). Show that \(P(X = 2) = P(X = 3)\) and hence state the mode(s) of \(X\).
A random variable \(X \sim B(8,\, p)\). Given that \(P(X = 2) = 4 \times P(X = 3)\), find the value of \(p\).
A bag contains a large number of beads, 30% of which are blue. Four beads are selected at random with replacement. Find the probability that none of the beads selected is blue.
A fair coin is tossed 6 times. Find the probability that all 6 tosses result in heads.
A machine produces components and each independently has a 0.9 probability of passing quality control. Five components are tested. Find the probability that all five pass.
In a large population, 40% of people support a new policy. A random sample of 7 people is selected. Find the probability that exactly 2 of them support the policy.
A random variable \(X \sim B(8,\, 0.25)\). Calculate \(P(X = 2)\) and \(P(X = 3)\), and hence determine which value of \(r\) is more likely.
A batch of 12 electronic components is tested. Each component independently has a 0.15 probability of being faulty. Find the probability that none of the 12 components is faulty.
A basketball player has a free-throw success rate of 35%. She attempts 10 free throws in a game. Find the probability that she makes exactly 4 of them.
A random variable \(X \sim B(10,\, 0.3)\). By calculating \(P(X = 2)\), \(P(X = 3)\) and \(P(X = 4)\), determine the mode of \(X\).
A tennis player wins each point on her serve with probability 0.6, independently. In a game she serves 5 points. Find the probability that she wins at least 4 of the 5 points.

In a genetics experiment, each offspring independently has a probability of \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) of displaying a recessive trait. A sample of 9 offspring is observed. Find the probability that exactly 3 display the recessive trait.
A fair spinner has 5 equal sectors, one of which is red. The spinner is spun 8 times. Find the probability that it lands on red at least once but no more than 3 times.

A system contains 10 independent components, each with a 0.95 probability of working. The system functions only if all 10 components work. (a) Find the probability that the system functions. (b) Three such systems operate independently. Find the probability that all three systems function.

Process A produces items in batches of 3, each independently defective with probability 0.5. Process B produces items in batches of 4, each independently defective with probability 0.4. For each process, find the probability that a batch contains no defective items and state which process is more likely to produce a defect-free batch.
A random variable \(X \sim B(9,\, 0.6)\). Show that \(P(X = 5) = P(X = 6)\) and hence state the mode(s) of \(X\).

In a medical trial, a treatment is effective for each patient independently with probability 0.45. Six patients receive the treatment. Find the probability that the treatment is effective for at least 2 but no more than 4 of the patients.

y1sd3.questionText: The random variable \(X \sim B(10, 0.3)\). Using the cumulative binomial probability table, \(P(X \le 4) = 0.8497\). State the probability that \(X\) is at most 4.
The random variable \(X \sim B(10, 0.3)\). Given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.3828\) and \(P(X \le 3) = 0.6496\), find \(P(X = 3)\).
The random variable \(X \sim B(12, 0.4)\). Given that \(P(X \le 5) = 0.6652\), find \(P(X > 5)\).
The random variable \(X \sim B(15, 0.25)\). Given that \(P(X \le 3) = 0.4613\), find \(P(X \ge 4)\).
The random variable \(X \sim B(10, 0.3)\). Given that \(P(X \le 3) = 0.6496\), find \(P(X < 4)\).

A coin is biased so that the probability of obtaining a head on each toss is \(0.4\). The coin is tossed 12 times. Let \(X\) denote the number of heads obtained. Given that \(P(X \le 6) = 0.8418\), find the probability of obtaining more than 6 heads.
The random variable \(X \sim B(20, 0.3)\). Given that \(P(X \le 4) = 0.2375\) and \(P(X \le 8) = 0.8867\), find \(P(5 \le X \le 8)\).

A multiple-choice test has 15 questions, each with 4 options. A student guesses every answer. Let \(X\) be the number of correct answers, so \(X \sim B(15, 0.25)\). Given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.2361\) and \(P(X \le 5) = 0.8516\), find the probability that the student gets between 3 and 5 correct answers (inclusive).

The random variable \(X \sim B(10, 0.3)\). Using the cumulative binomial table values: \(P(X \le 1) = 0.1493\), \(P(X \le 4) = 0.8497\), \(P(X \le 5) = 0.9527\). Find (a) \(P(X \ge 2)\), (b) the probability that \(X\) takes a value from 2 to 5 inclusive.

A factory produces bolts. The probability that any bolt is defective is \(0.1\). A random sample of 20 bolts is taken. Let \(X\) be the number of defective bolts, so \(X \sim B(20, 0.1)\). Given that \(P(X \le 1) = 0.3917\) and \(P(X \le 3) = 0.8670\), find (a) the probability that fewer than 2 bolts are defective, (b) the probability that more than 3 bolts are defective.

A company claims that 30% of adults in a town use their product. A market researcher surveys 20 adults at random. Let \(X\) be the number who use the product, so \(X \sim B(20, 0.3)\). Given: \(P(X \le 3) = 0.1071\), \(P(X \le 5) = 0.4164\), \(P(X \le 8) = 0.8867\), \(P(X \le 9) = 0.9520\). Find (a) \(P(X \le 5)\), (b) \(P(X > 8)\), (c) \(P(4 \le X \le 9)\).
The random variable \(X \sim B(5, 0.4)\). By calculating individual probabilities, find \(P(X \le 2)\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

A bag contains a large number of balls, 25% of which are red. Balls are drawn one at a time with replacement. Let \(X\) be the number of red balls in 8 draws, so \(X \sim B(8, 0.25)\). Given that \(P(X \le 1) = 0.3671\) and \(P(X \le 4) = 0.9727\), find (a) \(P(X \ge 5)\), (b) \(P(2 \le X \le 4)\), (c) \(P(X = 2)\) by first finding \(P(X \le 2)\), given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.6785\).

A quality inspector checks items from a production line where 20% are faulty. She inspects 6 items at random. Let \(X\) be the number of faulty items, so \(X \sim B(6, 0.2)\). (a) Find \(P(X \le 1)\) by calculating \(P(X = 0)\) and \(P(X = 1)\). (b) Hence find the probability that at least 2 items are faulty. Give answers to 4 decimal places.

A doctor believes that 40% of patients with a certain condition respond to a new treatment. In a trial of 20 patients, let \(X\) be the number who respond, so \(X \sim B(20, 0.4)\). Using the cumulative binomial table: \(P(X \le 5) = 0.1256\), \(P(X \le 6) = 0.2500\), \(P(X \le 9) = 0.7553\), \(P(X \le 10) = 0.8725\), \(P(X \le 11) = 0.9435\). Find (a) \(P(X > 10)\), (b) \(P(7 \le X \le 11)\), (c) \(P(X = 6)\), (d) the probability that at most 5 or more than 10 patients respond.
The random variable \(X \sim B(4, 0.3)\). By calculating individual probabilities, find \(P(X \le 1)\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
A fair coin is tossed 6 times. Let \(X\) be the number of heads, so \(X \sim B(6, 0.5)\). Given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.3438\), find the probability of obtaining no more than 2 heads.

In a call centre, the probability that any call is a complaint is \(0.35\). In a sample of 8 calls, let \(X\) be the number of complaints, so \(X \sim B(8, 0.35)\). Given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.4278\), find the probability that at least 3 calls are complaints.
The random variable \(X \sim B(15, 0.2)\). Given that \(P(X \le 3) = 0.6482\), find (a) \(P(X < 4)\), (b) \(P(X \ge 4)\).
The random variable \(X \sim B(10, 0.45)\). Given that \(P(X \le 3) = 0.2660\) and \(P(X \le 6) = 0.8980\), find \(P(3 < X < 7)\).

A manufacturer finds that 15% of components produced are slightly scratched. A random sample of 5 components is taken. Let \(X\) be the number of scratched components, so \(X \sim B(5, 0.15)\). By first calculating \(P(X = 0)\) and \(P(X = 1)\), find the probability that at least 2 components are scratched. Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

A customer service department finds that 35% of incoming emails require a response within one hour. In a batch of 20 emails, let \(X\) be the number requiring a fast response, so \(X \sim B(20, 0.35)\). Given that \(P(X \le 5) = 0.2454\) and \(P(X \le 10) = 0.9468\), find (a) \(P(X > 10)\), (b) \(P(6 \le X \le 10)\).

Students sit a test where each question is multiple choice with 5 options. A student guesses all answers on a 10-question test. Let \(X\) be the number of correct answers, so \(X \sim B(10, 0.2)\). Given that \(P(X \le 1) = 0.3758\) and \(P(X \le 4) = 0.9672\), find the probability that the student gets more than 1 but fewer than 5 correct answers.

In a school, 15% of students are left-handed. A class of 12 students is chosen at random. Let \(X\) be the number of left-handed students, so \(X \sim B(12, 0.15)\). Given: \(P(X \le 0) = 0.1422\), \(P(X \le 1) = 0.4435\), \(P(X \le 3) = 0.9078\), \(P(X \le 4) = 0.9761\). Find (a) \(P(X \ge 2)\), (b) \(P(2 \le X \le 4)\), (c) \(P(X > 3)\).
The random variable \(X \sim B(10, 0.5)\). Given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.0547\) and \(P(X \le 6) = 0.8281\), find (a) \(P(2 < X < 7)\), (b) \(P(X \ge 7)\).

The random variable \(X \sim B(20, 0.4)\). The following cumulative probabilities are given: \(P(X \le 8) = 0.5956\), \(P(X \le 9) = 0.7553\), \(P(X \le 10) = 0.8725\), \(P(X \le 11) = 0.9435\). Find the smallest integer \(c\) such that \(P(X \le c) \ge 0.9\).

In a factory, 60% of items pass a quality check on the first attempt. A random sample of 7 items is taken. Let \(X\) be the number that pass, so \(X \sim B(7, 0.6)\). By calculating \(P(X = 5)\), \(P(X = 6)\) and \(P(X = 7)\) directly, find \(P(X \ge 5)\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

A training programme has an 80% success rate. From a group of 18 trainees, let \(X\) be the number who complete successfully, so \(X \sim B(18, 0.8)\). Given: \(P(X \le 12) = 0.1329\), \(P(X \le 13) = 0.2836\), \(P(X \le 14) = 0.4990\), \(P(X \le 15) = 0.7287\), \(P(X \le 16) = 0.9009\). Find (a) \(P(X \ge 15)\), (b) \(P(13 < X < 17)\), (c) \(P(X = 14)\), (d) the probability that at most 13 or more than 16 trainees complete successfully.

The random variable \(X \sim B(10, 0.3)\). Given that \(P(X \le 2) = 0.3828\) and \(P(X \le 6) = 0.9894\), find (a) \(P(3 \le X \le 6)\), (b) \(P(X \le 2 \text{ or } X \ge 7)\). State which method you use for part (b) and explain why it works.

A machine produces electronic chips with a defect rate of 10%. A batch of 25 chips is inspected. Let \(X\) be the number of defective chips, so \(X \sim B(25, 0.1)\). Given: \(P(X \le 0) = 0.0718\), \(P(X \le 1) = 0.2712\), \(P(X \le 2) = 0.5371\), \(P(X \le 3) = 0.7636\), \(P(X \le 4) = 0.9020\), \(P(X \le 5) = 0.9666\). Find (a) \(P(X \ge 4)\), (b) \(P(1 \le X \le 4)\), (c) the smallest integer \(k\) such that \(P(X \le k) \ge 0.95\).

y1sd4.questionText: A fair six-sided die is rolled 60 times. Let \(X\) be the number of sixes obtained. Given that \(X \sim B(60, \tfrac{1}{6})\), find \(E(X)\).
A biased coin has probability \(0.3\) of landing heads. The coin is flipped 20 times and \(X\) is the number of heads. Find \(\text{Var}(X)\).

A manufacturer knows that 5% of items produced are defective. A sample of 80 items is taken and \(X\) is the number of defective items. Assuming \(X \sim B(80, 0.05)\), find the mean and standard deviation of \(X\).
Given that \(X \sim B(50, 0.4)\), find \(E(X)\) and \(\text{Var}(X)\).

In a large school, 15% of students are left-handed. A random sample of 40 students is selected and \(X\) is the number who are left-handed. Assuming a binomial model, find the mean, variance and standard deviation of \(X\).
A random variable \(X \sim B(25, p)\). Given that \(E(X) = 5\), find the value of \(p\) and hence find \(\text{Var}(X)\).
A random variable \(X \sim B(n, 0.3)\). Given that \(\text{Var}(X) = 6.3\), find the value of \(n\) and state \(E(X)\).
A student claims that the number of rainy days in a week in London can be modelled by \(B(7, 0.4)\). State two assumptions required for this model and comment on whether each is likely to be valid.

A factory produces bolts, and quality control records show that 2% are faulty. A box of 50 bolts is selected at random. Let \(X\) be the number of faulty bolts in the box. (a) State a suitable distribution for \(X\), giving its parameters. (b) Find \(E(X)\) and \(\text{Var}(X)\). (c) State one assumption you have made.

A new vaccine is trialled on 200 patients. It is believed that the probability of a patient experiencing side effects is 0.08, independently of other patients. Let \(X\) be the number of patients who experience side effects. (a) Write down the distribution of \(X\). (b) Calculate the mean and standard deviation of \(X\). (c) In the trial, 25 patients experienced side effects. Comment on the suitability of the model.
A teacher asks 30 students in her class whether they walk to school. She models the number who walk as \(X \sim B(30, 0.25)\). Explain why this binomial model might not be appropriate.
A random variable \(X \sim B(n, p)\). Given that \(E(X) = 9\) and \(\text{Var}(X) = 6.3\), find the values of \(n\) and \(p\).

A polling company surveys 500 randomly selected adults and asks whether they support a new policy. They model the number who support the policy as \(X \sim B(500, 0.35)\). (a) Find \(E(X)\) and \(\sigma\). (b) The survey found that 205 adults supported the policy. By comparing with the model, determine whether the result is consistent with \(p = 0.35\). (c) State two conditions required for the binomial model to be valid in this context.
A random variable \(X \sim B(n, p)\). Given that \(E(X) = 24\) and the standard deviation of \(X\) is \(\sqrt{4.8}\), find the values of \(n\) and \(p\).

A company manufactures circuit boards in batches of 100. Historically, each board has a 0.04 probability of being faulty, independently of other boards. Let \(X\) be the number of faulty boards in a batch. (a) State the distribution of \(X\) and find its mean, variance and standard deviation. (b) The company rejects a batch if it contains 8 or more faulty boards. Using the mean and standard deviation, explain why a batch being rejected would be an unusual event. (c) After a machine upgrade, batches of 100 boards are produced. Over many batches the mean number of faulty boards is found to be 2.1 and the variance is 1.89. Determine whether these observations are consistent with a binomial model, and if so, estimate \(p\).

An ecologist surveys 120 trees in a forest. Each tree has a probability of 0.15 of hosting a particular species of bird, independently of other trees. Let \(X\) be the number of trees hosting the bird species. Find \(E(X)\) and interpret your answer in context.

A shop finds that 12% of customers use a loyalty card. On a particular day, 75 customers visit the shop. Let \(X\) be the number of customers who use a loyalty card. Assuming \(X \sim B(75, 0.12)\), find the variance and standard deviation of \(X\).
