y2ld.topicTitle: Large Data Sets & Data in Context 71
y2ld.questionText: The journey times, \(t\) minutes, of commuters on two routes to a city were recorded. Route X (\(50\) commuters) and Route Y (\(50\) commuters) gave the grouped data:\[\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{Time } t\text{ (min)} & \text{Route X freq} & \text{Route Y freq}\\\hline 10\le t<20 & 9 & 4\\ 20\le t<30 & 18 & 14\\ 30\le t<40 & 15 & 20\\ 40\le t<50 & 6 & 9\\ 50\le t<60 & 2 & 3\end{array}\]\((a)\) Estimate the mean journey time for each route. \((b)\) Estimate the standard deviation of the journey times for Route X. \((c)\) Compare the two routes in context, referring to your statistics. \((d)\) A commuter who values reliability asks which route to take. Using your results, advise the commuter and state one further piece of information that would help the decision.

y2na.questionText: A binomial random variable \( X \) has \( n = 50 \) and \( p = 0.5 \). By checking the conditions \( np > 5 \) and \( n(1-p) > 5 \), determine whether a Normal approximation to \( X \) is valid.
A binomial random variable \( X \) has \( n = 12 \) and \( p = 0.3 \). By checking the conditions \( np > 5 \) and \( n(1-p) > 5 \), determine whether a Normal approximation to \( X \) is valid.
The random variable \( X \sim B(40, 0.45) \). State the Normal distribution \( N(\mu, \sigma^2) \) that approximates \( X \), giving the mean \( \mu = np \) and variance \( \sigma^2 = np(1-p) \).
When approximating the discrete \( X \sim B(n,p) \) by a continuous Normal variable \( Y \), a continuity correction is applied. Write the corrected Normal probability for \( P(X \ge 20) \).
The random variable \( X \sim B(100, 0.5) \). Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find \( P(X \le 45) \). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
The random variable \( X \sim B(80, 0.45) \). Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find \( P(X \ge 40) \). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
The random variable \( X \sim B(200, 0.4) \). Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find \( P(X < 75) \). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
The random variable \( X \sim B(150, 0.6) \). Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find \( P(X > 95) \). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
The random variable \( X \sim B(120, 0.55) \). Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find \( P(X = 70) \). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
The random variable \( X \sim B(64, 0.5) \). Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find \( P(X \ge 36) \). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

The random variable \( X \sim B(90, 0.5) \). First confirm a Normal approximation is valid using \( np > 5 \) and \( n(1-p) > 5 \), then with a continuity correction find \( P(X \le 40) \). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
The random variable \( X \sim B(80, 0.25) \) is to be approximated by a Normal distribution \( Y \). Write down the mean and variance of \( Y \).
The random variable \( X \sim B(150, 0.4) \) is approximated by a Normal distribution \( Y \). Find the mean and standard deviation of \( Y \).
A random variable follows \( X \sim B(50, 0.3) \). By considering \( np \) and \( n(1-p) \), state whether a Normal approximation is appropriate, giving a reason.
A random variable follows \( X \sim B(200, 0.01) \). By considering \( np \) and \( n(1-p) \), state whether a Normal approximation is appropriate, giving a reason.

The binomial random variable \( X \) is approximated by a Normal variable \( Y \). Write down the continuity correction needed to approximate \( P(X \le 30) \), and the resulting probability statement in terms of \( Y \).

The binomial random variable \( X \) is approximated by a Normal variable \( Y \). Write down the continuity correction needed to approximate \( P(X \ge 18) \), and the resulting probability statement in terms of \( Y \).

The binomial random variable \( X \) is approximated by a Normal variable \( Y \). Write down the continuity correction needed to approximate \( P(X = 22) \), and the resulting probability statement in terms of \( Y \).
The random variable \( X \sim B(100, 0.4) \) is approximated by a Normal variable \( Y \). Using a continuity correction, find \( P(X \le 45) \).
The random variable \( X \sim B(120, 0.45) \) is approximated by a Normal variable \( Y \). Using a continuity correction, find \( P(X \ge 60) \).
The random variable \( X \sim B(90, 0.3) \) is approximated by a Normal variable \( Y \). Using a continuity correction, find \( P(X = 25) \).
The random variable \( X \sim B(100, 0.45) \) is approximated by a Normal variable \( Y \). Using a continuity correction, find \( P(40 \le X \le 50) \).

A machine produces components, each independently defective with probability \( 0.12 \). In a batch of \( 200 \) components, let \( X \) be the number that are defective. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X \le 30) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

In an election, \( 45\% \) of all voters support a particular candidate. A random sample of \( 500 \) voters is taken and \( X \) is the number in the sample who support the candidate. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X \ge 240) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

A packet contains \( 300 \) seeds, each germinating independently with probability \( 0.8 \). Let \( X \) be the number of seeds that germinate. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(230 \le X \le 250) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.
A fair coin is flipped \( 400 \) times and \( X \) is the number of heads obtained. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X = 210) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

A large delivery of light bulbs has each bulb independently faulty with probability \( 0.08 \). A sample of \( 250 \) bulbs is tested and \( X \) is the number found to be faulty. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X \le 25) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

A tray holds \( 400 \) seeds, each germinating independently with probability \( 0.85 \). Let \( X \) be the number that germinate. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X \ge 350) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.
A fair coin is flipped \( 1000 \) times and \( X \) is the number of heads obtained. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(480 \le X \le 520) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

A production line makes microchips, each independently defective with probability \( 0.10 \). In a run of \( 600 \) chips, let \( X \) be the number that are defective. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X = 55) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

In a town, \( 30\% \) of residents say they would vote yes in a referendum. A random sample of \( 800 \) residents is surveyed and \( X \) is the number who say yes. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X \le 230) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

A fair six-sided die is rolled \( 720 \) times and \( X \) is the number of times a six is obtained. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X \ge 130) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

An airline finds that each passenger holding a reservation independently shows up for a flight with probability \( 0.92 \). On a day with \( 450 \) reservations, let \( X \) be the number who show up. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(405 \le X \le 420) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

In a large bag of sweets, each sweet is independently red with probability \( 0.40 \). A sample of \( 350 \) sweets is taken and \( X \) is the number that are red. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X = 145) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

An email filter classifies incoming messages, and each message is independently spam with probability \( 0.20 \). On a day with \( 1200 \) messages, let \( X \) be the number that are spam. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X \le 230) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

In a population, each person is independently left-handed with probability \( 0.10 \). A random sample of \( 900 \) people is taken and \( X \) is the number who are left-handed. Using a suitable Normal approximation, find \( P(X \ge 100) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.

In a large town, \( 55\% \) of households own a pet. A random sample of \( 100 \) households is taken and the number that own a pet, \( X \), is recorded, where \( X \sim B(100, 0.55) \). Using a suitable Normal approximation, estimate the probability that more than \( 60 \) households own a pet.

A biased coin shows heads with probability \( 0.4 \). The coin is tossed \( 120 \) times and the number of heads, \( X \), is recorded, where \( X \sim B(120, 0.4) \). Using a suitable Normal approximation, estimate the probability of obtaining fewer than \( 40 \) heads.

In a manufacturing process, each item is independently classified as type A with probability \( 0.5 \). In a batch of \( 200 \) items the number of type A items, \( X \), follows \( X \sim B(200, 0.5) \). Using a suitable Normal approximation, estimate the probability that the number of type A items is between \( 95 \) and \( 110 \) inclusive.

On a commuter route, each train is late with probability \( 0.45 \), independently of other trains. Over a period of \( 80 \) trains, let \( X \) be the number that are late, so \( X \sim B(80, 0.45) \). Find the expected number of late trains, and then use a suitable Normal approximation to estimate the probability that at least \( 40 \) trains are late.

A fair spinner lands on red with probability \( 0.5 \). It is spun \( 50 \) times and the number of reds, \( X \), follows \( X \sim B(50, 0.5) \). First check that a Normal approximation is appropriate, then use it to estimate the probability that at most \( 20 \) reds are obtained.

The random variable \( X \sim B(40, 0.5) \). The exact value of \( P(X \le 15) \) is \( 0.0769 \) to 4 decimal places. Use a Normal approximation with a continuity correction to estimate \( P(X \le 15) \), and comment on how close your estimate is to the exact value.

A researcher models the number of voters in a sample of \( 150 \) who support a particular policy as \( X \sim B(150, 0.48) \), and approximates this distribution by \( N(72, 37.44) \). Explain why a Normal approximation to this binomial distribution is reasonable in this case.

An online retailer finds that \( 52\% \) of customers opt in to marketing emails. In a random sample of \( 300 \) customers the number who opt in, \( X \), follows \( X \sim B(300, 0.52) \). Using a suitable Normal approximation, estimate the probability that more than \( 170 \) customers opt in.

A seed supplier states that each seed germinates with probability \( 0.6 \), independently. A tray contains \( 90 \) seeds and the number that germinate, \( X \), follows \( X \sim B(90, 0.6) \). Using a suitable Normal approximation, estimate the probability that fewer than \( 50 \) seeds germinate.

In a survey, each respondent independently chooses option X with probability \( 0.44 \). For a sample of \( 250 \) respondents the number choosing option X, \( X \), follows \( X \sim B(250, 0.44) \). Using a suitable Normal approximation, estimate the probability that strictly between \( 100 \) and \( 120 \) respondents choose option X.

A call centre finds that \( 35\% \) of calls result in a sale. On a busy day there are \( 160 \) independent calls, and the number resulting in a sale, \( X \), follows \( X \sim B(160, 0.35) \). Find the expected number of sales, and then use a suitable Normal approximation to estimate the probability of at least \( 70 \) sales.

A test consists of \( 400 \) true/false questions and a candidate guesses every answer, so the number of correct answers \( X \) follows \( X \sim B(400, 0.5) \). First check that a Normal approximation is appropriate, then use it to estimate the probability that the candidate gets at least \( 210 \) answers correct.

The random variable \( X \sim B(60, 0.5) \). The exact value of \( P(X = 30) \) is \( 0.1026 \) to 4 decimal places. Use a Normal approximation with a continuity correction to estimate \( P(X = 30) \), and comment on how close your estimate is to the exact value.

A factory produces components and the number that pass inspection in a batch of \( 200 \) is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(200, 0.4) \). Using a suitable Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find the smallest integer \( k \) such that \( \mathrm{P}(X \ge k) \le 0.05 \).

In a survey, each of \( 150 \) people independently answers 'yes' with probability \( 0.5 \). Let \( X \) be the number who answer 'yes', so \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(150, 0.5) \). Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find the smallest integer \( k \) for which \( \mathrm{P}(X \le k) \ge 0.90 \).

A machine fills \( 400 \) jars per hour, and each jar is correctly filled independently with probability \( 0.55 \). Let \( X \) be the number of correctly filled jars in an hour, so \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(400, 0.55) \). Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find the smallest integer \( k \) such that \( \mathrm{P}(X \ge k) \le 0.01 \).

On any given day, \( 180 \) trains run on a line and each arrives on time independently with probability \( 0.5 \). Let \( X \) be the number arriving on time, so \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(180, 0.5) \). (a) Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, estimate \( \mathrm{P}(X \ge 100) \). (b) Hence, assuming days are independent, estimate the probability that on at least \( 2 \) of the next \( 3 \) days at least \( 100 \) trains arrive on time.

A call centre receives \( 250 \) calls in a shift, and each call independently is resolved on the first attempt with probability \( 0.32 \). Let \( X \) be the number resolved on the first attempt, so \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(250, 0.32) \). Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, estimate \( \mathrm{P}(70 \le X \le 90) \).

A fair coin is tossed \( 50 \) times and \( X \) is the number of heads, so \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(50, 0.5) \). (a) Find the exact value of \( \mathrm{P}(X \ge 30) \). (b) Use a Normal approximation with a continuity correction to estimate \( \mathrm{P}(X \ge 30) \), and comment on the size of the error.

The random variable \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(40, 0.45) \). (a) Find the exact value of \( \mathrm{P}(X = 18) \). (b) Use a Normal approximation with a continuity correction to estimate \( \mathrm{P}(X = 18) \), and comment on the accuracy of the approximation.

The random variable \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(100, 0.5) \), with exact probability \( \mathrm{P}(X \le 45) = 0.1841 \) (to 4 d.p.). A student estimates \( \mathrm{P}(X \le 45) \) using a Normal approximation but forgets the continuity correction, computing \( \mathrm{P}(Y \le 45) \). Find the value the student obtains and the value obtained with the correct continuity correction, and comment on the effect of omitting the correction.

A retailer sends out \( 320 \) marketing emails, and each is opened independently with probability \( 0.35 \). Let \( X \) be the number opened, so \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(320, 0.35) \). (a) Show that a suitable Normal approximation to the distribution of \( X \) is \( \mathrm{N}(112, 72.8) \). (b) Hence use this approximation, with a continuity correction, to estimate \( \mathrm{P}(X \le 100) \).

A large quiz platform has \( 600 \) users attempt a question, and each answers correctly independently with probability \( 0.6 \). Let \( X \) be the number of correct answers, so \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(600, 0.6) \). (a) Show that the approximating Normal distribution is \( \mathrm{N}(360, 144) \), and hence write down its standard deviation. (b) Using this approximation with a continuity correction, find the smallest integer \( k \) such that \( \mathrm{P}(X \le k) \ge 0.975 \).

A fair coin is tossed \( 500 \) times each day and \( X \) is the number of heads, so \( X \sim \mathrm{B}(500, 0.5) \). (a) Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, estimate \( \mathrm{P}(230 \le X \le 270) \). (b) Hence, assuming days are independent, estimate the probability that \( X \) lies in the interval \( [230, 270] \) on each of \( 4 \) consecutive days.

A fair process produces successes with probability \( 0.34 \) on each of \( 200 \) independent trials, so \( X\sim B(200,0.34) \). \( X \) is to be approximated by a Normal distribution. (a) State the approximating distribution. (b) Use it, with a continuity correction, to estimate \( P(X\le 60) \). (c) The exact binomial value is \( 0.1310 \). By also computing the estimate without a continuity correction, comment on the size of the error introduced by omitting the correction.

The random variable \( X\sim B(80,0.45) \) is approximated by a suitable Normal distribution. (a) Justify briefly why the Normal approximation is reasonable here. (b) Using a continuity correction, estimate \( P(30\le X\le 40) \).

A student wants to estimate \( P(X\le 6) \) for \( X\sim B(15,0.3) \) by using a Normal approximation. Critically assess whether the Normal approximation is appropriate here. State clearly the condition you are checking, what it evaluates to, and what method should be used instead.

On each of \( 150 \) independent days a machine has probability \( 0.4 \) of needing a reset, so \( X\sim B(150,0.4) \) is the number of reset days in a period. Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find the smallest integer \( k \) for which \( P(X\ge k)\le 0.05 \).

A batch contains \( 500 \) electronic components, each independently faulty with probability \( 0.06 \). Let \( X \) be the number of faulty components. (a) Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, estimate \( P(X>40) \). (b) The supplier claims that 'more than \( 40 \) faults in a batch is a typical occurrence'. Using your answer, comment on this claim.

A web server handles \( 2000 \) independent requests, each failing with probability \( 0.001 \). Let \( X \) be the number of failures, so \( X\sim B(2000,0.001) \). A colleague suggests approximating \( X \) by a Normal distribution to find \( P(X\le 3) \). Critically evaluate this suggestion: state which approximation is appropriate and why, and carry out the more suitable approximation to estimate \( P(X\le 3) \).

A binomial random variable \( X\sim B(n,p) \) is approximated by a Normal distribution with mean \( 48 \) and variance \( 28.8 \). (a) By relating the Normal parameters back to \( np \) and \( np(1-p) \), find the values of \( n \) and \( p \). (b) Hence use the approximation, with a continuity correction, to estimate \( P(X\le 45) \).

A fair coin is tossed \( 100 \) times and \( X\sim B(100,0.5) \) is the number of heads. (a) Use a Normal approximation with a continuity correction to estimate \( P(X = 50) \). (b) Explain why any attempt to estimate this single-value probability without a continuity correction must fail, and state the size of error that omitting the correction would produce here (the exact value is \( 0.0796 \)).

A grower sows \( 300 \) seeds, each germinating independently with probability \( 0.85 \). Let \( X \) be the number that germinate. (a) Using a Normal approximation with a continuity correction, estimate \( P(X < 250) \). (b) The grower needs at least \( 250 \) seedlings to fill an order. Interpret your answer in this context, and state whether the order is likely to be met.

In a quality survey, each of \( 400 \) independently selected items is non-conforming with probability \( 0.2 \), so \( X\sim B(400,0.2) \). Using a Normal approximation, find values \( a \) and \( b \) (symmetric about the mean) such that the central region \( P(a\le X\le b)\approx 0.90 \). Give \( a \) and \( b \) as integers, applying a continuity correction.

For \( X\sim B(1000,0.5) \) the probability \( P(X\le 480) \) is to be estimated by a Normal approximation. The exact binomial value is \( 0.1087 \). (a) Compute the Normal estimate both with and without a continuity correction. (b) Hence discuss whether the continuity correction is worth applying when \( n \) is this large, justifying your answer with the sizes of the two errors.

y2nm.questionText: The random variable \( X \) has a Normal distribution with mean \( 30 \) and variance \( 25 \). Write down the value of \( \mu \) and the value of \( \sigma \) for \( X \).
A Normal distribution is symmetrical about its mean. Explain why this symmetry means that the mean and the median of a Normal distribution are equal.
The random variable \( X \sim N(40, 6^2) \). Write down the value of \( P(X < 40) \) and explain your answer.
The random variable \( X \sim N(50, 16) \). Find \( P(X < 56) \).
The random variable \( X \sim N(20, 25) \). Find \( P(X > 27) \).
The heights, \( H\,\mathrm{cm} \), of a large group of plants are modelled by \( H \sim N(100, 225) \). Find the probability that a randomly chosen plant is shorter than \( 118\,\mathrm{cm} \).
The times, \( T \) minutes, taken to complete a puzzle are modelled by \( T \sim N(8, 4) \). Find the probability that a randomly chosen person takes more than \( 11 \) minutes.
The random variable \( X \sim N(70, 64) \). Find the standardised value (the \( z \)-score) of \( X = 82 \).
The masses, \( M\,\mathrm{g} \), of apples from an orchard are modelled by \( M \sim N(60, 100) \). Find the probability that a randomly chosen apple has a mass less than \( 75\,\mathrm{g} \).

A data set is well modelled by a Normal distribution. A student claims that for this model the mean, the median and the mode are all equal. State whether the student is correct, and give a reason involving the shape of the distribution.
The lifetimes, \( L \) hours, of a type of battery are modelled by \( L \sim N(500, 1600) \). Find the probability that a randomly chosen battery lasts less than \( 540 \) hours.
The random variable \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(50,\ 4^2) \). Find \( P(46 < X < 54) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.
The random variable \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(70,\ 5^2) \). Find \( P(X < 78) \), giving your answer to 4 decimal places.
IQ scores are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(100,\ 15^2) \). Find the probability that a randomly chosen person has an IQ greater than \( 120 \). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

The heights of a species of plant (in cm) are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(160,\ 8^2) \). Using the empirical (68–95–99.7) rule, state the proportion of plants with heights between \( 152\ \mathrm{cm} \) and \( 168\ \mathrm{cm} \).

A machine fills bottles with a mean of \( 200\ \mathrm{ml} \) and standard deviation \( 10\ \mathrm{ml} \), modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(200,\ 10^2) \). Using the empirical rule, find the proportion of bottles containing between \( 180\ \mathrm{ml} \) and \( 220\ \mathrm{ml} \).

The lifetimes of a battery (in hours) are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(500,\ 20^2) \). Using the empirical rule, find the proportion of batteries with lifetimes between \( 440 \) hours and \( 560 \) hours.

The bell-shaped curve of a normal distribution \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu,\ \sigma^2) \) has two points of inflection. State, in terms of \( \mu \) and \( \sigma \), where these points occur and explain what they represent about the distribution.
The masses of apples (in grams) are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(50,\ 4^2) \). In a crate of \( 200 \) apples, estimate the number of apples with a mass greater than \( 58\ \mathrm{g} \).
The random variable \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(60,\ 5^2) \). Find the value of \( x \) such that \( P(X < x) = 0.90 \), giving your answer to 2 decimal places.
The random variable \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(75,\ 6^2) \). Find the value of \( x \) such that \( P(X > x) = 0.10 \), giving your answer to 2 decimal places.
The test scores of \( 500 \) students are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(75,\ 4^2) \). Estimate the number of students scoring between \( 70 \) and \( 80 \).

The heights of adult men in a population are modelled by a Normal distribution \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(175,\,8^2) \), where \( X \) is the height in \( \mathrm{cm} \). Find, to the nearest \( \mathrm{cm} \), the height \( a \) exceeded by only the tallest \( 10\% \) of men, i.e. the value \( a \) for which \( P(X<a)=0.90 \).
The mass of flour, in grams, dispensed by a machine into bags is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(500,\,12^2) \). Find, to \( 1 \) decimal place, the value \( a \) such that \( P(X>a)=0.05 \).

The time, in minutes, taken by athletes to complete a training circuit is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(42,\,6^2) \). Find the lower quartile of these times, giving your answer to \( 1 \) decimal place.

The marks scored by candidates in an examination are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(58,\,14^2) \). A distinction is awarded to the top \( 10\% \) of candidates. Find, to the nearest mark, the lowest mark that earns a distinction.

The lengths, in centimetres, of metal rods produced by a factory are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(20,\,2.5^2) \). The shortest \( 15\% \) of rods are rejected. Find, to \( 2 \) decimal places, the greatest length of a rejected rod.
The time, in seconds, taken for a chemical reaction to complete is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(68,\,3^2) \). Find \( P(65<X<70) \), giving your answer to \( 4 \) decimal places.

The volume of juice, in millilitres, dispensed into cartons is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(350,\,20^2) \). A carton is underfilled if it contains less than \( 340\ \mathrm{ml} \). In a batch of \( 200 \) cartons, find the expected number that are underfilled.
The mass, in kilograms, of newborn lambs on a farm is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(12.4,\,1.8^2) \). Find the upper quartile of these masses, giving your answer to \( 2 \) decimal places.
The mass, in kilograms, of bags of compost is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(2.5,\,0.4^2) \). Find the 80th percentile of the masses, giving your answer to \( 2 \) decimal places.
Scores on a standardised aptitude test are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(100,\,15^2) \). Find \( P(112<X<130) \), giving your answer to \( 4 \) decimal places.

The marks scored by \( 2000 \) candidates in a national test are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(512,\,85^2) \). A scholarship is offered to anyone scoring more than \( 650 \) marks. Estimate the number of candidates offered a scholarship.

The daily maximum temperature, in \( {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C} \), at a resort in summer is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(24,\,3^2) \). On the hottest \( 5\% \) of days the temperature exceeds \( a\ {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C} \). Find \( a \) to \( 1 \) decimal place.
The time, in minutes, that customers spend waiting in a queue is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(15.2,\,2.4^2) \). Find the value \( a \), to \( 1 \) decimal place, for which \( P(X>a)=0.30 \).

The heights, in centimetres, of sunflowers grown in a trial are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(180,\,10^2) \). In a field of \( 500 \) sunflowers, estimate the number whose height is between \( 170\ \mathrm{cm} \) and \( 195\ \mathrm{cm} \).

The lifetime, in hours, of a brand of LED bulb is modelled by a normal distribution with standard deviation \( 120\,\mathrm{hours} \). It is found that \( 30\% \) of bulbs last longer than \( 1000\,\mathrm{hours} \). Find the mean lifetime \( \mu \), giving your answer to the nearest hour.

A machine fills bags with sugar. The mass of sugar, in grams, is normally distributed with standard deviation \( 8\,\mathrm{g} \). Only \( 10\% \) of bags contain less than \( 500\,\mathrm{g} \). Find the mean mass \( \mu \) of a bag, to 1 decimal place.

A component is manufactured to a target length with mean \( 50\,\mathrm{mm} \). The length is normally distributed and \( 2.5\% \) of components are longer than \( 53\,\mathrm{mm} \). Find the standard deviation \( \sigma \), to 2 decimal places.

The reaction time of a driver, in seconds, is normally distributed with mean \( 0.30\,\mathrm{s} \). It is known that \( 20\% \) of drivers react in less than \( 0.25\,\mathrm{s} \). Find the standard deviation \( \sigma \), to 3 decimal places.

A factory produces bolts whose diameter is normally distributed with mean \( 10.00\,\mathrm{mm} \) and standard deviation \( 0.04\,\mathrm{mm} \). A bolt is accepted only if its diameter lies between \( 9.95\,\mathrm{mm} \) and \( 10.05\,\mathrm{mm} \). Find the proportion of bolts that are rejected.

A bottling machine dispenses a drink with mean volume \( 250\,\mathrm{ml} \), normally distributed. The manufacturer requires \( 99\% \) of bottles to contain between \( 245\,\mathrm{ml} \) and \( 255\,\mathrm{ml} \). Assuming this band is symmetric about the mean, find the largest permitted standard deviation \( \sigma \), to 3 decimal places.

The mass of an adult male of a certain species, in kilograms, is normally distributed with mean \( 70\,\mathrm{kg} \) and standard deviation \( 10\,\mathrm{kg} \). (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen male has mass greater than \( 85\,\mathrm{kg} \). (b) The heaviest \( 5\% \) are classed as "large". Find the minimum mass for a male to be classed as large.

Marks in an examination are normally distributed with mean \( 55 \) and standard deviation \( 12 \). (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen candidate scores between \( 40 \) and \( 70 \) marks. (b) A distinction is awarded to the top \( 10\% \). Find the minimum mark needed for a distinction.

The daily rainfall at a weather station in winter, in millimetres, is modelled by a normal distribution with mean \( 2.4\,\mathrm{mm} \) and standard deviation \( 0.8\,\mathrm{mm} \). Find the probability that on a randomly chosen winter day the rainfall exceeds \( 3.5\,\mathrm{mm} \).

A factory cuts steel pipes whose length is normally distributed with mean \( 2.50\,\mathrm{m} \) and standard deviation \( 0.02\,\mathrm{m} \). Find the probability that a randomly chosen pipe has length between \( 2.46\,\mathrm{m} \) and \( 2.53\,\mathrm{m} \).

A coffee machine dispenses coffee with a volume that is normally distributed with standard deviation \( 5\,\mathrm{ml} \). The machine is set so that only \( 2\% \) of cups contain less than \( 200\,\mathrm{ml} \). (a) Find the mean volume \( \mu \) dispensed, to 2 decimal places. (b) Using this mean, find the probability that a cup contains more than \( 215\,\mathrm{ml} \).

The heights of adult women in a large population have mean \( 163\,\mathrm{cm} \) and standard deviation \( 7\,\mathrm{cm} \). A statistician proposes modelling height with a normal distribution. State, with two reasons, whether a normal model is suitable here.

At a clinic, the waiting time for patients has mean \( 4\,\mathrm{minutes} \) and standard deviation \( 3\,\mathrm{minutes} \). A student suggests modelling waiting time with a normal distribution. Discuss whether this is appropriate, justifying your answer.

The random variable \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \). It is given that \( \mathrm{P}(X < 20) = 0.1056 \) and \( \mathrm{P}(X > 40) = 0.1056 \). Find the value of \( \mu \) and the value of \( \sigma \).

The masses, in grams, of a population of birds are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \). It is found that \( \mathrm{P}(X < 460) = 0.0228 \) and \( \mathrm{P}(X > 530) = 0.0668 \). Find the value of \( \mu \) and the value of \( \sigma \).

The diameters, in millimetres, of ball bearings produced by a machine follow \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(160, 12^2) \). A bearing is selected at random. Given that its diameter exceeds \( 145\,\mathrm{mm} \), find the probability that its diameter also exceeds \( 175\,\mathrm{mm} \).

A machine dispenses coffee into cups. The volume dispensed, \( V\,\mathrm{ml} \), is modelled by \( V \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \). The machine is known to underfill (dispense less than \( 500\,\mathrm{ml} \)) on \( 2\% \) of cups, and to overfill (dispense more than \( 520\,\mathrm{ml} \)) on \( 10\% \) of cups. Find \( \mu \) and \( \sigma \), giving your answers to 3 significant figures.

The scores in a test are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(72, 15^2) \). A distinction is awarded to the top \( 10\% \) of candidates. (a) Find the minimum whole-number score needed for a distinction. (b) A cohort contains \( 250 \) candidates. Find the expected number who achieve a distinction.

The times, in minutes, taken by customers to complete a survey are modelled by \( T \sim \mathrm{N}(50, 8^2) \). (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen customer takes between \( 45 \) and \( 60 \) minutes. (b) On a day when \( 400 \) customers complete the survey, find the expected number who take between \( 45 \) and \( 60 \) minutes.

The number of minutes by which a daily train is late is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(8.5, 2^2) \). On a given day the train is known to be more than \( 10 \) minutes late. Find the probability that it is in fact more than \( 12 \) minutes late.

The operating lifetimes, in hours, of a brand of light bulb are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(1200, 150^2) \). The manufacturer offers a warranty and wishes only \( 2.5\% \) of bulbs to fail before the warranty period ends. (a) Find the warranty period, to the nearest hour. (b) In a batch of \( 5000 \) bulbs, find the expected number that fail before this warranty period.

The amount of rainfall, \( X\,\mathrm{mm} \), recorded at a weather station on a rainy day is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \). Records show that \( 20\% \) of rainy days have more than \( 30\,\mathrm{mm} \) of rain, and \( 10\% \) have less than \( 20\,\mathrm{mm} \). Find \( \mu \) and \( \sigma \), giving your answers to 3 significant figures.

The heights, in centimetres, of adult males in a population are modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(178, 7^2) \). A man is chosen at random from those taller than \( 183\,\mathrm{cm} \). Find the probability that he is taller than \( 190\,\mathrm{cm} \).

The annual rainfall, \( X\,\mathrm{mm} \), at a location is modelled by \( X \sim \mathrm{N}(850, 120^2) \). The middle \( 80\% \) of years (those between the \( 10\text{th} \) and \( 90\text{th} \) percentiles) are classed as typical. (a) Find the two rainfall values that bound a typical year, to the nearest \( \mathrm{mm} \). (b) Over a \( 50 \)-year period, find the expected number of years that are not typical.

The lifetime, in hours, of a certain brand of battery is modelled by a Normal distribution with mean \( \mu \) and standard deviation \( \sigma \). It is known that \( 2.5\% \) of batteries last less than \( 10\,\mathrm{hours} \) and \( 10\% \) last more than \( 20\,\mathrm{hours} \). Find the values of \( \mu \) and \( \sigma \), giving your answers to \( 3 \) significant figures.

The diameter, in \( \mathrm{mm} \), of a machined component is modelled as \( X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^{2}) \). The manufacturer finds that \( P(X>105)=0.20 \) and \( P(X<90)=0.10 \). Find \( \mu \) and \( \sigma \), giving your answers to \( 3 \) significant figures.

A greengrocer models the mass, \( W\,\mathrm{kg} \), of fruit in a randomly chosen bag by \( W\sim N(5,\,3^{2}) \). (a) Calculate \( P(W<0) \). (b) Hence comment on the suitability of the Normal distribution as a model for \( W \), and state one further assumption required for the Normal model to be reasonable here.

An economist proposes modelling the annual salary, \( S \) (in pounds), of employees at a large firm by \( S\sim N(30000,\,12000^{2}) \). (a) Find \( P(S<0) \). (b) Salary data are typically positively skewed with a long upper tail. With reference to your answer to (a) and to skewness, critique the appropriateness of this Normal model.

The probability density function of \( X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^{2}) \) has points of inflection at \( x=42 \) and \( x=58 \). (a) Write down \( \mu \) and \( \sigma \). (b) Hence find \( P(X>62) \), giving your answer to \( 4 \) decimal places.
The mass, \( M\,\mathrm{g} \), of an apple is modelled by \( M\sim N(60,\sigma^{2}) \). Given that \( P(M<70)=0.8413 \), show that \( \sigma=10 \).

The length, \( X\,\mathrm{cm} \), of a manufactured rod is modelled by \( X\sim N(50,\,2^{2}) \). A rod is accepted if its length lies between \( 47\,\mathrm{cm} \) and \( 53\,\mathrm{cm} \), and is rejected otherwise. (a) Find the probability \( p \) that a randomly chosen rod is rejected. (b) A batch of \( 8 \) rods is selected at random. Using a suitable binomial model, find the probability that at least one rod in the batch is rejected. Give answers to \( 4 \) decimal places.

Scores on a standardised test are modelled by \( X\sim N(500,\,100^{2}) \). A score above \( 650 \) is classed as 'distinction'. (a) Find the probability \( p \) that a randomly chosen candidate gains a distinction. (b) In a randomly selected group of \( 12 \) candidates, find the probability that exactly \( 2 \) gain a distinction. Give answers to \( 4 \) decimal places.

A psychologist models the reaction time, \( T \) seconds, of participants by \( T\sim N(0.30,\,0.10^{2}) \). (a) Find \( P(T<0.25) \). (b) Find \( P(T<0) \) and explain why this reveals a weakness of the Normal model here. (c) Reaction-time data are usually positively skewed. State, with a reason, whether this makes the Normal model more or less appropriate. Give probabilities to \( 4 \) decimal places.

The volume, \( X\,\mathrm{ml} \), dispensed by a drinks machine is modelled by \( X\sim N(\mu,\,15^{2}) \). Find the value of \( a \) such that the central interval \( (\mu-a,\ \mu+a) \) contains exactly \( 99\% \) of dispensed volumes. Give \( a \) to \( 3 \) significant figures.

The mass, \( X\,\mathrm{g} \), of a packet of seeds is modelled by \( X\sim N(250,\,20^{2}) \). A packet is labelled 'non-standard' if its mass is below \( 220\,\mathrm{g} \) or above \( 280\,\mathrm{g} \). (a) Find the probability \( p \) that a packet is non-standard. (b) A random sample of \( 6 \) packets is taken. Using a binomial model, find the probability that at most one packet is non-standard. Give answers to \( 4 \) decimal places.

y2nm1.questionText: State, in your own words, what the change of sign method tells you about a continuous function \(f\) on an interval \([a, b]\).
Show that the equation \(x^3 - x - 1 = 0\) has a root in the interval \([1, 2]\).
Show that \(x^3 - 3x + 1 = 0\) has a root in \([0, 1]\).
Show that \(f(x) = e^{x} - 2x - 1\) has a root in the interval \([1, 2]\).
Show that \(\ln x + x - 2 = 0\) has a root in \([1, 2]\).
Show that \(\cos x = x\) has a solution in the interval \([0, 1]\). Work in radians.
Show that \(x^3 = 20\) has a root in the interval \([2, 3]\).
The equation \(2^x = 3x\) has a root in the interval \([3, 4]\). Verify this result using the change of sign method.
The function \(f(x) = x^3 - 5x + 1\) has three real roots. Show that one of them lies in the interval \([-3, -2]\).
Given \(f(x) = x^3 - 5x + 1\), find an interval of width 1 that contains each of the other two real roots.
Use the change of sign method on \(f(x) = x^3 - x - 1\) to show that the root in \([1, 2]\) actually lies in the interval \([1.3, 1.4]\).
The equation \(x^3 - x - 1 = 0\) has a root \(\alpha\) in the interval \((1.32, 1.33)\). Use the change of sign method to show that, to 2 decimal places, \(\alpha = 1.32\).
The equation \(\sin x = 0.5 x\) has a root in \([1, 2]\). Show this and narrow the root to an interval of width 0.1. Work in radians.
The equation \(x^{x} = 100\) has a unique root. Show that it lies in the interval \([3, 4]\).
A student claims that \(f(x) = \tfrac{1}{x - 2}\) has a root in \([1, 3]\) because \(f(1) = -1 < 0\) and \(f(3) = 1 > 0\). Explain why the change of sign method does not apply here.
The function \(f(x) = (x - 1)^{2}(x - 3)\) has \(f(0) = -3\) and \(f(2) = -1\). Explain why this does not mean there are no roots in \([0, 2]\).
Show that the equation \(x^{4} - 3x + 1 = 0\) has at least two real roots in the interval \([0, 2]\).
Show that the equation \(\ln(x + 3) = x\) has a root between \(x = 1\) and \(x = 2\), and use bisection once to narrow this interval.
The equation \(f(x) = x^{3} + x^{2} - 5 = 0\) has a root \(\alpha\) in \([1, 2]\). Using bisection, show that \(\alpha\) lies in \((1.4, 1.5)\).
The equation \(x^{3} - 2x^{2} - 5 = 0\) has a root \(\alpha\). Using the change of sign method, determine \(\alpha\) to 1 decimal place.

A function \(g\) is continuous on \([-1, 4]\) and satisfies \(g(-1) = 2,\ g(1) = -3,\ g(2) = -1,\ g(3) = 2,\ g(4) = 5\). State, with reasons, how many distinct real roots \(g\) is guaranteed to have in \([-1, 4]\).
Show that \(\tan x = 2x\) has a root in \([1, 1.4]\). Work in radians.

A student claims \(\tan x - 2x = 0\) has a root in \([1, 2]\) because \(\tan 1 - 2 \approx -0.443\) and \(\tan 2 - 4 \approx -6.19\)... Reconsider: actually \(\tan 1.5 \approx 14.1\), so the student instead claims the interval \([1.5, 2]\) contains a root. Explain whether the change of sign method applies.
Given \(f(x) = x^{3} - 4x^{2} + x + 6\), show that \(f\) has three real roots and locate each in an interval of width 1.
The equation \(e^{-x} = x\) has a unique real root \(\alpha\). Show that \(\alpha\) lies in \([0.5, 0.6]\) and narrow this to an interval of width 0.01 using bisection.
The equation \(3x^{3} - 10x + 4 = 0\) has a root between \(x = 1\) and \(x = 2\). Use the change of sign method to show that, correct to 1 decimal place, this root is \(1.6\).
Show that the equation \(x^{2}\!\sin x = 1\) has a root in \([1, 2]\) and narrow this root to an interval of width 0.1. Work in radians.

A function \(f\) is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\) with \(f(0) = 2,\ f(1) = -1,\ f(2) = 3\) and \(f(3) = -4\). Alice claims \(f\) must have exactly three distinct real roots in \((0, 3)\). State whether Alice is correct and justify your answer.
The equation \(\ln x = \tfrac{1}{x}\) has a unique root \(\alpha\). Show that \(\alpha\) lies in \([1, 2]\) and find \(\alpha\) to 2 decimal places using the change of sign method.

Let \(f(x) = x^{3} - 2x - k\), where \(k\) is a real constant. Find the set of values of \(k\) for which the change of sign method applied to \([0, 2]\) guarantees that \(f\) has a root in this interval.

y2nm2.questionText: Show that the equation \(x^{3} - x - 1 = 0\) can be rearranged into the form \(x = \sqrt[3]{x + 1}\).
The iteration \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{x_{n} + 1}\) is used with \(x_{0} = 1\). Find \(x_{1},\ x_{2}\) and \(x_{3}\), giving each to 4 decimal places.
Continuing the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{x_{n} + 1}\) from Q2, find \(x_{4}\) to 4 decimal places and state the root of \(x^{3} - x - 1 = 0\) to 2 decimal places.
State the iteration formula obtained by rearranging \(x^{2} - 5 = 0\) into \(x = \tfrac{5}{x}\). Apply the iteration with \(x_{0} = 2\) and compute \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\).
Use the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \cos x_{n}\) with \(x_{0} = 0.5\) (radians). Find \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 4 decimal places.
Continuing Q5, compute \(x_{3},\ x_{4}\) and \(x_{5}\) to 4 decimal places.
Show that the equation \(x^{2} - 3x - 5 = 0\) can be rearranged into \(x = 3 + \tfrac{5}{x}\).
Apply the iteration \(x_{n+1} = 3 + \tfrac{5}{x_{n}}\) with \(x_{0} = 4\). Find \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 4 decimal places.
Verify that \(x = \tfrac{1}{2}(x^{2} + 1)\) is a rearrangement of \(x^{2} - 2x + 1 = 0\).
Rearrange the equation \(x^{3} + 2x - 5 = 0\) into the iterative form \(x = \sqrt[3]{5 - 2x}\).
Apply \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt{x_{n} + 1}\) with \(x_{0} = 1\). Find \(x_{1},\ x_{2}\) and \(x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places.
The iteration \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt{x_{n} + 1}\) converges to a root \(\alpha\). State the equation satisfied by \(\alpha\).
A fixed point of the iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) satisfies which equation? Explain in one line.
Explain why solving \(x = g(x)\) is equivalent to finding a root of \(x - g(x) = 0\).
Show that \(x^{2} - 6 = 0\) can be rearranged as \(x = \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(x + \tfrac{6}{x}\right)\).
Apply the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(x_{n} + \tfrac{6}{x_{n}}\right)\) with \(x_{0} = 2\). Find \(x_{1},\ x_{2}\) and \(x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places and compare with \(\sqrt{6}\).
Apply \(x_{n+1} = \ln(x_{n} + 3)\) with \(x_{0} = 2\). Find \(x_{1},\ x_{2}\) and \(x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places.
Rearrange \(e^{x} - x - 2 = 0\) into \(x = \ln(x + 2)\) and apply the iteration with \(x_{0} = 1\) to find \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 4 decimal places.
Show that \(x^{3} - 5x + 1 = 0\) can be rearranged as (a) \(x = \tfrac{x^{3} + 1}{5}\) and (b) \(x = \sqrt[3]{5x - 1}\).
Apply \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{x_{n}^{3} + 1}{5}\) with \(x_{0} = 0\). Find \(x_{1},\ x_{2},\ x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places and state what they appear to converge to.
Apply the second rearrangement \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{5x_{n} - 1}\) with \(x_{0} = 2\). Compute \(x_{1},\ x_{2},\ x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places.
The cubic \(x^{3} - 5x + 1 = 0\) has three real roots. Use the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{5x_{n} - 1}\) with \(x_{0} = -2\) to find, to 2 decimal places, the negative root.
The iteration \(x_{n+1} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{x_{n}}\) has a fixed point \(\alpha\). Show that \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\alpha^{2} - \alpha - 1 = 0\) and state the positive value of \(\alpha\) in exact form.
Apply \(x_{n+1} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{x_{n}}\) with \(x_{0} = 1\) and find \(x_{1},\ x_{2},\ x_{3},\ x_{4}\) to 4 decimal places.
Let \(f(x) = x^{3} - 2x - 5\). Show that the rearrangement \(x = \sqrt[3]{2x + 5}\) is equivalent to \(f(x) = 0\), and use iteration with \(x_{0} = 2\) to find the root to 2 decimal places.
Show that \(2x - \cos x = 0\) can be rearranged as \(x = \tfrac{1}{2}\cos x\). Use iteration with \(x_{0} = 0.5\) to find \(x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places.
Verify that \(\tan x - x = 0\) can be rearranged as \(x = \arctan(x + n\pi)\) for integer \(n\), but that \(x_{n+1} = \tan x_{n}\) does not converge near the nonzero roots. Explain briefly.
For the iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\), state the condition on \(g'(\alpha)\) that guarantees convergence near the fixed point \(\alpha\).
For the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{x_{n} + 1}\), show that near the fixed point \(\alpha \approx 1.3247\) the convergence condition \(|g'(\alpha)| < 1\) is satisfied.
For the iteration \(x_{n+1} = x_{n}^{3} - 1\), show that the fixed points are roots of \(x^{3} - x - 1 = 0\) but that iteration from a nearby start diverges.
Apply \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}(x_{n} + \tfrac{20}{x_{n}})\) with \(x_{0} = 4\). Find \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 4 decimal places, and state what \(x_{n}\) is approximating.
Using \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{x_{n} + 1}\) with \(x_{0} = 1\), find the root \(\alpha\) of \(x^{3} - x - 1 = 0\) correct to 3 decimal places. State how many iterations are required.

An iteration converges linearly when \(|x_{n+1} - \alpha| \approx k|x_{n} - \alpha|\) for some constant \(k\) with \(|k| < 1\). State the value of \(k\) for the iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) near a fixed point \(\alpha\).
Given \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{4}(x_{n}^{2} + 3)\), show that the fixed points are \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\), and determine which fixed point is attractive.
A root of \(\sin x = x - 1\) lies near \(x = 2\). Write this as \(x = \sin x + 1\) and apply three iterations with \(x_{0} = 2\) to 4 decimal places. Work in radians.
Starting from \(x_{0} = 1\), apply the iteration \(x_{n+1} = 3 - \tfrac{1}{x_{n}^{2}}\) until two successive values agree to 3 decimal places. Give the final value.
Show that \(x^{3} - 3x + 1 = 0\) can be rearranged as \(x = \tfrac{x^{3} + 1}{3}\). Apply this iteration with \(x_{0} = 0\) and find the root it converges to, to 3 decimal places.
Given \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{2 + x_{n}^{2}}{2x_{n}}\) with \(x_{0} = 1\), show that \(x_{n}\) converges to \(\sqrt{2}\) and compute \(x_{3}\) to 6 decimal places.

Use the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{3}{x_{n} + 1}\) with \(x_{0} = 1\). Compute \(x_{1},\ x_{2},\ x_{3}\) and \(x_{4}\) to 4 decimal places, and find the equation whose root the iteration converges to.
Describe, in one sentence, the difference between a staircase diagram and a cobweb diagram for an iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\).
The iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(1 + \tfrac{3}{x_{n}}\right)\) is applied to solve \(2x^{2} - x - 3 = 0\). Verify that a fixed point satisfies \(2x^{2} - x - 3 = 0\).
An iteration is given by \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{x_{n} + 2}{x_{n}^{2}}\) with \(x_{0} = 2\). Compute \(x_{1},\ x_{2},\ x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places.
Given \(f(x) = x^{2} - 7\), derive the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(x_{n} + \tfrac{7}{x_{n}}\right)\) and use it to estimate \(\sqrt{7}\) to 4 decimal places starting from \(x_{0} = 3\).
Apply the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + x_{n}}\) with \(x_{0} = 0\). Compute \(x_{1}\) to \(x_{5}\) to 4 decimal places and state the limit.
For the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}(x_{n} + a/x_{n})\) (the Babylonian method for \(\sqrt{a}\)), show that \(g'(\sqrt{a}) = 0\) and explain why this gives faster than linear convergence.
Show that \(x = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{x + 1}}\) is equivalent to \(x^{2}(x + 1) = 1\) and apply this iteration with \(x_{0} = 1\). Compute \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 4 decimal places.

For the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{x_{n} + 1}}\) with fixed point \(\alpha\) satisfying \(\alpha^{2}(\alpha + 1) = 1\) (so \(\alpha \approx 0.7549\)), find \(g'(\alpha)\) to 3 decimal places and state whether the iteration converges.
The iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{4x_{n} - 1}{x_{n}^{2}}\) has a fixed point \(\alpha > 0\). Find the equation satisfied by \(\alpha\).
Starting from \(x_{0} = 2\), use \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{4x_{n} - 1}{x_{n}^{2}}\) to find a root of \(x^{3} - 4x + 1 = 0\) to 3 decimal places.
Use the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[5]{3x_{n} + 2}\) with \(x_{0} = 1\) and find \(x_{1},\ x_{2},\ x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places.
Use \(x_{n+1} = \ln(5x_{n})\) with \(x_{0} = 2\) and compute \(x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places.

Two students wish to solve \(x^{3} + x - 3 = 0\). One uses \(x_{n+1} = 3 - x_{n}^{3}\); the other uses \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{3 - x_{n}}\). Explain, using the condition on \(g'\), which is more likely to converge near the root \(\alpha \approx 1.21\).
The iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) with \(g(x) = \tfrac{2x + 3}{x^{2}}\) has a fixed point \(\alpha > 0\). Find the polynomial equation satisfied by \(\alpha\).
Starting from \(x_{0} = 2\), apply \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{2x_{n} + 3}{x_{n}^{2}}\) three times. Compute \(x_{1},\ x_{2},\ x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places.

The iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{a}{x_{n} + b}\) has a fixed point \(\alpha\). Show that \(\alpha = \tfrac{-b + \sqrt{b^{2} + 4a}}{2}\) (positive root), and find the condition on \(a,\ b\) such that \(|g'(\alpha)| < 1\).

A sequence defined by \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{3}(x_{n}^{2} + 2)\) converges to \(\alpha = 1\) if started close enough. Find the interval of starting values \(x_{0}\) for which \(|g'(x_{0})| < 1\) near \(\alpha = 1\).
Apply the iteration \(x_{n+1} = (x_{n} + \tfrac{5}{x_{n}^{2}})/2\) with \(x_{0} = 1\). Compute \(x_{1},\ x_{2},\ x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places and state which root the iteration approximates.

Given the iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) and a fixed point \(\alpha\), show that if \(g\) is differentiable and \(g'(\alpha) = 0\) then \(|x_{n+1} - \alpha| \leq C|x_{n} - \alpha|^{2}\) for some constant \(C\) and for \(x_{n}\) close to \(\alpha\).
Consider \(f(x) = x^{3} - 2x - 2\). Use any convergent iterative formula, starting from a suitable \(x_{0}\), to find the real root to 3 decimal places.
For the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \cos x_{n}\), show that there is exactly one fixed point in \([0, 1]\) and that convergence from \(x_{0} = 0\) is guaranteed.
A root of \(e^{-x} = x\) lies near \(x = 0.57\). Use iteration \(x_{n+1} = e^{-x_{n}}\) with \(x_{0} = 0.5\) and compute \(x_{1}\) to \(x_{5}\) to 5 decimal places.

Show that the iteration \(x_{n+1} = x_{n} - \tfrac{f(x_{n})}{f'(x_{n})}\) (Newton–Raphson) is a fixed-point iteration with \(g(x) = x - f(x)/f'(x)\), and verify that \(g'(\alpha) = 0\) for a simple root \(\alpha\) of \(f\).
A sequence satisfies \(x_{n+1} = x_{n}^{2} - 0.5\). Find the two fixed points and classify each as attracting or repelling.

Consider \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt{5 - x_{n}}\). Show that the fixed point \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\alpha^{2} + \alpha - 5 = 0\) and find the value of \(\alpha > 0\) correct to 3 decimal places using iteration with \(x_{0} = 2\).
The equation \(x^{3} + x - 1 = 0\) has a single real root \(\alpha\). Rearrange as \(x = \tfrac{1}{x^{2} + 1}\) and, starting from \(x_{0} = 0.5\), compute \(x_{5}\) to 5 decimal places.
Suggest a rearrangement of \(x^{3} + x - 1 = 0\) that gives more rapid convergence than \(x = \tfrac{1}{x^{2} + 1}\), and justify your answer using \(g'(\alpha)\).

Let \(g(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}(x + \tfrac{c}{x})\) for \(c > 0\). Show that the sequence \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) has error \(\epsilon_{n+1} = x_{n+1} - \sqrt{c}\) satisfying \(\epsilon_{n+1} = \tfrac{\epsilon_{n}^{2}}{2x_{n}}\), and interpret this as quadratic convergence.
The iteration \(x_{n+1} = 1.5 x_{n}(1 - x_{n})\) (a logistic map with parameter 1.5) has fixed points 0 and \(\tfrac{1}{3}\). Determine which of these is attracting.

A calculator repeats the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \cos x_{n}\) (radians) starting from any value \(x_{0}\). Show that for any starting value in \(\mathbb{R}\) the sequence converges to the same limit, and give this limit to 4 decimal places.
Use the iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) of your choice to find, to 4 decimal places, the positive real root of \(e^{x} + 3x - 4 = 0\). Justify that your chosen rearrangement converges.

y2nm3.questionText: Describe, in your own words, what a staircase diagram represents for the iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\).
State the difference between a staircase diagram and a cobweb diagram.
State the condition on \(g'(\alpha)\) for the iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) to converge to the fixed point \(\alpha\).
Where on a sketch does the fixed point \(\alpha\) of \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) appear?
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{x_{n} + 3}{4}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\), and state the fixed point.
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = 0.6 x_{n} + 1\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\).
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = 0.8 x_{n} + 1\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\).
Sketch the cobweb diagram for \(x_{n+1} = -\tfrac{1}{2} x_{n} + 1\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\).
Sketch the cobweb diagram for \(x_{n+1} = 2 - \tfrac{1}{2} x_{n}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\).
Describe the behaviour of the iteration \(x_{n+1} = 1.5 x_{n} - 0.5\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1.1\).
Describe the behaviour of the iteration \(x_{n+1} = -2 x_{n} + 3\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1.1\).
If \(g'(\alpha) = 0\), describe the shape of the staircase diagram near the fixed point.
On a staircase diagram, from which element of the diagram do you read the value of \(x_{1}\)?
State the slope of the line \(y = x\) and explain why it always appears on a staircase diagram.
A diagram shows \(y = g(x)\) crossing \(y = x\) at \(\alpha\) with slope approximately 0.2. Classify the iteration's behaviour.
A diagram shows \(y = g(x)\) crossing \(y = x\) at \(\alpha\) with slope approximately \(-0.3\). Classify the iteration's behaviour.
A diagram shows \(y = g(x)\) crossing \(y = x\) at \(\alpha\) with slope approximately 1.4. Classify the iteration's behaviour.
A diagram shows \(y = g(x)\) crossing \(y = x\) at \(\alpha\) with slope approximately \(-1.5\). Classify the iteration's behaviour.
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt{x_{n} + 2}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\). State the fixed point.
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{x_{n} + 1}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1\).
Sketch the cobweb diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \cos x_{n}\) (radians) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\).
Sketch the cobweb diagram for \(x_{n+1} = e^{-x_{n}}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\).
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \ln(x_{n} + 2)\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\).
Sketch the cobweb diagram for \(x_{n+1} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{x_{n}}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1\). State the fixed point.
Sketch the staircase diagram for the Babylonian iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}(x_{n} + \tfrac{5}{x_{n}})\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1\).
Sketch the cobweb diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\cos x_{n}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\). Work in radians.
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt{3 x_{n} - 2}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1.5\) and show convergence to \(\alpha = 2\).
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = 3 - \tfrac{2}{x_{n}}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 2\).
For the iteration in Q28, show that starting from \(x_{0} = 1.2\) iteration diverges away from \(\alpha = 1\) and lands on the other fixed point.
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{2 x_{n} + 5}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 2\).
Sketch the diagram for \(x_{n+1} = -x_{n}^{3} + 3\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1.2\). Does the iteration converge near the fixed point \(\alpha \approx 1.2134\)?
Sketch the cobweb diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{x_{n} + 1}}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1\).
The iteration \(x_{n+1} = 1 - x_{n}\) starts from \(x_{0} = 0.2\). Sketch the diagram and describe the behaviour.
Describe the behaviour of \(x_{n+1} = x_{n}^{2}\) from \(x_{0} = 0.5\). Include the fixed points.
Describe the behaviour of \(x_{n+1} = x_{n}^{2}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1.1\).
Identify the two fixed points of \(x_{n+1} = x_{n}^{2} - 0.5\) and state which is attracting.
Sketch the diagram for the iteration in Q36 starting from \(x_{0} = -0.2\) and confirm convergence to the stable fixed point.
Describe the behaviour of \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{5}{x_{n}}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 2\).

The diagram below shows \(y = g(x)\) and \(y = x\) with a fixed point at \(\alpha \approx 1\). The tangent to \(g\) at \(\alpha\) has gradient roughly \(0.7\). Starting from \(x_{0} = 0.3\), describe the iteration's behaviour. Include a sketch.
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{3}(x_{n}^{2} + 1)\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\).
For the iteration in Q40, explain what would happen if we started from \(x_{0} = 3\).
Sketch the cobweb diagram for the logistic iteration \(x_{n+1} = 2x_{n}(1 - x_{n})\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0.1\).
Describe the behaviour of the iteration \(x_{n+1} = 3.2 x_{n}(1 - x_{n})\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0.2\).
Sketch the diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(x_{n} + \tfrac{3}{x_{n}}\right)\) starting from \(x_{0} = 3\). Explain why convergence is so rapid.
For the iteration \(x_{n+1} = 0.4 x_{n} + 3\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\), state the fixed point and sketch the staircase.
Sketch \(y = \sin x\) and \(y = x\) together and explain why the only fixed point of \(x_{n+1} = \sin x_{n}\) is \(x = 0\), and show that it is a borderline case.
Sketch the staircase diagram for \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{4}(x_{n}^{2} + 3)\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0.5\).
Use the sketched iteration in Q47 to estimate, to 1 decimal place, the value of \(x_{3}\) when \(x_{0} = 0.5\).
Sketch and describe the behaviour of \(x_{n+1} = 3\sqrt{x_{n}} - 2\) starting from \(x_{0} = 2\).
Give an example of an iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) whose diagram is a diverging staircase. State the fixed point and the slope of \(g\) there.
Give an example of an iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) whose diagram is a diverging cobweb.
Sketch the cobweb for \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{x_{n} + 1}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0.5\).
On a single sketch, show \(y = x^{3}\) and \(y = x\). State the fixed points and use the slope of \(g\) at each to classify the behaviour of \(x_{n+1} = x_{n}^{3}\).
Sketch the diagram for \(x_{n+1} = x_{n}^{3}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0.9\) and describe what happens.
Sketch the diagram for \(x_{n+1} = x_{n}^{3}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1.1\). Describe the behaviour.

A diagram shows \(y = g(x)\) cutting \(y = x\) at two points \(\alpha_{1} < \alpha_{2}\). The slope of \(g\) at \(\alpha_{1}\) is \(0.5\), and at \(\alpha_{2}\) is \(1.8\). Describe the behaviour of the iteration starting from a point just below \(\alpha_{1}\), between \(\alpha_{1}\) and \(\alpha_{2}\), and just above \(\alpha_{2}\).
For the iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) with \(g(x) = 1 + \tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\), sketch the cobweb starting from \(x_{0} = 1\). State the equation satisfied by the fixed point.
On axes, sketch both \(y = g(x) = 1 - x^{2}\) and \(y = x\). Identify the fixed points and classify each.
Given the iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{x_{n}^{2} + a}{b x_{n}}\) for positive constants \(a,\ b\), find the fixed points and the condition on \(g'(\alpha)\) for convergence.
Sketch the staircase for \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}(x_{n} + \tfrac{10}{x_{n}})\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1\). Compute \(x_{1},\ x_{2}\) to 4 decimal places.

A diagram shows the iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) being used to solve \(f(x) = 0\). Explain why the points \((x_{n}, x_{n+1})\) all lie on the curve \(y = g(x)\) but the horizontal transfer to \(y = x\) is what converts \(x_{n+1}\) into the next input.
Sketch the diagram for \(x_{n+1} = 4x_{n}(1 - x_{n})\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0.2\). Comment on the behaviour.
Sketch the staircase for \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}(x_{n} + 1)^{1/2}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0.5\). State the fixed-point equation.
Sketch the cobweb for \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{3}{x_{n} + 2}\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0\) and state the fixed-point equation.
Draw sketches showing each of: (a) a converging staircase, (b) a converging cobweb, (c) a diverging staircase, (d) a diverging cobweb. Label the slope of \(g\) at the fixed point in each case.
A company models its monthly sales by \(S_{n+1} = 0.7 S_{n} + 30\) (thousand pounds). Sketch the staircase diagram from \(S_{0} = 0\) and state the long-run equilibrium.
The iteration \(x_{n+1} = \tfrac{x_{n}}{2} + \tfrac{1}{x_{n}}\) has fixed point \(\alpha = \sqrt{2}\). Verify using the slope that convergence is fast, and sketch the staircase from \(x_{0} = 1\).

An iteration \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) has the sketch of \(y = g(x)\) shown as a curve steeper than \(y = x\) at the fixed point. If we change to the rearrangement \(y = g^{-1}(x)\), explain what happens to the slope and whether this new iteration might converge.
Sketch the staircase diagram for the Newton–Raphson iteration applied to \(f(x) = x^{2} - 5\), starting from \(x_{0} = 3\). What is the slope of \(g\) at the fixed point?

Two iterations for solving \(x^{3} - x - 1 = 0\) are proposed: (i) \(x_{n+1} = x_{n}^{3} - 1\), (ii) \(x_{n+1} = \sqrt[3]{x_{n} + 1}\). Sketch the diagram near the fixed point \(\alpha \approx 1.325\) for each and state which iteration converges.

y2nm4.questionText: State the Newton-Raphson iterative formula for finding a root of \(f(x) = 0\).
Explain geometrically how each Newton-Raphson step obtains \(x_{n+1}\) from \(x_{n}\).
Apply one step of Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = x^{2} - 2\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1.5\). Give \(x_{1}\) to 4 decimal places.
Continuing Q3, compute \(x_{2}\) and \(x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places. Compare with \(\sqrt{2}\).
Apply one step of Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = x^{3} - 7\) starting from \(x_{0} = 2\). Give \(x_{1}\) to 4 decimal places.
Continuing Q5, compute \(x_{2}\) and \(x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places.
Show that the Newton-Raphson iteration for \(f(x) = x^{2} - k\) simplifies to \(x_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}\!\left(x_{n} + \frac{k}{x_{n}}\right)\).
Use Newton-Raphson on \(f(x) = x^{2} - 11\) with \(x_{0} = 3\) to estimate \(\sqrt{11}\) to 4 decimal places.
The equation \(x^{3} - x - 1 = 0\) has a root near \(x = 1.3\). Apply one Newton-Raphson step from \(x_{0} = 1.3\) to find \(x_{1}\) to 4 decimal places.
Continuing Q9, compute \(x_{2}\) to 4 decimal places and state the root to 3 decimal places.
Write the Newton-Raphson iteration for \(f(x) = x^{3} - 5\) and apply it once from \(x_{0} = 2\).
Show that the Newton-Raphson iteration for \(f(x) = x^{n} - k\) is \(x_{n+1} = \frac{(n-1)x_{n}^{n} + k}{n \cdot x_{n}^{n-1}}\).
Use Newton-Raphson on \(f(x) = x^{2} - 3x - 2\) with \(x_{0} = 4\). Compute \(x_{1}\) to 4 decimal places.
Continuing Q13, compute \(x_{2}\) and \(x_{3}\) to 4 decimal places and state the positive root of \(x^{2} - 3x - 2 = 0\) to 3 decimal places.
The Newton-Raphson method can fail if \(f'(x_{n}) = 0\). Explain why.
For \(f(x) = x^{2} - 4\) with \(x_{0} = 0\), explain what goes wrong.
Explain why starting Newton-Raphson for \(f(x) = x^{3} - 3x + 1\) at a turning point (\(x = 1\) or \(x = -1\)) fails.
Explain why Newton-Raphson may overshoot and diverge if \(x_{0}\) is far from the root.
Apply Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = \cos x - x\) with \(x_{0} = 0.5\) (radians). Find \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 5 decimal places.
Apply Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = e^{x} - 3x\) with \(x_{0} = 1\). Find \(x_{1}\) to 4 decimal places.
Based on Q20, suggest a better starting value and compute \(x_{1}\) to 4 decimal places. (There is a root between 0 and 1.)
Use Newton-Raphson on \(f(x) = x - \cos x\) from \(x_{0} = 0.7\) (radians). Find \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 5 decimal places.
Use Newton-Raphson on \(f(x) = \ln x - 1\) with \(x_{0} = 2\). Find \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 4 decimal places. (The root is \(e\).)
The equation \(x e^{x} = 1\) has a root near \(x = 0.5\). Apply Newton-Raphson once to find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
Use Newton-Raphson on \(f(x) = x^{3} - 2x - 5\) with \(x_{0} = 2\). Find \(x_{1},\ x_{2}\) and \(x_{3}\) to 5 decimal places.
Apply Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = \sin x - \frac{x}{2}\) with \(x_{0} = 2\) (radians). Give \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
Explain why \(x_{n+1} = g(x_{n})\) with \(g(x) = x - f(x)/f'(x)\) satisfies \(g'(\alpha) = 0\) at any simple root \(\alpha\) of \(f\).
State what is meant by quadratic convergence.
The Newton-Raphson iteration for \(f(x) = x^{4} - 3\) is \(x_{n+1} = \frac{3 x_{n}^{4} + 3}{4 x_{n}^{3}}\). Apply it with \(x_{0} = 1.5\). Compute \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
Continuing Q29, compute \(x_{2}\) to 5 decimal places. Compare with \(\sqrt[4]{3}\).
Use Newton-Raphson on \(f(x) = \tan x - 1\) with \(x_{0} = 0.8\) (radians). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
Apply Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = x^{2} - 2\sin x - 1\) with \(x_{0} = 2\) (radians). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
Apply Newton-Raphson to the equation \(x^{5} - x - 1 = 0\) from \(x_{0} = 1\). Compute \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 5 decimal places.
Use Newton-Raphson to find the positive root of \(f(x) = 2^{x} - 3x\). Use \(x_{0} = 1\) and compute \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
Apply Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = x \ln x - 1\) starting from \(x_{0} = 2\). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
For \(f(x) = x^{3} - 3x + 1\), apply Newton-Raphson with \(x_{0} = 2\). Compute \(x_{1},\ x_{2}\) and state the root to 4 decimal places.
For \(f(x) = x^{3} - 3x + 1\), start Newton-Raphson at \(x_{0} = 1\). Explain what happens and why.
Use Newton-Raphson on \(f(x) = \cos x\) with \(x_{0} = 1.5\) (radians). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places. State the exact root.
Show that applying Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = 1/x - a\) gives \(x_{n+1} = x_{n}(2 - a x_{n})\).
Use the iteration in Q39 with \(a = 3\) and \(x_{0} = 0.3\) to approximate \(1/3\). Compute \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 5 decimal places.
Apply Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = x \sin x - 1\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1\) (radians). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
A Newton-Raphson sketch shows the tangent at \((x_{n}, f(x_{n}))\) meeting the x-axis at \(x_{n+1}\). Given \(f(x_{n}) = 2\) and \(f'(x_{n}) = 5\), calculate \(x_{n+1} - x_{n}\).
Starting from \(x_{0} = 0\), apply Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = x^{3} + 2x - 1\). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
Continuing Q43, compute \(x_{2}\) and \(x_{3}\) to 5 decimal places.
Use Newton-Raphson to solve \(x = \ln(3 - x)\) from \(x_{0} = 1\). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places. (Rewrite as \(f(x) = x - \ln(3 - x)\).)
Apply Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = x^{4} + x - 3\) starting from \(x_{0} = 1\). Compute \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 5 decimal places.
For \(f(x) = x^{2} - 5x + 6\), apply Newton-Raphson starting from \(x_{0} = 2.5\). Find \(x_{1}\) and explain what happens.
Starting from \(x_{0} = 2\) for \(f(x) = x^{3} - x^{2} - 1\), compute \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 5 decimal places. State the root to 4 d.p.
For \(f(x) = \sqrt{x} - 2\), apply Newton-Raphson with \(x_{0} = 3\). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
A root of \(f(x) = x + \tan x\) lies between 2 and 2.1 (radians). Apply Newton-Raphson from \(x_{0} = 2\). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
For \(f(x) = x^{3}\), apply Newton-Raphson from \(x_{0} = 1\). Compute \(x_{1}\) and explain why convergence to the root \(\alpha = 0\) is only linear.
Prove that if \(\alpha\) is a double root of \(f\), then Newton-Raphson converges linearly with factor \(\frac{1}{2}\).
For \(f(x) = \arctan x\), applying Newton-Raphson from a sufficiently large \(x_{0}\) can produce divergent oscillations. Explain why intuitively.
Use Newton-Raphson to find the real root of \(f(x) = e^{x} - 4x\) to 4 decimal places, choosing a sensible \(x_{0}\).
Use Newton-Raphson to find \(\ln 2\) by solving \(e^{x} - 2 = 0\) starting from \(x_{0} = 0.5\). Give \(x_{3}\) to 6 decimal places.
Given that \(\alpha\) is a root of \(f(x) = x - \cos x\), show that Newton-Raphson from \(x_{0} = 1\) produces errors that roughly square each step.

The polynomial \(f(x) = x^{3} - 5x^{2} + 7x - 3\) has a repeated root at \(x = 1\) and a simple root at \(x = 3\). Apply Newton-Raphson from \(x_{0} = 2\). Compute \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 5 decimal places and comment.
Describe a practical strategy to choose a good starting value \(x_{0}\) for Newton-Raphson on a given equation \(f(x) = 0\).
Use Newton-Raphson on \(f(x) = \sin x - \frac{x}{3}\) from \(x_{0} = 2.5\) (radians). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.

Show that the Newton-Raphson iteration for \(f(x) = x^{3} - a\) is \(x_{n+1} = \frac{2 x_{n}^{3} + a}{3 x_{n}^{2}}\), and apply it with \(a = 20,\ x_{0} = 3\) to find \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) to 5 decimal places.
An engineer solves \(x^{2} + 3x - 7 = 0\) using Newton-Raphson from \(x_{0} = 2\). Compute the positive root to 4 decimal places.
Use Newton-Raphson on the equation \(x^{4} = 10x - 5\) from \(x_{0} = 1\). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
Continuing Q62, compute \(x_{2}\) and comment on the iteration's behaviour.
The equation \(x = \tan x\) has a root near \(x = 4.49\) (radians). Apply Newton-Raphson from \(x_{0} = 4.5\). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
Use Newton-Raphson on \(f(x) = x^{3} - 4x - 9\) from \(x_{0} = 3\). Find the root to 4 decimal places.
Consider the iteration applied to \(f(x) = (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3)\). Starting from \(x_{0} = 1.5\), compute \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places and discuss which root the iteration ultimately finds.
Apply Newton-Raphson to \(f(x) = x^{2} - \sqrt{x} - 2\) starting from \(x_{0} = 2\). Find \(x_{1}\) to 5 decimal places.
Prove that, if Newton-Raphson converges, then the limit \(\alpha\) satisfies \(f(\alpha) = 0\).
Use Newton-Raphson to find the real root of \(f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1\) to 5 decimal places, starting from \(x_{0} = 0.5\).

Newton-Raphson is used to find a root of \(f(x) = x^{3} - 2x + c\) for a parameter \(c\). Starting from \(x_{0} = 0\), show that \(x_{1} = c/2\), and discuss what happens to the iteration for \(c = 0.5\) and \(c = 2\).

y2nm5.questionText: State the trapezium rule for estimating \(\int_{a}^{b} y\,dx\) using \(n\) strips of equal width.
Explain what is meant by a "strip" and an "ordinate" in the trapezium rule.
A trapezium-rule calculation uses 4 strips on \([1, 5]\). State the strip width \(h\) and list the \(x\)-values of the ordinates.
Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{4} x^{2}\,dx\).
Compare the estimate from Q4 with the exact value of \(\int_{0}^{4} x^{2}\,dx\), and state the percentage error.
Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate \(\int_{1}^{5} \sqrt{x}\,dx\). Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
Use the trapezium rule with 2 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{2} \tfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\,dx\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{2} \tfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\,dx\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
Using the estimates from Q7 and Q8, compare them with the exact value \(\arctan 2 \approx 1.1071\).
Use the trapezium rule with 5 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{1} e^{x}\,dx\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
Using Q10, compare the estimate with the exact value \(e - 1 \approx 1.71828\) and compute the absolute error.
Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x\,dx\). Work in radians and give your answer to 4 decimal places.
Compare the estimate from Q12 with the exact value \(\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x\,dx = 2\).
State what is meant by an over-estimate and an under-estimate of \(\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx\) by the trapezium rule, and relate these to the concavity of \(f\).
Using concavity, state whether the trapezium rule over- or under-estimates \(\int_{0}^{1} e^{x}\,dx\).
Using concavity, state whether the trapezium rule over- or under-estimates \(\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x\,dx\).
Use the trapezium rule with 3 strips to estimate \(\int_{1}^{4} \ln x\,dx\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
The trapezium rule is applied to \(\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{1 + x^{3}}\,dx\) using 2 strips. Find the estimate to 4 decimal places.
Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{2} 2^{x}\,dx\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
Continuing Q19, compare with the exact value \(\int_{0}^{2} 2^{x}\,dx = \tfrac{3}{\ln 2}\).
Use the trapezium rule with 5 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{1} \tfrac{1}{1 + x}\,dx\). Give your answer to 5 decimal places.
The integral \(\int_{0}^{1} \tfrac{1}{1 + x}\,dx = \ln 2 \approx 0.69315\). Using Q21, comment on the accuracy.
Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{2} x e^{-x}\,dx\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
Use the trapezium rule with 3 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{3} \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x}}\,dx\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
A student writes \(T = \tfrac{h}{2}(y_{0} + y_{1} + y_{2} + \cdots + y_{n})\) for the trapezium rule. Identify the error and correct it.
Use the trapezium rule with 6 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{6} \tfrac{1}{x + 1}\,dx\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{2} (x^{3} - 2x + 3)\,dx\). Give your answer exactly.
Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{2} \cos(x^{2})\,dx\). Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
Use the trapezium rule with 8 strips to estimate \(\int_{0}^{2} \tfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\,dx\). Give your answer to 5 decimal places.
Doubling the number of strips in the trapezium rule typically improves the absolute error by what factor?
A table gives \(f(x)\) at \(x = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2\) with values \(3, 4, 6, 9, 13\). Use the trapezium rule to estimate \(\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\,dx\).

Find the self-intersection point of the curve \(x = 2 - t^2,\ y = t^3 - 3t\).
Describe the curve \(x = t\cos t,\ y = t\sin t\).

y2pe4.questionText: The curve \(x = t^2,\ y = 2t\) meets the line \(y = x\). Find the point(s) of intersection.
Find where the curve \(x = t^2 - 4,\ y = t^2 - 9\) crosses the \(x\)-axis.
Find where the curve \(x = t^2 - 4,\ y = t + 1\) crosses the \(y\)-axis.
Find where the curve \(x = t,\ y = 2t + 3\) meets the line \(y = 7\).
Find where the curve \(x = 2t + 1,\ y = t^2\) meets the line \(y = 4\).
Find where the curve \(x = t^2,\ y = 2t\) meets the line \(x = 9\).
Find where the curve \(x = 3t,\ y = t + 1\) meets the line \(y = 3\).
Find the points where the curve \(x = t^2,\ y = 2t\) meets the line \(y = x - 3\).
Find where the curve \(x = t,\ y = 2t^2\) meets the line \(y = x\).
Find the points where the curve \(x = t,\ y = t^2\) meets the line \(y = x + 4\).
Find where the circle \(x = \cos t,\ y = \sin t\) meets the line \(y = x\).

Find where the line \(x = 2t,\ y = t\) meets the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 6\).
Show that the curve \(x = \cos t,\ y = \sin t\) is the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\).

Find where the curve \(x = t + 2,\ y = t^2\) meets the line \(y = 2x - 3\).

Find the self-intersection point of the curve \(x = t^2 - 1,\ y = t^3 - t\).
Find the self-intersection point of the curve \(x = t^2 - 1,\ y = t^3 - t + 1\).
Find the self-intersection point of the curve \(x = \sin 2t,\ y = \sin t\) on \(t \in [0, 2\pi]\).
Find where the curve \(x = 3t,\ y = t^2 - 1\) meets the line \(y = \tfrac{1}{3}(x + 3)\).
Find where the curve \(x = t^2,\ y = 2t\) meets the line \(y = 3x - 5\).
Find where the curve \(x = t + 2,\ y = t - 1\) meets the line \(y = -x\).
Find where the curve \(x = t + 2,\ y = t^2 + 1\) meets the line \(y = 5\).

Show that the curves \(x = t^2,\ y = t\) and \(x = 2s + 1,\ y = s + 1\) touch, and find the point of contact.
The curves \(x = \cos t,\ y = \sin t\) and \(x = \sin s,\ y = \cos s\) are given. Find their points of intersection.
Find where the curve \(x = t + 1,\ y = t^3\) meets the parabola \(y = (x - 1)^2\).
Find where the curve \(x = t,\ y = t^2 - \tfrac{1}{4}\) meets the line \(y = x\), and state whether the line is tangent to the curve.
